paragraphs.text: II.A. Human Factors
Introduction
How
Hypoxia 												AI.II.A.K1a
Hypoxia: “Reduced oxygen” or “not enough oxygen” – 4 Types: Hypoxic, Hypemic, Stagnant, Histotoxic
Hypoxic Hypoxia
A result of insufficient oxygen available to the lungs - e.g. blocked airway or drowning
Pilots: The reduction in partial pressure of oxygen at high altitude is a common example
Hypemic Hypoxia
The blood is not able to take up and transport sufficient oxygen to the cells in the body
Causes: Not enough blood volume, Blood diseases, Hemoglobin (the molecule that transports oxygen) is unable to bind oxygen molecules, Carbon monoxide poisoning
Stagnant Hypoxia
The blood isn’t moving to the tissues - ex. when your arm “falls asleep”
Results from G-forces, shock, the heart failing to pump effectively, a constricted artery
Histotoxic Hypoxia
“Histo” refers to tissues or cells, and “Toxic” means poison
Oxygen is being transported to the cells, but they are unable to use it
Causes: Alcohol and other drugs, such as narcotics and poison
Symptoms of Hypoxia
Cyanosis (blue fingernails and lips)
Headache
Delayed reactions
Impaired judgment
Euphoria
Visual Impairment
Drowsiness
Lightheaded or dizzy sensation
Tingling in fingers or toes
Numbness
Useful Consciousness (See table)
Max time to make and carry out rational decisions without supplemental oxygen
Treatment
Lower altitude and supplemental oxygen
FAA Physiology Training
One day course in OK with altitude chamber & vertigo demonstrations
Hyperventilation 										AI.II.A.K1b
Occurs when experiencing emotional stress, fright, or pain, and the breathing rate and depth increase – caused by an excessive loss of carbon dioxide from the body, which can lead to unconsciousness
Symptoms (very similar to hypoxia):
Visual Impairment
Lightheaded or dizzy sensation
Tingling sensations
Hot and cold sensations
Muscle spasms
Unconsciousness
Treatment
Breathing normally is both the best prevention and the best cure for hyperventilation
Breath into a paper bag or talking aloud
If unsure, treat for hypoxia (the more dangerous situation)
Middle Ear & Sinus Problems 								AI.II.A.K1c
Middle Ear Problems
Explanation
Difference in the pressure of the air outside the body and inside the middle ear/nasal sinuses
Symptoms
Pain is the primary indicator
Temporary reduction in hearing sensitivity
Relation to flying
During a climb, the difference in pressure causes the eardrum to bulge outward
During a descent, the difference in pressure causes the eardrum to bulge inward
Excessive pressure in either situation can result in pain and a ruptured ear drum
Treatment
Chew gum, stretch the jaw
Valsalva
Medicines, nasal sprays, if approved for flight
Sinus Problems
Explanation
Congestion prevents pressure in the sinuses equalizing with the pressure in the flight deck
Symptoms
Sinus pain/Upper teeth ache
Bloody mucus from the nasal passages
Treatment
Slower descent rates can reduce the pain
Do not fly with sinus problems
Spatial Disorientation 									AI.II.A.K1d
Lack of orientation of the position/attitude/movement of the plane in space
Orientation – The body uses 3 systems to orient itself:
Visual: The eye, by far the largest source of information
Somatosensory: Nerves that sense position based on gravity, feeling, and sound
Vestibular System: Motion sensing system in inner ears
Reports head position, orientation, movement
Spatial Disorientation & Flight
Flying can result in conflicting information between the systems leading to disorientation
Visual System (eyes)
VMC - Eyes prevail over false sensations
IMC - Eyes can’t correct for false sensations
Vestibular System (inner ear)
Senses movement & determines orientation
Semicircular Canals
Detect angular acceleration (turns)
Only detects turns of a short duration
After approx. 20 seconds, the feeling of turning stops (pictured, right)
Otolith Organs (pictured, bottom right)
Detect linear acceleration/gravity
Forward acceleration can give the illusion of the head tilting backward (climb)
Deceleration can give the illusion of the head tilting forward (descent)
Somatosensory System (nerves)
Nerves in the body constantly send info to the brain, which signals the body’s relation to gravity
The brain can’t differentiate between the forces of a turn or turbulence, and the force of gravity
Countering the sensations
Recognize the problem, disregard the false sensations, and rely on the flight instruments
Motion Sickness 										AI.II.A.K1e
Causes
Brain receiving conflicting messages about the body’s state
Anxiety and stress
Symptoms
General discomfort, Nausea, Dizziness, Paleness, Sweating, Vomiting
Treatment
Open fresh air vents
Focus on objects outside the airplane and avoid unnecessary head movement
Take control of the aircraft and fly smooth, straight, and level
Carbon Monoxide Poisoning 								AI.II.A.K1f
How it Happens – In the Plane
Carbon Monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas produced by all internal combustion engines
Exhaust leak can allow CO to enter the cabin
How it Happens – In the Body
CO attaches itself to the hemoglobin in the blood, preventing it from carrying oxygen to the cells
Effects of CO poisoning
Hypemic hypoxia, Headache, Blurred vision, Dizziness, Drowsiness, Loss of muscle power
Detecting & Correcting
CO detector
If a strong odor of exhaust gases is detected, assume CO is present
If suspected:
Turn off the heater and open fresh air vents and windows
Use supplemental oxygen, if available
Land
Fatigue & Stress
Fatigue 											AI.II.A.K1h
Acute Fatigue (short term)
Short term, and a normal occurrence in everyday life
Skill Fatigue: A special type of acute fatigue affecting piloting skill. Effects include:
Timing Disruption: Performing a task, but the timing of each element is slightly off
Concentrating attention on the center of vision and neglecting the periphery
Causes: Physical and Psychological stress, mild hypoxia
Prevention: Proper diet, Adequate rest and sleep
Chronic Fatigue
Fatigue over a long period of time – usually has psychological roots or underlying disease
Causes: Continuous high-stress levels
Symptoms
Weakness, Tiredness, Headaches, Irritability, Breathlessness, Aches and pains
Heart palpitations, Stomach or intestinal problems
Emotional Illness (when conditions become serious enough)
Prevention: Usually requires treatment by a physician
Stress 												AI.II.A.K1g
The body’s response to physical and psychological demands placed upon it
Stressors
Physical Stress – Noise or vibration
Physiological Stress – Fatigue
Psychological Stress – Difficult work or personal situations
Two Categories of Stress (Acute and Chronic)
Acute Stress (short term)
Involves an immediate threat that is perceived as danger (fight or flight response)
Normally, a healthy person can cope with acute stress and prevent stress overload
On-going acute stress can develop into chronic stress
Chronic Stress (long term)
Stress that exceeds the ability to cope, and causes performance to fall sharply
Unrelenting psychological pressures (ex. loneliness, financial worries, relationship problems)
Not safe to fly. Consult a physician
Dehydration & Nutrition									AI.II.A.K1i
Dehydration: Critical loss of water from the body
Causes: Hot flight decks/flight lines, wind, humidity, diuretic drinks (coffee, tea, alcohol, soda)
Effects: Fatigue, inability to concentrate, headaches, cramps, tingling, sleepiness, and dizziness
Prevention: Primarily water
Keep the flight deck well-ventilated and protect yourself from the sun
Limit daily caffeine and alcohol intake
Nutrition
Ensure properly fed and nourished
Causes: Missing/postponing meals and/or poor eating habits
Effects: Low energy and/or low blood sugar, stomach contractions, distraction, breakdown in habit patterns, and shortened attention span
Insufficient vitamin A can impair night vision
Prevention: Eat healthy, regularly spaced & sized meals
Hypothermia 											AI.II.A.K1j
The body loses heat faster than it can be produced (Normal: 98.6o F/37o C, Hypothermia: < 95o F/35o C)
Mechanisms of heat loss
Radiated Heat: Most heat loss is due to heat radiated from unprotected parts of the body
Direct Contact: In contact with something very cold, heat is conducted away from the body
Heat is lost much faster in cold water than cold air and if clothes are wet vs dry
Wind: Carries away the thin layer of warm air at the surface of your skin
Causes
Clothes that aren’t warm enough for the weather, or unable to get out of wet clothes
Too much time in the cold or cold water
Symptoms
Shivering, Slurred speech or mumbling, Slow, shallow breathing, Weak pulse, Clumsiness, Drowsiness, Confusion or memory loss, Bright red, cold skin
Prevention (COLD)
Cover: Wear protective clothing
Overexertion: Avoid activities that result in a lot of sweat
Layers: Loose fitting, layered, lightweight clothing (wool, silk or polypropylene)
Tightly woven, water repellent material is best for wind protection
Dry: Stay dry – get out of wet clothing as soon as possible
Optical Illusions 										AI.II.A.K1k
Runway Width Illusion
Reason: A narrower or wider than usual runway
Illusion: Narrow – Appear to be at a higher altitude than you are (appear lower with a wide runway)
Result: Narrow – A lower than normal approach; Wider – A higher than normal approach
Runway and Terrain Slope Illusion
Reason: A sloping runway, sloping terrain, or both
Illusion: Upslope – Appear to be higher than you are (appear to be lower with a downslope)
Result: Upslope – A lower than normal approach; Downslope – A higher than normal approach
Featureless Terrain Illusion
Reason: An absence of ground features, as when landing over water, or darkened areas
Illusion: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it is
Result: The pilot who doesn’t recognize this will fly a lower approach
Atmospheric Illusions
Reason: Rain on the windscreen, Atmospheric Haze, Penetration of fog
Illusion: Rain - Illusion of greater height; Haze –Greater distance; Fog – Pitching up
Result: Rain & Haze - A lower than normal approach; Fog – steepens the approach, often abruptly
Ground Lighting Illusions
Reason: Lights along a straight path, such as a road, and even lights on moving trains
Illusions: Can create the illusion of runway and approach lights
Result: The pilot may attempt to land on a path, road, or train
Reason: Bright runway and approach lighting systems
Illusion: Can create the illusion of less distance to the runway
Result: The pilot who does not recognize this illusion will fly a higher approach
Preventing landing Illusions
Anticipate them during approaches; Use glide slope or VASI/PAPI systems whenever possible
Nitrogen & Scuba Diving 									AI.II.A.K1l
Why it’s a Danger
Scuba diving results in a significant increase in the amount of nitrogen dissolved in the body
Scuba Diving and Flying
If enough time isn’t allowed for excess nitrogen elimination, decompression sickness (DCS) can occur
Symptoms: severe pain and impairment, extreme cases can result in death
Wait times:
Wait 12 hrs. before flight up to 8,000’ MSL – 24 hrs. for flight above 8,000’
Wait 24 hrs. after a dive that requires a controlled ascent before flight up to 8,000’ MSL
Alcohol & Other Drugs 								AI.II.A.K2, AI.II.A.K3
DON’T drink and fly
Alcohol interferes with the brains ability to utilize oxygen (histotoxic hypoxia)
Altitude multiples the effects of alcohol on the brain
FAR 91.17 – 8 hrs. ‘from bottle to throttle’ (8 hrs. and not feeling the effects of alcohol is better)
Medications
FAR 61.53 prohibits flying if using meds/getting treatment that would prevent obtaining a medical
FAR 91.17 prohibits the use of drugs that affect you in any way contrary to safety
Do not fly while taking any medication(s), unless approved by the FAA
ADM, CRM, & SRM 										AI.II.A.K4
RM: Distractions (Task Prioritization, Loss of SA, Disorientation) 				AI.II.A.R3
Human factors can present significant, distractions, disorientation, and an inability to manage tasks
IMSAFE:
Illness – Symptoms?
Medication – Taking any?
Stress – Family, money, relationships, work, etc.
Alcohol – Been drinking?
Fatigue – Well rested?
Emotion – Emotionally upset?
In flight, be alert to factors that can affect performance and lead to disorientation, etc.
RM: Combat expectation bias 								AI.II.A.R4
Your expectations can influence behavior
Individuals are vulnerable to thinking they see (or hear) what they expect to see (or hear)
RM: Hazardous Attitudes (pictured, right) 							AI.II.A.R2
Attitude affects the quality of decisions
Spot hazardous attitudes and remove them
Stress Management (stressors pictured, right)
A certain amount of stress is normal/good
Too much can be very bad – stress is cumulative
3 types of stress that affect performance
Physical: Associated with the environment (temperature, noise, vibration, lack of oxygen)
Physiological: Physical conditions (fatigue, lack of physical fitness, missed meals)
Psychological: Social or emotional factors (divorce, death in the family, sick child)
Recognize when stress is affecting a learner
Distracted or has a difficult time accomplishing tasks
Try to determine the cause (doesn’t have to be specific, could be a private matter)
Have them self-assess then set realistic goals - Delay training, if necessary
Put the learner and their progress first
Use all Resources
Use all available resources (think outside the box)
Internal Resources
Equipment, systems, charts, books, ingenuity, knowledge, skill, other passengers
External Resources
ATC, flight service specialists, guard, etc.
Workload Management
Plan, prioritize, and sequence to prevent overload
Prepare for high workload situations
Be able to recognize high workloads
“Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing/threatening issue
RM: Aeromedical & Physiological Issues 							AI.II.A.R2
The lesson as a whole is a discussion of managing risk associated with aeromedical issues
Conclusion: Brief review of the main

WHAT
The human factors concepts involve several health and physiological factors that can affect a pilot and their ability to fly safely. Some are minor, while others require special attention to ensure safety and survival and avoid incapacitation.

WHY
Many of these factors not only affect the health and well-being of the pilot but could quickly lead to in-flight emergencies if unrecognized and/or untreated.

Lack of orientation of the position/attitude/movement of the plane in space
Orientation – The body uses 3 systems to orient itself:
Visual: The eye, by far the largest source of information
Somatosensory: Nerves that sense position based on gravity, feeling, and sound
Vestibular System: Motion sensing system in inner ears
Reports head position, orientation, movement
Spatial Disorientation & Flight
Flying can result in conflicting information between the systems leading to disorientation
Visual System (eyes)
VMC - Eyes prevail over false sensations
IMC - Eyes can’t correct for false sensations
Vestibular System (inner ear)
Senses movement & determines orientation
Semicircular Canals
Detect angular acceleration (turns)
Only detects turns of a short duration
After approx. 20 seconds, the feeling of turning stops (pictured, right)
Otolith Organs (pictured, bottom right)
Detect linear acceleration/gravity
Forward acceleration can give the illusion of the head tilting backward (climb)
Deceleration can give the illusion of the head tilting forward (descent)
Somatosensory System (nerves)
Nerves in the body constantly send info to the brain, which signals the body’s relation to gravity
The brain can’t differentiate between the forces of a turn or turbulence, and the force of gravity
Countering the sensations
Recognize the problem, disregard the false sensations, and rely on the flight instruments
Motion Sickness 										AI.II.A.K1e
Causes
Brain receiving conflicting messages about the body’s state
Anxiety and stress
Symptoms
General discomfort, Nausea, Dizziness, Paleness, Sweating, Vomiting
Treatment
Open fresh air vents
Focus on objects outside the airplane and avoid unnecessary head movement
Take control of the aircraft and fly smooth, straight, and level
Carbon Monoxide Poisoning 								AI.II.A.K1f
How it Happens – In the Plane
Carbon Monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas produced by all internal combustion engines
Exhaust leak can allow CO to enter the cabin
How it Happens – In the Body
CO attaches itself to the hemoglobin in the blood, preventing it from carrying oxygen to the cells
Effects of CO poisoning
Hypemic hypoxia, Headache, Blurred vision, Dizziness, Drowsiness, Loss of muscle power
Detecting & Correcting
CO detector
If a strong odor of exhaust gases is detected, assume CO is present
If suspected:
Turn off the heater and open fresh air vents and windows
Use supplemental oxygen, if available
Land
Fatigue & Stress
Fatigue 											AI.II.A.K1h
Acute Fatigue (short term)
Short term, and a normal occurrence in everyday life
Skill Fatigue: A special type of acute fatigue affecting piloting skill. Effects include:
Timing Disruption: Performing a task, but the timing of each element is slightly off
Concentrating attention on the center of vision and neglecting the periphery
Causes: Physical and Psychological stress, mild hypoxia
Prevention: Proper diet, Adequate rest and sleep
Chronic Fatigue
Fatigue over a long period of time – usually has psychological roots or underlying disease
Causes: Continuous high-stress levels
Symptoms
Weakness, Tiredness, Headaches, Irritability, Breathlessness, Aches and pains
Heart palpitations, Stomach or intestinal problems
Emotional Illness (when conditions become serious enough)
Prevention: Usually requires treatment by a physician
Stress 												AI.II.A.K1g
The body’s response to physical and psychological demands placed upon it
Stressors
Physical Stress – Noise or vibration
Physiological Stress – Fatigue
Psychological Stress – Difficult work or personal situations
Two Categories of Stress (Acute and Chronic)
Acute Stress (short term)
Involves an immediate threat that is perceived as danger (fight or flight response)
Normally, a healthy person can cope with acute stress and prevent stress overload
On-going acute stress can develop into chronic stress
Chronic Stress (long term)
Stress that exceeds the ability to cope, and causes performance to fall sharply
Unrelenting psychological pressures (ex. loneliness, financial worries, relationship problems)
Not safe to fly. Consult a physician
Dehydration & Nutrition									AI.II.A.K1i
Dehydration: Critical loss of water from the body
Causes: Hot flight decks/flight lines, wind, humidity, diuretic drinks (coffee, tea, alcohol, soda)
Effects: Fatigue, inability to concentrate, headaches, cramps, tingling, sleepiness, and dizziness
Prevention: Primarily water
Keep the flight deck well-ventilated and protect yourself from the sun
Limit daily caffeine and alcohol intake
Nutrition
Ensure properly fed and nourished
Causes: Missing/postponing meals and/or poor eating habits
Effects: Low energy and/or low blood sugar, stomach contractions, distraction, breakdown in habit patterns, and shortened attention span
Insufficient vitamin A can impair night vision
Prevention: Eat healthy, regularly spaced & sized meals
Hypothermia 											AI.II.A.K1j
The body loses heat faster than it can be produced (Normal: 98.6o F/37o C, Hypothermia: < 95o F/35o C)
Mechanisms of heat loss
Radiated Heat: Most heat loss is due to heat radiated from unprotected parts of the body
Direct Contact: In contact with something very cold, heat is conducted away from the body
Heat is lost much faster in cold water than cold air and if clothes are wet vs dry
Wind: Carries away the thin layer of warm air at the surface of your skin
Causes
Clothes that aren’t warm enough for the weather, or unable to get out of wet clothes
Too much time in the cold or cold water
Symptoms
Shivering, Slurred speech or mumbling, Slow, shallow breathing, Weak pulse, Clumsiness, Drowsiness, Confusion or memory loss, Bright red, cold skin
Prevention (COLD)
Cover: Wear protective clothing
Overexertion: Avoid activities that result in a lot of sweat
Layers: Loose fitting, layered, lightweight clothing (wool, silk or polypropylene)
Tightly woven, water repellent material is best for wind protection
Dry: Stay dry – get out of wet clothing as soon as possible
Optical Illusions 										AI.II.A.K1k
Runway Width Illusion
Reason: A narrower or wider than usual runway
Illusion: Narrow – Appear to be at a higher altitude than you are (appear lower with a wide runway)
Result: Narrow – A lower than normal approach; Wider – A higher than normal approach
Runway and Terrain Slope Illusion
Reason: A sloping runway, sloping terrain, or both
Illusion: Upslope – Appear to be higher than you are (appear to be lower with a downslope)
Result: Upslope – A lower than normal approach; Downslope – A higher than normal approach
Featureless Terrain Illusion
Reason: An absence of ground features, as when landing over water, or darkened areas
Illusion: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it is
Result: The pilot who doesn’t recognize this will fly a lower approach
Atmospheric Illusions
Reason: Rain on the windscreen, Atmospheric Haze, Penetration of fog
Illusion: Rain - Illusion of greater height; Haze –Greater distance; Fog – Pitching up
Result: Rain & Haze - A lower than normal approach; Fog – steepens the approach, often abruptly
Ground Lighting Illusions
Reason: Lights along a straight path, such as a road, and even lights on moving trains
Illusions: Can create the illusion of runway and approach lights
Result: The pilot may attempt to land on a path, road, or train
Reason: Bright runway and approach lighting systems
Illusion: Can create the illusion of less distance to the runway
Result: The pilot who does not recognize this illusion will fly a higher approach
Preventing landing Illusions
Anticipate them during approaches; Use glide slope or VASI/PAPI systems whenever possible
Nitrogen & Scuba Diving 									AI.II.A.K1l
Why it’s a Danger
Scuba diving results in a significant increase in the amount of nitrogen dissolved in the body
Scuba Diving and Flying
If enough time isn’t allowed for excess nitrogen elimination, decompression sickness (DCS) can occur
Symptoms: severe pain and impairment, extreme cases can result in death
Wait times:
Wait 12 hrs. before flight up to 8,000’ MSL – 24 hrs. for flight above 8,000’
Wait 24 hrs. after a dive that requires a controlled ascent before flight up to 8,000’ MSL
Alcohol & Other Drugs 								AI.II.A.K2, AI.II.A.K3
DON’T drink and fly
Alcohol interferes with the brains ability to utilize oxygen (histotoxic hypoxia)
Altitude multiples the effects of alcohol on the brain
FAR 91.17 – 8 hrs. ‘from bottle to throttle’ (8 hrs. and not feeling the effects of alcohol is better)
Medications
FAR 61.53 prohibits flying if using meds/getting treatment that would prevent obtaining a medical
FAR 91.17 prohibits the use of drugs that affect you in any way contrary to safety
Do not fly while taking any medication(s), unless approved by the FAA
ADM, CRM, & SRM 										AI.II.A.K4
RM: Distractions (Task Prioritization, Loss of SA, Disorientation) 				AI.II.A.R3
Human factors can present significant, distractions, disorientation, and an inability to manage tasks
IMSAFE:
Illness – Symptoms?
Medication – Taking any?
Stress – Family, money, relationships, work, etc.
Alcohol – Been drinking?
Fatigue – Well rested?
Emotion – Emotionally upset?
In flight, be alert to factors that can affect performance and lead to disorientation, etc.
RM: Combat expectation bias 								AI.II.A.R4
Your expectations can influence behavior
Individuals are vulnerable to thinking they see (or hear) what they expect to see (or hear)
RM: Hazardous Attitudes (pictured, right) 							AI.II.A.R2
Attitude affects the quality of decisions
Spot hazardous attitudes and remove them
Stress Management (stressors pictured, right)
A certain amount of stress is normal/good
Too much can be very bad – stress is cumulative
3 types of stress that affect performance
Physical: Associated with the environment (temperature, noise, vibration, lack of oxygen)
Physiological: Physical conditions (fatigue, lack of physical fitness, missed meals)
Psychological: Social or emotional factors (divorce, death in the family, sick child)
Recognize when stress is affecting a learner
Distracted or has a difficult time accomplishing tasks
Try to determine the cause (doesn’t have to be specific, could be a private matter)
Have them self-assess then set realistic goals - Delay training, if necessary
Put the learner and their progress first
Use all Resources
Use all available resources (think outside the box)
Internal Resources
Equipment, systems, charts, books, ingenuity, knowledge, skill, other passengers
External Resources
ATC, flight service specialists, guard, etc.
Workload Management
Plan, prioritize, and sequence to prevent overload
Prepare for high workload situations
Be able to recognize high workloads
“Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing/threatening issue
RM: Aeromedical & Physiological Issues 							AI.II.A.R2
The lesson as a whole is a discussion of managing risk associated with aeromedical issues
Conclusion: Brief review of the main

paragraphs.text: II.B. Visual Scanning & Collision Avoidance
Introduction
How
“See and Avoid” (FAR 91.113, AC 90-48) 							AI.II.B.K3
Vigilance shall be maintained at all times, by each person operating an aircraft
Although often a shared job, the pilot is always responsible to see and avoid traffic
Proper Visual Scanning (AIM 8-1-6) 								AI.II.B.K4
Fovea vs Peripheral Viewing
Fovea (center of vision) – sends a clear, sharp image to the brain
Effective in daylight, but effectively a blind spot at night
Peripherals – outside of the center of vision, good for detecting motion/collision threats, and most effective at night
Effective scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements (10o per sec) bringing successive areas of the sky into view
Day – Use the fovea/center of vision; Night – Use peripherals
Poor visual scanning and/or a lack of visual scanning increases the risk of midair collisions
RM: Distractions to Visual Scanning 		     	        AI.II.B.R1
90% outside, 10% inside
Imperative to fly based on outside references with short glances inside
Remove distractions
if it’s a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Collision Risks											AI.II.B.K7
RM: High Traffic Areas (RM: High Volume Operational Environments)			AI.II.B.R3
Class B, C, D & E surface areas, VORs, VFR waypoints, VFR corridors, training areas, airways, etc.
Distractions
Overconcentration on instruments, maps, tablet, conversation, a problem, or anything other the scan
Poor visibility conditions such as rain, reduced visibility/haze, and the position of the sun
Division of Attention 										AI.II.B.K8
90% outside, 10% inside
Clearing Procedures 									AI.II.B.K5
Before Takeoff - Scan the approach/departure areas for traffic
Climbs & Descents - Use gentle banks left and right to permit scanning
Straight & Level - Execute clearing procedures at periodic intervals
Traffic Patterns - Scan judiciously; Do not enter the pattern while descending
Traffic at VOR Sites - Hight traffic area. Scan judiciously
Training Operations – Be vigilant at all times. Use clearing turns prior to each maneuver
Blind Spots - Momentarily raise/lower the wing as necessary to clear for traffic before turning
Visual Cues / Recognizing Hazards (AC 90-48, AIM 8-1-8) 					AI.II.B.K6
RM: Aircraft Speed and Collision Risk (RM: Collision reaction time)				AI.II.B.R4
Minimum time to spot traffic, identify it, realize it’s a threat, and respond – 12.5 seconds
Determining Relative Altitude
If the aircraft is above the horizon, it is probably on a higher flight path, and vice versa
Any aircraft that appears to have no relative motion is likely to be on a collision course
Taking Appropriate Action
If on a collision course, take immediate action
Safety comes first, but be familiar with Right-of-Way rules (FAR 91.113)
Collision Avoidance (AIM 8-1-8)
Flight deck Management
Plan ahead/organize to minimize time spent with your eyes inside/head down
Visual obstructions in the Flight deck
Adjust for blind spots, do not block windows, keep windscreens clean
Keep the windscreen clean
Be More Visible
Use exterior lights & keep interior lights low at night to maintain night vision
ADS-B
Other traffic is displayed on the MFD, often with visual and/or audio alerts
ATC Support
Use flight following for radar traffic advisories whenever possible
RM: Safety Pilot/Another set of Eyes (RM: Use of a safety pilot) 				AI.II.B.R5
Conditions that Degrade Vision (AIM 8-1-6) 						AI.II.B.K1
Physical Conditions
Medicine/drugs, exhaustion, poor physical conditioning, diet, missing meals, alcohol, tobacco, stressors, fatigue, lack of oxygen (hypoxia), etc.
CO poisoning, smoking, alcohol/drugs, and a lack of oxygen can decrease night vision
Environmental Conditions
Dim illumination: Small print and colors become unreadable unless adequate lighting is available
Dark Adaptation: Vision becomes more sensitive to light (30 min to adapt, few second to lose)
Excessive Illumination: Glare results in squinting, watering eyes, even temporary blindness
Visibility Conditions: Smoke, haze, dust, etc.
RM: Relaxed Intermediate Focal Distance 						AI.II.B.R2
With nothing to focus on, the eyes focus on a point slightly ahead of the plane (10-30’)
Prevention
Day: Force your eyes to focus farther ahead, maintain your scan
Night: Search out and focus on distant light sources, no matter how dim
Vestibular / In Flight / Visual Illusions 							AI.II.B.K2
The Leans: Abrupt correction of a bank entered too slowly to stimulate the senses in the inner ear
Illusion: Can create the illusion of banking in the opposite direction
Result: Roll the back into the original attitude (turn), thinking it’s straight and level
Coriolis Illusion
Reason: Abrupt head movement in a turn that has stopped stimulating the motion sensing system
Illusion: Can create the illusion of rotation or movement in an entirely different axis
Result: The pilot may maneuver into a dangerous attitude in order to stop the perceived rotation
Graveyard Spin
Reason: Recovery from a spin that has ceased stimulating the motion sensing system
Illusion: Can create the illusion of being in a spin in the opposite direction
Result: The disoriented pilot will return the aircraft to its original spin
Graveyard Spiral
Reason: Loss of altitude during a turn that has stopped stimulating the motion sensing system
Illusion: Can create the illusion of a wings level descent
Result: Pilot may pull back on the controls, tightening the spiral and increasing the loss of altitude
Somatogravic Illusion
Reason: A rapid acceleration, or a rapid deceleration
Illusion: Rapid acceleration can create the illusion of a nose up attitude (deceleration = nose down)
Result: May put the aircraft in a nose low/dive attitude (deceleration = nose up/stall attitude)
Inversion Illusion
Reason: An abrupt change from a climb to straight and level flight
Illusion: Can create the illusion of tumbling backwards
Result: The disoriented pilot will push the aircraft abruptly into a nose low attitude
Elevator Illusion
Reason: Abrupt upward/downward vertical acceleration, due to an updraft /downdraft
Illusion: Upward vertical acceleration can create the illusion of being in a climb (downward = decent)
Result: The disoriented pilot will push the aircraft into a nose low attitude (downward = nose up)
False Horizon
Reason: Sloping clouds, obscured horizon, certain patterns of lights
Illusions: Can create the illusion of not being aligned correctly with the horizon
Result: The disoriented pilot will put the aircraft in a dangerous attitude
Autokinesis
Reason: Darkness
Illusion: A static light when stared at for many seconds will appear to move about
Result: The disoriented pilot may lose control of the aircraft in attempting to align it with the light
Preventing Spatial Disorientation
Prevented by reference to flight instruments or reliable, fixed points on the ground
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

Additionally, we’ll discuss various illusions, how they affect the pilot, and how to counter them.

WHY
Safety. Visual scanning and collision avoidance is very important in creating safe skies. A diligent visual scan to avoid collision threats and the ability to recognize and counter illusions is paramount to the safety of all pilots.

Class B, C, D & E surface areas, VORs, VFR waypoints, VFR corridors, training areas, airways, etc.
Distractions
Overconcentration on instruments, maps, tablet, conversation, a problem, or anything other the scan
Poor visibility conditions such as rain, reduced visibility/haze, and the position of the sun
Division of Attention 										AI.II.B.K8
90% outside, 10% inside
Clearing Procedures 									AI.II.B.K5
Before Takeoff - Scan the approach/departure areas for traffic
Climbs & Descents - Use gentle banks left and right to permit scanning
Straight & Level - Execute clearing procedures at periodic intervals
Traffic Patterns - Scan judiciously; Do not enter the pattern while descending
Traffic at VOR Sites - Hight traffic area. Scan judiciously
Training Operations – Be vigilant at all times. Use clearing turns prior to each maneuver
Blind Spots - Momentarily raise/lower the wing as necessary to clear for traffic before turning
Visual Cues / Recognizing Hazards (AC 90-48, AIM 8-1-8) 					AI.II.B.K6
RM: Aircraft Speed and Collision Risk (RM: Collision reaction time)				AI.II.B.R4
Minimum time to spot traffic, identify it, realize it’s a threat, and respond – 12.5 seconds
Determining Relative Altitude
If the aircraft is above the horizon, it is probably on a higher flight path, and vice versa
Any aircraft that appears to have no relative motion is likely to be on a collision course
Taking Appropriate Action
If on a collision course, take immediate action
Safety comes first, but be familiar with Right-of-Way rules (FAR 91.113)
Collision Avoidance (AIM 8-1-8)
Flight deck Management
Plan ahead/organize to minimize time spent with your eyes inside/head down
Visual obstructions in the Flight deck
Adjust for blind spots, do not block windows, keep windscreens clean
Keep the windscreen clean
Be More Visible
Use exterior lights & keep interior lights low at night to maintain night vision
ADS-B
Other traffic is displayed on the MFD, often with visual and/or audio alerts
ATC Support
Use flight following for radar traffic advisories whenever possible
RM: Safety Pilot/Another set of Eyes (RM: Use of a safety pilot) 				AI.II.B.R5
Conditions that Degrade Vision (AIM 8-1-6) 						AI.II.B.K1
Physical Conditions
Medicine/drugs, exhaustion, poor physical conditioning, diet, missing meals, alcohol, tobacco, stressors, fatigue, lack of oxygen (hypoxia), etc.
CO poisoning, smoking, alcohol/drugs, and a lack of oxygen can decrease night vision
Environmental Conditions
Dim illumination: Small print and colors become unreadable unless adequate lighting is available
Dark Adaptation: Vision becomes more sensitive to light (30 min to adapt, few second to lose)
Excessive Illumination: Glare results in squinting, watering eyes, even temporary blindness
Visibility Conditions: Smoke, haze, dust, etc.
RM: Relaxed Intermediate Focal Distance 						AI.II.B.R2
With nothing to focus on, the eyes focus on a point slightly ahead of the plane (10-30’)
Prevention
Day: Force your eyes to focus farther ahead, maintain your scan
Night: Search out and focus on distant light sources, no matter how dim
Vestibular / In Flight / Visual Illusions 							AI.II.B.K2
The Leans: Abrupt correction of a bank entered too slowly to stimulate the senses in the inner ear
Illusion: Can create the illusion of banking in the opposite direction
Result: Roll the back into the original attitude (turn), thinking it’s straight and level
Coriolis Illusion
Reason: Abrupt head movement in a turn that has stopped stimulating the motion sensing system
Illusion: Can create the illusion of rotation or movement in an entirely different axis
Result: The pilot may maneuver into a dangerous attitude in order to stop the perceived rotation
Graveyard Spin
Reason: Recovery from a spin that has ceased stimulating the motion sensing system
Illusion: Can create the illusion of being in a spin in the opposite direction
Result: The disoriented pilot will return the aircraft to its original spin
Graveyard Spiral
Reason: Loss of altitude during a turn that has stopped stimulating the motion sensing system
Illusion: Can create the illusion of a wings level descent
Result: Pilot may pull back on the controls, tightening the spiral and increasing the loss of altitude
Somatogravic Illusion
Reason: A rapid acceleration, or a rapid deceleration
Illusion: Rapid acceleration can create the illusion of a nose up attitude (deceleration = nose down)
Result: May put the aircraft in a nose low/dive attitude (deceleration = nose up/stall attitude)
Inversion Illusion
Reason: An abrupt change from a climb to straight and level flight
Illusion: Can create the illusion of tumbling backwards
Result: The disoriented pilot will push the aircraft abruptly into a nose low attitude
Elevator Illusion
Reason: Abrupt upward/downward vertical acceleration, due to an updraft /downdraft
Illusion: Upward vertical acceleration can create the illusion of being in a climb (downward = decent)
Result: The disoriented pilot will push the aircraft into a nose low attitude (downward = nose up)
False Horizon
Reason: Sloping clouds, obscured horizon, certain patterns of lights
Illusions: Can create the illusion of not being aligned correctly with the horizon
Result: The disoriented pilot will put the aircraft in a dangerous attitude
Autokinesis
Reason: Darkness
Illusion: A static light when stared at for many seconds will appear to move about
Result: The disoriented pilot may lose control of the aircraft in attempting to align it with the light
Preventing Spatial Disorientation
Prevented by reference to flight instruments or reliable, fixed points on the ground
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: II.C. Runway Incursion Avoidance
Introduction
How
Runway Incursion 										AI.II.C.K1

Any occurrence at an airport involving an aircraft, vehicle, person, or object on the ground that creates a collision hazard or results in a loss of separation with an aircraft taking off, landing, or intending to land
Approximately 3 runway incursions occur each day at towered airports in the US
About 65% of all incursions are caused by pilots (about half of those are caused by GA pilots)
Airport/Taxiing Challenges
Situational Awareness: Complex layouts, increased traffic
Distractions: Checklists, radio calls, cell phone/iPad, passengers/people, airplane, etc.
Causal Factors
Failure to comply with ATC instructions
Lack of airport familiarity
Nonconformance with standard operating procedures (SOPs)
Preventive Practices
Maintain SA (your position & other aircraft)
Review airport layouts & know airport signage
Review NOTAMs
Study & use proper phraseology
Write down complex taxi instructions
Readback all runway crossing and/or hold short instructions
Request progressive taxi instructions when necessary
Turn on lights and rotating beacon or strobes when taxiing
Check for traffic before crossing any runway hold line or entering any taxiway
When landing, clear the runway as soon as possible and wait for taxi instructions before moving
Taxi Instructions & Clearances								AI.II.C.K2
Approval must be obtained prior to moving onto the movement area while tower is in operation
Clearance must be obtained prior to crossing any runway
When assigned taxi instructions, ATC will specify:
The runway or point to taxi to
Taxi instructions
Hold short instructions or runway crossing clearances if the route will cross a runway
When instructions are received from the controller, always read back:
The runway assignment
RM: Any clearance to enter a specific runway (RM: Entering or crossing runways) 	AI.II.C.R3
Any instruction to hold short of a specific runway
Uncontrolled Field 										AI.II.C.K6
Announce intentions on CTAF
Always have a taxi diagram
Monitor CTAF and maintain SA (your position & other aircraft)
Apply the right-of-way rules, and give way when appropriate, or when safety dictates
Plan, Brief, Review
Route Planning
Have a current copy of the Airport Diagram & review expected routes/closed taxiways
Check for pre-designated, or standard, taxi routes, review these for familiarity
Taxi Briefing (AC 91-73)
Ground Procedures
Timing and execution of checklists/communications that will not interfere with taxiing
Expected route/any abnormalities or unusual procedures
Previous experience/unusual procedures or techniques
Critical locations on the taxi route (hold short, hot spots, etc.)
During low visibility operations, brief the requirements and considerations
Expectations of others (pilots of passengers) in the plane
Sterile flight deck procedures - encourage others to speak up if they see a potential conflict
Use of airport diagrams (pilots)
Cell phones/electronic devices should be off
Record & Review 										AI.II.C.K3
Write down ATC taxi instructions to prevent mistakes
RM: Combats expectation bias 							AI.II.C.R2
Review the route given by ATC, query ATC in case of confusion
RM: Appropriate Flightdeck Activities (RM: Distractions, Task Prioritization)	AI.II.C.K5, AI.II.C.R1
For safety reasons the pilot’s workload should be at a minimum during taxi operations
All heads down activities should be done only when the aircraft is stopped
RM: Task prioritization – taxiing comes first, handle all other tasks when safely stopped
Sterile flight deck
Taxiing Near Other Aircraft
Keep eyes outside, taxi slowly and be alert to what’s going on around you and the taxi route
Use a “continuous loop” process to monitor and update other aircraft progress and location
Be especially vigilant if another aircraft with a similar call sign is on frequency
Airport Markings, Signs, & Lights 								AI.II.C.K4
Airport Markings
Overview
Taxiways should have centerline/runway holding position markings whenever intersecting a runway
Edge markings separate the taxiway from areas not for aircraft use or define taxiway edges
Taxiway Centerline Markings
Normal Centerline
Purpose - Visual cue to permit taxiing along a designated path
Markings - Single continuous yellow line, 6” - 12” wide
Enhanced Centerline
Purpose - Same as above but at larger commercial airports to warn that a runway hold position marking is being approached
Markings - Parallel line of yellow dashes on both sides of the taxiway centerline
Taxiway Edge Markings
Defines the edge of the taxiway (usually when the edge doesn’t match with the pavement)
Continuous Markings
Purpose - Define the taxiway edge from the shoulder/paved surface not for use by aircraft
Markings - Continuous double yellow line
Dashed Markings
Purpose - Define the taxiway edge when adjoining pavement is intended for aircraft (apron)
Markings - Broken double yellow line
Taxi Shoulder Markings
Purpose - Shoulders prevent erosion but they may not support aircraft
Markings - Taxiway edge markings will usually define this area
Surface Painted Taxiway Direction Signs
Purpose - When it isn’t possible to offer direction signs at intersections, or to supplement such signs
Markings - Surface painted location signs with a yellow background and black inscription
Surface Painted Location Signs
Purpose - Location signs assisting in confirming the taxiway
Markings - Black background with a yellow inscription
Geographic Position Markings
Purpose - Identifies aircraft location during low visibility operations
Markings - Left of the taxiway centerline in the direction of taxiing
A circle with an outer black ring, inner white ring, and a pink circle
On dark pavement, the white/black ring are reversed
Holding Position Markings
Show where an aircraft is supposed to stop when approaching a runway (hold on the solid side) - 4 yellow lines (2 solid/2 dashed) across the width of the taxiway, runway, or approach area
Runway Holding Position Markings on Taxiways
Purpose - Show where to stop without a clearance onto the runway
Markings – Same as described above
Runway Holding Position Markings on Runways (depicted, right)
Purpose - Installed if normally used for LAHSO or taxi ops
Markings - White inscription/red background next to hold markings
Taxiways Located in Runway Approach Area
Holding Position Markings for Instrument Landing System (ILS)
Purpose - Hold aircraft when the ILS critical area is being protected
Markings - 2 yellow solid lines 2’ apart joined by pairs of solid lines 10’ apart across the taxiway
Holding Position Markings for Taxiway/Taxiway Intersections
Purpose - Installed on taxiways where ATC normally holds aircraft short of an intersection
Markings - Single dashed line extending across the width of the taxiway
Surface Painted Holding Position Signs (pictured, right)
Purpose - Supplements signs located at the holding position
Markings - Red background/white text on hold side before hold lines
Other Markings
VOR Receiver Checkpoint Markings
Purpose - Allow the pilot to check aircraft instruments with navigational aid signals
Markings - Painted circle with an arrow in the middle (arrow is aligned toward the facility)
Located with a sign on the apron/taxiway, Black text on a yellow background
Vehicle Roadway Markings
Purpose - Defines a path for vehicle operations on the airport
Markings - White solid line delineates each edge and a dashed line separates lanes
Marking and Lighting of Permanently Closed Runways
Purpose – For permanently closed runways and taxiways
Markings - Lighting circuits will be disconnected
Yellow crosses at each end and at 1,000’ intervals
Temporarily Closed Runways & Taxiways
Purpose – Indication that a runway is temporarily closed
Markings - Yellow crosses at each end
A visual indication may not be present (check NOTAMs/ATIS)
Closed taxiways are blockaded (yellow cross may also be used)
Nonmovement Area Boundary Markings (pictured, right)
Purpose - Delineates movement area (area under control)
Markings - 2 yellow lines (one solid and one dashed)
Runway Markings
Three Types of Runway Markings (see diagram, below)
Visual; Non-precision Instrument; Precision Instrument
Diagram Notes
Note 1: Required on runways serving category C/D aircraft, & runways for international commercial transport
Note 2: Required on 4,200’ or longer runways serving categories C & D airplanes
Note 3: Required on 4,200’ or longer instrumented runways
Note 4: Used when the full runway pavement width may not be available for use as a runway
Runway Designators
Purpose - To identify / differentiate runways from the approach end
To Magnetic North; whole number to the nearest one-tenth of the runway course
L, R, C differentiate multiple parallel runways
Markings - Large white numbers
Runway Centerline Marking
Purpose - Identifies the center of the runway providing alignment guidance
Markings - A line of uniformly spaced stripes and gaps
Runway Aiming Point Markings
Purpose - Visual aiming point for landing aircraft
Markings - Broad white stripe on each side of the centerline, approximately 1,000’ from threshold
Runway Touchdown Zone Markers
Purpose - Identifies touchdown zone for landing; provide distance info in 500’ increments
Markings - Groups of 1, 2, and 3 rectangular bars in pairs about the runway centerline
Runway Side Stripe Markings
Purpose - Delineate edges of the runway providing a contrast between the runway and shoulder
Markings - Continuous white stripes located on each side of the runway
Runway Shoulder Markings
Purpose - Identify pavement areas not intended for aircraft use
Markings - Yellow stripes
Runway Threshold Markings (stripes vary with width, see table)
Purpose – Identifies the beginning of the runway available for landing
Markings – Stripes about the centerline
Displaced Threshold (DT)
Landing threshold starts at a point other than the beginning of the runway - Used for taxiing, takeoff, landing rollout (not to be landed on, reduces landing distance)
Markings
A 10’ wide white threshold bar across the runway at the displaced threshold
White arrow heads are located across the runway just prior to the threshold bar
White arrows down the centerline between the start of the runway and displaced threshold
Relocated Threshold
Explanation – Construction / other activities require the threshold to be relocated (NOTAM)
Markings – Normally a 10’ wide white threshold bar across the runway, but can vary
Airport Signs
Mandatory Instruction Signs
Purpose - Denote entrance to runway or critical area / area where aircraft are prohibited
Markings - Red background with a white text
Typical Mandatory Signs and Applications
Runway Holding Position Sign
Runway Approach Area Holding Position Sign
ILS Critical Area Holding Position Sign
No Entry Sign
Location Signs
Purpose - Identify either a taxiway or runway on which the aircraft is located
Taxiway Location Sign
Purpose - Along taxiways to indicate location
Markings - Black background with yellow inscription and border
Runway Location Sign
Purpose - Complement compass/heading info; typically, in areas with multiple runways
Markings - Black background with yellow text
Runway Boundary Sign
Purpose - Visual cue depicting when “clear of the runway”
Markings - Yellow background / black lines
ILS Critical Area Boundary Sign (pictured, right)
Purpose - Depicts where clear of the ILS critical area
Markings - Yellow background / black lines
Direction Signs
Purpose - Identify taxiways out of an intersection
Designations / arrows are arranged clockwise from the 1st taxiway on the pilot’s left
Markings - Yellow background / black text
Destination Signs
Purpose - Indicates a destination on the airport
Markings - Yellow background/black text
Information Signs
Purpose – Provide information on things such as: Areas the tower can’t see, radio frequencies, noise procedures
Markings - Yellow Background / black text
Runway Distance Remaining Signs
Purpose – Informs the distance remaining on the runway
Number indicates the thousands of feet of landing runway remaining
Markings - Black background / white number
Airport Lighting
Taxiway Lighting
Taxiway Edge Lights: Steady blue lights outlining the edges of taxiways
Taxiway Centerline Lights: Steady green lights installed along the centerline of the taxiway
Clearance Bar Lights: Three in-pavement steady-burning yellow lights
Installed at holding positions on taxiways to increase visibility of the holding position
Runway Guard Lights: Pair of elevated flashing yellow lights on either side of the taxiway, or a row of in-pavement yellow lights across the entire taxiway at the runway holding position marking
Installed at taxiway/runway intersections to make them more noticeable
Stop Bar Lights: A row of red, unidirectional, steady-burning in-pavement lights across the taxiway at the runway holding position, and elevated steady-burning red lights on each side
A controlled stop bar operates in conjunction with the taxiway centerline lead-on lights
Following ATC clearance, the stop bar is turned off and the lead-on lights are turned on
Used to confirm the ATC clearance to enter or cross the active runway in low visibility
Runway Lighting
Runway End Identifier Lights (REIL)
Installed to provide rapid / positive identification of the approach end of a runway
Configuration - Pair of synchronized flashing lights on each side of the runway threshold
Runway Edge Light Systems (HIRL, MIRL, LIRL)
Outline the edges of runways during dark / restricted visibility conditions
Classified according to the intensity or brightness: High (HIRL); Medium (MIRL); Low (LIRL)
Configuration
Runway edge lights – White
Instrument runways – Yellow for the last 2,000,’ or half the runway, whichever is shorter
Lights marking the end of the runway – Red / Green
Red indicates the end of the runway to a departing aircraft
Green indicates the threshold to landing aircraft
Runway Centerline Lighting System (RCLS)
Installed on some precision runways to facilitate landing under adverse conditions
Configuration
Along runway centerline at 50’ intervals
From the threshold, the lights are white until the last 3,000’ of the runway
White lights alternate with red for 2,000’, and the last 1,000’ all lights are red
Touchdown Zone Lights (TDZL)
On some precision runways to indicate touchdown zone in low visibility conditions
Configuration
Rows of (usually 3) lights on both sides of the runway centerline
Rows begin 100’ beyond the landing threshold and extend to 3,000’ beyond the landing threshold or the midpoint of the runway, whichever is less
Taxiway Centerline Lead-Off Lights
Provide visual guidance to exit the runway
Configuration:
Alternate green & yellow lights, beginning with green, from the runway centerline to 1 light position beyond the runway hold position/ILS critical area hold position
Taxiway Centerline Lead-on Lights
Provide visual guidance for entering the runway
Configuration
Color coded with the same pattern as lead-off lights
Bidirectional (1 side emits light for the lead-on function the other for the lead-off)
Land and Hold Short Lights
Used to indicate the hold short point on certain runways approved for LAHSO
When installed, the lights will be on anytime LAHSO is in effect and off when not
Configuration - A row of pulsing white lights installed across the runway
Runway Status Lights (RWSL)
Fully automated system providing indication it’s unsafe to enter, cross, takeoff, or land on a runway
Installed at several major US airports
Processes information from surveillance systems to turn red warning lights on/off
Used in conjunction with ATC – lights and ATC instructions must agree
Runway Entrance Lights (REL)
In-pavement red lights
Warns aircraft waiting to cross/enter a runway that there is conflicting traffic
Takeoff Hold Lights (THL)
In-pavement red lights
Warns aircraft in the takeoff position that the runway is occupied & takeoff is unsafe
More details: FAA Runway Status Lights
Airport Operations & Runway Incursions
Hold Lines
Show where stop when approaching a runway. Cross the dashed side, stop on the solid side
Always have a clearance to cross any runway
RM: During taxi: (Entering or crossing runways) 						AI.II.C.R3
Approaching from the dashed side, cross (no clearance required) & stop fully passed the solid lines
If approaching hold lines from the solid side, do not cross without a clearance
Always clear both directions and turn on all exterior lights when crossing
RM: Landing & Rollout 								AI.II.C.R6, AI.II.C.R7
Brief the landing and runway exit/taxi plan (sterile flight deck during taxi)
Exit the runway entirely, do not cross another runway without clearance
RM: Night Operations 									AI.II.C.R4
Exterior Lights - Make an aircraft easier to see (use day and night)
Starting Engines/Engines Running: Rotating beacon on
Taxiing: Prior to taxi, turn on navigation, position, and anti-collision lights
Strobes should not be used during taxi if they adversely affect the vision of others
Crossing a Runway: All exterior lights should be illuminated when crossing a runway
Entering the Runway for Takeoff: Turn on all lights, except for landing lights
Night: Line up 3’ off centerline to allow landing aircraft to differentiate you from runway lights
Takeoff: Turn on landing lights when cleared for takeoff/starting the takeoff roll if no control tower
Be more cautious at night
Taxi slower, allow more time to stop
Ensure you remain on the assigned route – lights and signs can be confusing
RM: Low Visibility 										AI.II.C.R5
AIM 4-3-19 Taxi During Low Visibility
Focus entire attention on the safe operation of the aircraft while it is moving
Taxi slowly with focus outside
Sterile flight deck
Notify the controller of difficulties or at the first indication of becoming disoriented
Lack of visibility from the tower can prevent visual confirmation of adherence to taxi instructions
RM: Loss of SA & Disorientation 								AI.II.C.R1
Stop if disoriented or SA is lost and inform ATC (or CTAF)
Regain orientation before proceeding
Ask for help from ATC - Request progressive, if necessary
Case Study: United 1448 (PVD Airport)
YouTube Animation & Audio Transcript
NTSB Safety Recommendation – July 6, 2000
Page 6 has a short summary and diagram
RM Concepts
Low visibility taxi, night operations, loss of SA/disorientation, entering/crossing runways
Discuss options to mitigate these risks
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

Location Signs

Taxiway Lighting

Hold Lines
Show where stop when approaching a runway. Cross the dashed side, stop on the solid side
Always have a clearance to cross any runway

RM: Landing & Rollout 								AI.II.C.R6, AI.II.C.R7
