paragraphs.text: II.E. Flight Controls & Operation of Systems
Introduction
How
Terms
Chord Line: An imaginary straight line drawn through an airfoil from the leading to the trailing edge
Camber: The characteristic curve of an airfoil’s upper and lower surfaces
Primary Flight Controls 									AI.II.E.K1a
Primary flight controls are those required to safely control an airplane during flight
Ailerons: Control roll about the longitudinal axis
Elevator: Controls pitch about the lateral axis
Rudder: Controls yaw about the vertical axis
Ailerons
Control roll about the longitudinal axis
Operated by cables, bell cranks, pulleys and/or push-pull tubes
How they Work
Attached to the outboard trailing edge of each wing and move in opposite directions
Right Turn: Right aileron up, Left aileron down
Left Turn: Left aileron up, Right aileron down
Upward deflection decreases camber/lift, lowering the wing
Downward deflection increases camber/lift, raising the wing
The difference in lift between the wings causes the aircraft to roll
Adverse Yaw
Sine the down deflected aileron produces more lift it also produces more induced drag
The added drag attempts to yaw the nose in the direction of the raised wing (adverse yaw)
Rudder is used to counter and maintain coordinated flight
The amount of rudder is greatest at low speeds, high AIA, and with large aileron deflections
4 Types of Ailerons to counter Adverse Yaw
Differential Ailerons
The upward moving aileron raises higher than the downward moving aileron lowers
Produces increased drag on the descending wing (raised aileron) to reduce adverse yaw
Frise-Type Ailerons
Raised aileron projects its leading edge into the airflow which creates drag and reduces adverse yaw
Also forms a slot so air flows smoothly over the lowered aileron (more effective at high AOA)
Reduces, but does not eliminate, adverse yaw
Coupled Ailerons & Rudder
Ailerons & rudder are linked – rudder automatically deflects with aileron input
Ex: When rolling left, the interconnect cable and springs pull forward on the left rudder pedal just enough to prevent right yaw
Flaperons (combine flaps and ailerons)
Control bank but can also be lowered together to act as flaps
Separate controls for ailerons & flaps
A mixer combines the separate pilot inputs into the single set of control surfaces
Elevator
Controls pitch about the lateral axis
How It Works
Pulling back deflects the trailing edge up
Changes the camber of the horizontal stab, creating a downward aerodynamic force
Tail moves down and the nose moves up
Pushing forward deflects the trailing edge down
Changes the camber of the horizontal stab, creating an upward force
Tail moves up and the nose moves down
Strength of the movement is determined by the distance, or arm, between the CG & horizontal tail surface
Types of Elevators
T-Tail
Elevator is mounted above most effects of prop downwash/fuselage and wing airflow
Makes for consistent control movements in most flight regimes
At slow speeds, the elevator must be moved a greater degree to raise the nose a given amount vs a conventional tail (which has prop downwash assisting in raising the nose)
Design Considerations
Designed stiffer and heavier than conventional
Longer moment arm creates high loads that can result in flutter
Susceptible to a deep stall when slow/high AOA (pictured)
The wing’s airflow, when fully stalled, creates a wake of decelerated, turbulent air blanketing the horizontal tail – Elevator control is reduced, or possibly eliminated
Stabilator - “All-moving tail”
Essentially a one-piece horizontal stabilizer that pivots from a central hinge point
When the controls are pulled back, the trailing edge raises, rotating the nose up
Pushing forward lowers the trailing edge, pitching the nose down
Anti-servo tabs decrease sensitivity
Stabilators are easier to move, anti-servo tabs add resistance

By pivoting around a central hinge point, a stabilator allows the pilot to generate a given pitching moment with less force. Because they are easier to move, to be certified, an aircraft must show an increasing resistance to increasing pilot input.

To provide this resistance, stabilators on small aircraft contain an anti-servo trim tab that deflects in the same direction as the stabilator and provides an aerodynamic force resisting the pilot’s input and making it less prone to overcontrolling (more info on anti-servo tabs below)
Safety Systems
Control Stops: Limit the movement of the elevator control
Some can adjust to allow more/less elevator control movement based on the situation
Elevator Down Spring: Assists in lowering the nose to prevent a stall caused by an aft CG position
Produces a mechanical load on the elevator causing it to move toward the nose-down position
Stick Pusher: Commonly used on transport category jets
If the computers recognize an approaching stall, they automatically push forward on the stick to prevent reaching a critical AOA
Rudder
Controls yaw about the vertical axis - used to maintain coordination
How it Works
Often operated through cables, but can be operated by various mechanisms
Pushing the left pedal moves the rudder left and vice versa
When deflected into the airflow, a horizontal force is exerted in the opposite direction

Moving the rudder in either direction increases the camber and therefore increases lift on one side of the rudder. Additionally, pushing the rudder into the relative wind creates a force which moves the aircraft’s nose in the same direction
V-Tail
Utilizes two slanted tail surfaces to perform the same functions as a conventional elevator and rudder
The fixed surfaces act as both horizontal and vertical stabilizers
The movable portion of the V-tail (ruddervators) are connected through a linkage allowing the control wheel to move both surfaces together
When both the rudder & elevator are moved, a mixing mechanism moves each one the appropriate amount
Drawbacks
More complex than for a conventional tail
More susceptible to Dutch roll
Total reduction in drag is minimal
Secondary Flight Controls 								AI.II.E.K1b
Improve performance characteristics – Flaps, Spoilers & Leading-Edge Devices
Flaps
The most common high lift devices used on practically all airplanes
Attached to the trailing edge of each wing to increase lift and induced drag for a given AOA
Functions
Takeoff: Get airborne at lower speeds, reduce the runway required, improve climb performance
Approach: Increased drag allows for steeper approaches
Landing: Reduced landing speeds and landing distance
Flap Types
Plain Flaps - Simplest of the types
Increase camber results in a significant increase in lift and drag at a given AOA
Drag is greatly increased, and the center of pressure moves aft resulting in a nose down pitch
Split Flaps
Deflect from the lower surface of the airfoil
Slightly more lift and drag vs plain flap
When fully extended, both plain and split flaps produce high drag with little additional lift
Slotted Flap (most popular on airplanes today)
Increase lift significantly more vs plain/split flaps
High energy air is ducted to the top, accelerating the boundary layer/delaying separation
Large aircraft have double- or even triple-slotted flaps
Allows for max increase in drag without destroying the flap’s added lift
Fowler Flaps
Type of slotted flap which changes the camber of the wing and increases the wing area
Slide backward, then downward
The first portion of extension considerably increases lift but has little effect on drag
From there, drag increases with little change in lift
Flap Control
Mechanical, electrical, or hydraulic operation (can be a combination)
Be aware of any flap operating speeds
Spoilers
High drag devices that spoil the smooth airflow over the wing, reducing lift & increasing drag
Reduce airspeed at a higher-than-normal rate (in the air and during landing)
Landing: Spoilers destroy lift and more efficiently transfer the weight from the wings to the wheels, improving braking effectiveness
Increased rate of descent - The aircraft can descend at a faster rate without increasing airspeed
Roll control – One wing’s spoiler is used to reduce lift and create drag (eliminates adverse yaw)
Trim Systems
Relieves the need for constant pressure on the flight controls
How a Trim Tab Works
Consists of flight deck controls & small, hinged devices on the trailing edge of one or more primary control surfaces
Most common is a single trim tab attached to the trailing edge of the elevator
Minimize workload by aerodynamically assisting the movement and position of the flight controls
Operation
Often operated manually through a vertically mounted control wheel (or trim crank)
Tim tab moves opposite the elevator surface
With the tab up, into the airstream, airflow over the tail forces the elevator down, moving the nose down
Note: Bottom pic should say “Tab Down – Elevator Up”
Flight Deck Operation
Establish desired power/pitch/configuration, then trim to relieve pressures
Re-trim any time power/pitch/configuration is changed
Types of Trim Tabs
Balance Tabs
Function like trim tabs, but coupled to the control rod
When the controls are deflected, the tab automatically moves in the  opposite direction
If adjustable by the pilot, it can be used as a trim tab too
Servo Tabs (primarily used in large aircraft)
Very similar in operation and appearance to trim/balance tabs
A small portion of a flight control that helps to move the entire control surface in the direction the pilot wishes
Only the servo tab moves in response the flight controls
Airflow on the servo tab then moves the control surface
Antiservo Tabs
Decrease stabilator sensitivity/act as a trim device
Like a balance tab, but moves in the same direction as the flight control
Ground Adjustable Tabs
Metal trim tab on the rudder bent in either direction while on the ground to apply a trim force
Proper placement is found through trial & error
Adjustable Stabilizer
Some aircraft can adjust the entire stabilizer
Driven by a jackscrew
Motor driven on large aircraft / Crank on small aircraft
Using Trim Tabs
Establish the desired power, pitch attitude, and configuration, then trim to relieve pressures
Any time power, pitch attitude, or configuration is changed, re-trim for the new condition
Power Plant (four stroke reciprocating engines)						AI.II.E.K1c
General
Converts chemical energy (fuel) into mechanical energy
Occurs in the cylinders through combustion
Pistons produce mechanical energy to accomplish work
Basic Components & Operation
Cylinders
Contain intake/exhaust valves, sparks plugs, pistons
Intake / exhaust valves allow the fuel-air mixture to enter / exit the combustion chamber
Spark plugs ignite the fuel air mixture
Pistons move up and down in the cylinder and drive the crankshaft which drives the propeller
Crankcase
Contains crankshaft, and connecting rods
Pistons connect to the crankshaft via connecting rods
Crankshaft is connected to the propeller
Accessory Housing
Contains magnetos
Power source for the spark plugs
More information in 4. Ignition System
Four-Stroke Operating Cycle
Intake
Piston moves to the bottom
Fuel-air mixture enters combustion chamber
Compression
Intake valve closes
Piston moves up, compressing mixture
Spark plug ignites mixture
Power
Mixture is ignited, increasing pressure
Pressure increases, forcing the piston back down
Turns the crankshaft which drives the propeller
Exhaust
Exhaust valve opens as piston reaches bottom
As piston moves back up, exhaust gas is pushed out
Two Primary Engine Designs
Spark Ignition – Most popular for many years
Compression Ignition – Becoming more popular – Reduced costs, simpler designs, more reliable
Compression systems can run on diesel or jet fuel (Diamond DA42, for example)
Components
Main mechanical components of spark and compression systems are essentially the same
Primary difference is the process of igniting the fuel
Spark Ignition: Uses spark plug to ignite mixture
Compression Ignition: Compression of the air raises its temperature to allow for automatic ignition when fuel is injected into the cylinder
Horizontally Opposed Cylinder Arrangement
Most popular reciprocating engine for smaller aircraft
Cylinder on one side “opposes” a cylinder on the other
Generally, air cooled / mounted in a horizontal position
Compact arrangement allows for a more streamlined installation, minimizing aerodynamic drag
High power-to-weight ratios
Ignition System
Provides the spark that ignites the fuel-air mixture in the cylinders
Components
Magnetos
Self-contained, engine driven unit that supplies electrical current to the spark plugs
A permanent magnet generates the electrical current
Completely independent of the airplane’s electrical system
Normally two magnetos per engine (left and right)
Spark Plugs
Deliver electric current from the magnetos to the combustion chamber to ignite the mixture
High-Tension Leads: The wires that connect the magnetos to the spark plugs
Ignition Switch: Controls the operation of the magnetos
5 positions: Off, R - Only runs R magneto, L - Only runs L magneto, Both - Runs both magnetos, and Start - Engages the starter using battery power. The starter rotates the crankshaft
The ignition system begins to fire when the crankshaft begins to turn
Operation
Normal Operation
The system begins to fire when the starter is engaged, and the crankshaft begins to turn
Initially powered by the battery
Crankshaft rotation activates the magnetos which send power to the spark plugs, producing a spark in the combustion chamber
Combustion in the chamber produces piston movement which rotates the crankshaft
Once the engine can move the pistons on its own the starter is no longer necessary
If the crankshaft is rotating, the magnetos/ignition system continues to operate
As long as the magnetos/ignition system are operating, the crankshaft continues rotating
Dual Ignition System
Two individual magnetos, separate sets of wires, and two separate spark plugs in each cylinder
Each magneto operates independently to fire one of the two spark plugs in each cylinder
Firing two spark plugs improves combustion and provides slightly higher power output
If one magneto fails, the other is unaffected
The engine will continue to run but with a slight decrease in power
The same is true if one of the two spark plugs in a cylinder fails
Induction Systems
General
Air enters through an intake, is filtered, mixed with fuel and delivered to the cylinders
Two types of induction systems
Fuel Injection: Mixes fuel/air before entry into cylinders, or injects fuel directly into cylinders
Carburetor System: Mixes the fuel and air in the carburetor before it enters the intake manifold
Carburetor System (older system)
General
Mixes the fuel and air in the carburetor before entering the intake manifold
Two categories of carburetors – Float-Type (most common) and Pressure-Type (rare)
Basic difference is delivery of fuel – pressure type delivers fuel under pressure by a pump
Float-type Carburetors
Operation
Fuel is sent from the fuel tank(s) to the carburetor float chamber
Float chamber stores & meters the fuel that will be mixed with the air and sent to the engine
At the same time, outside air enters through an air filter
The filtered air flows into the carburetor and through a venturi
A low-pressure area is created forcing fuel to flow through the discharge nozzle
The fuel/air mix and flow to the combustion chambers based on the throttle valve position
Increasing power opens the valve, decreasing closes the valve
Disadvantages
Do not function well with abrupt maneuvers
Discharge of fuel at low pressure leads to incomplete vaporization and difficulty in discharging fuel into some supercharged systems
Chief Disadvantage – Icing tendencies
Carburetor Icing
Fuel vaporization & decreased pressure in the venturi can cause a sharp drop in temperature
If water vapor in the air condenses with temperatures at/below freezing, ice can form
Carburetor icing restricts the flow of fuel-air mixture and reduces power
If enough ice builds up, the engine can stop operating
Most likely to occur at temperatures below 70o F with relative humidity greater than 80%
Fixed Pitch Propellers: First indication is a decrease in rpm, then possibly engine roughness
Constant speed propeller: First indication is a decrease in manifold pressure, but not RPM
Carburetor heat is used to combat carburetor icing
Carburetor Heat
Preheats the air before it reaches the carburetor
Primarily prevents formation of ice, but can be used to melt ice that has already formed
Decreases engine power, sometimes up to 15%
Fuel Injection System
General
Fuel is injected directly into the cylinders, or just ahead of the intake valve
Advantages
Reduction in evaporation icing, better fuel flow, faster throttle response, precise control of mixture, better fuel distribution, easier cold weather starts
Disadvantages
Difficulty in starting a hot engine, vapor locks during ground operation on hot days, problems associated with restarting an engine that quit because of fuel starvation
Components & Operation
Engine-Driven Fuel Pump: Provides fuel to the fuel-air control unit after the engine is started
Auxiliary Fuel Pump: Provides fuel to the fuel-air control unit for engine start / emergency use
Fuel-Air Control Unit: Meters fuel based on the mixture / throttle settings
Fuel Manifold (Distributor): Distributes the fuel to the individual fuel discharge nozzles
Discharge Nozzles: Inject the fuel-air mixture directly into each cylinder intake port
Fuel Pressure/Flow Indicators: Provide the pilot information regarding the fuel system
Oil Systems 											AI.II.E.K1e
Functions
Lubricates the engine’s moving parts
Cools the engine – Reduces friction and removes heat from cylinders
Provides a seal between the cylinder walls and pistons
Carries away contaminants
Two types: Wet-sump & Dry-sump
Wet-Sump System
Oil is in a sump that is part of the engine (usually at the base of the engine)
Operation
Oil pump draws oil from the sump and routes it to the engine
In some engines the rotating crankshaft splashes oil onto portions of the engine
After oil passes through the engine, it returns to the sump (generally returned by gravity)
Dry-Sump System
Oil is stored in a tank, outside of the engine, and circulated through the engine by pumps
A greater volume of oil can be supplied to the engine (suitable for large reciprocating engines)
Operation
Oil pump supplies pressure to pump oil from the external tank through the engine
Scavenge pumps return oil from various locations in the engine to the oil tank
Indications
Oil Pressure Gauge: Provides a direct indication of the oil system operation
Oil Temperature Gauge: Measures the temperature of the oil
High temps may signal a plugged line, low quantity, a blocked cooler, or defective temp gauge
Low oil temperatures may signal improper oil viscosity during cold weather operations
Cooling Systems
Types of Engine Cooling
Air Cooling (most small aircraft are air cooled)
Air flows into the engine compartment, is routed over the hottest parts of the engine and expelled through the lower, aft portion of the cowling
Liquid Cooling
Cooling liquid (usually water, ethylene glycol, or a combination of the two) is pumped around the engine to cool the hot components
Benefits: Less chance of shock cooling, ability to direct coolant to specific, critical areas
Negatives: Added weight, increased complexity and increased cost
Air Cooling
Operation
Outside air enters the engine compartment where baffles direct it to the hottest parts of the engine
Dependent on air flow so it is less effective at low speeds
Conversely, high-speed descents provide excess air and can shock cool the engine
Monitoring & Controlling Engine Temperature
Monitoring Temperature
Oil temperature gauge gives an indirect and delayed indication of rising engine temperature
Cylinder head temperature (CHT) indicates a direct / immediate cylinder temperature change
Controlling Temperature
Increase airspeed, Enrich the fuel air mixture, Reduce power, and/or Open cowl flaps
Exhaust Systems
Vents burned combustion gases overboard, provides heat for the cabin & defrosts the wind screen
Operation
Engine Exhaust
After combustion, exhaust gases are pushed out of the cylinder through the exhaust valve and travel through the exhaust manifold/piping, and muffler to the atmosphere
Cabin Heat
Outside air is ducted through a shroud around the muffler
Exiting exhaust gases heat the muffler, which in turn heats the air around the muffler
Heated air is ducted to the cabin for heat and defrost
Exhaust must be in good condition / free of cracks to ensure gases don’t enter the cabin
EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) Probe
Measures the temperature of the gases at the exhaust manifold
Temperature varies based on the ratio of fuel and air entering the cylinders and can be used for regulating the fuel-air mixture (highly accurate in indicating the proper mixture setting)
FADEC (Full Authority Digital Engine Control)
System consisting of a digital computer and ancillary components that control the engine & propeller
What it does
Optimizes Performance
Uses speed, temperature and pressure sensors to monitor the status of each cylinder
Calculates ideal pulse for each injector, and adjusts ignition timing / fuel flow as necessary
Simplifies Systems
Eliminates pilot controls for magnetos, carburetor heat, mixture, propeller, and engine priming
A single throttle is characteristic of FADEC aircraft (pilot sets throttle, computer does the rest)
Safety
Two separate and identical digital channels are incorporated for redundancy
Losing FADEC could result in loss of engine power
A backup electrical source must be available to prevent this
In many aircraft, the FADEC uses power from a separate generator connected to the engine
Propeller 											AI.II.E.K1c
General
Rotating airfoil – Subject to induced drag, stalls, and other aerodynamic principles
Engine power rotates the propeller
Rotation generates thrust similar to how a wing produces lift
The amount of thrust depends on the shape of the airfoil, the AOA, and RPM
Prop is twisted – blade angle changes from hub to tip to provide uniform lift from hub to tip
The greatest angle of incidence (highest pitch) is at the hub, smallest (lowest pitch) is at the tip
A prop that wasn’t twisted would be inefficient
As airspeed increased, the hub would have a negative AOA and the tip would be stalled
Installation
Mounted on a shaft connected to the engine
If it directly connected to the crankshaft, the propeller rpm matches crankshaft rpm
On some engines, the propeller is geared to the engine crankshaft
In this case, the propeller RPM is different than that of the engine
Ex. the Diamond DA42 is geared at a ratio of 1.69:1 (engine to prop ratio)
Fixed Pitch Propellers
Overview
Fixed blade angle
Pitch is set by the manufacturer and cannot be changed
Achieve best efficiency only at a given combination of airspeed and RPM
Not ideal for cruise or climb; performance suffers a bit in each category
Used when low weight, simplicity, and low cost are needed
Two types of fixed-pitch propellers: Climb and Cruise
Climb Propeller
Lower pitch, and therefore less drag
Less drag results in higher RPM and more horsepower capability
Increases performance during takeoffs and climbs, decreases performance during cruise
Cruise Propeller
Higher pitch, and therefore more drag
More drag results in lower RPM and less horsepower capability
Decreases performance during takeoff and climbs, increases performance during cruise
Control & Indications
Tachometer: Indicator of power
Direct indication of the engine / propeller rpm
Controlling RPM
RPM is regulated by the throttle which controls the amount of fuel-air to the engine
At a given altitude, the higher the tachometer reading, the higher the power output of the engine
Adjustable Pitch Propellers (Constant-speed propellers)
Overview
A governor adjusts propeller pitch to maintain a specific RPM
More efficient because it allows selection of the best RPM for the given phase of flight
How it Works
Once an RPM is selected, the governor adjusts the propeller blade to maintain the selected RPM
An increase in airspeed or decrease in propeller load causes the governor to increase the propeller blade angle to maintain RPM
A reduction in airspeed or increase in load causes the propeller blade to decrease
As long as the propeller blade angle is within its rpm range, a constant rpm is maintained
If it reaches a pitch stop, rpm will increase / decrease (like a fixed pitch prop)
Controls & Indications
Controls
Throttle controls power output
Propeller control regulates rpm through the governor (rpm is shown on the tachometer)
Manifold Pressure Gauge
Indicates power, and controlled by the throttle
At a constant RPM / altitude, power is directly related to the fuel-air mixture
Increased throttle = increased fuel/air = increased manifold pressure (and vice versa)
Adjusting Power & RPM
Decreasing: Reduce manifold pressure, then RPM
Lower = Left to right (Throttle then Prop)
If rpm is reduced first, manifold pressure increases and could exceed engine tolerances
Increasing: Increase RPM, then manifold pressure
Raise = Right to left (Prop then throttle)
Landing Gear & Brakes (Hydraulics) 						AI.II.E.K1d, AI.II.E.K1e
Landing Gear
Overview
Principal support of the aircraft
Types: Wheels, floats for water, skis for snow, etc.
Generally, Two main wheels, one on either side of the fuselage, and a third wheel at the front or rear
Conventional (tailwheel) – When the third wheel is positioned at the rear
Tricycle – When the third wheel is positioned at the nose
Fixed and Retractable Landing Gear
Fixed – Always remains extended. Advantages: Simplicity and low maintenance
Retractable – Streamlines the airplane / reduces drag
Tricycle Landing Gear
Advantages:
Allows more forceful brake application without causing the aircraft to nose over
Permits better forward visibility during takeoff, landing, and taxiing
Tends to prevent ground loop since the center of gravity is forward of the main wheels
Nosewheel
Steerable nosewheels are linked to the rudders by cables or rods
Castering nosewheels are free to swivel
In either case, steering is done with rudder pedals (and brake application, if needed)
Tailwheel Landing Gear
Two main wheels attached to the airframe, ahead of the center of gravity
Support most of the weight of the structure
Tailwheel at the very back of the fuselage provides a third point of support
Advantages:
Ground clearance for a larger propeller
More desirable for operations on unimproved fields
Disadvantages:
Directional control is more difficult on the ground with the CG behind the main gear
Diminished forward visibility when the tailwheel is on or near the ground
Hydraulics
Standard Components:
Reservoir
Pump
Filter
Selector Valve and Relief Valve
Actuator or servo
Operation
Hydraulic fluid is pumped from the reservoir through a filter to an actuator or servo
Servo – cylinder with a piston inside used to move a system or flight control
Servos can be single- or double-acting
Fluid can be applied to one or both sides
Selector valve allows the fluid direction to be controlled
Relief valve provides an outlet for the system in case of excessive fluid pressure
Brakes
Located on the main wheels
Applied by either a hand control or foot pedal (most common)
Foot pedals operate independently and allow for differential braking
Differential braking can supplement steering
Fuel Systems 											AI.II.E.K1e
Provides uninterrupted, clean fuel from the tanks to the engine – fuel must be available under all conditions
Types
Gravity Feed System
Gravity transfers fuel from the tank(s) to the engine(s)
Many high wing aircraft
Fuel-Pump System
Fuel pumps transfer the fuel to the engine
Two fuel pumps per engine
Engine driven pump – Primary fuel pump
Operates when the engine is operating
Electrically-driven auxiliary pump – For engine start and backup to the main pump
Fuel Tank & Strainer
Fuel Tank(s)
Normally located in the wings
Vented to maintain atmospheric pressure in tank
Include an overflow drain
Fuel can expand and not damage the tank
Strainer
After leaving the fuel tank, fuel passes through a strainer that removes moisture / sediment
Contaminants are heavier than aviation fuel and settle at the bottom of the strainer
Strainer should be drained before each flight
Water is the principal fuel contaminant
In cold weather it can freeze and block fuel lines
In warm weather it can flow into the carburetor and stop the engine
If water is present, drain until there is no evidence of water
Indicated by cloudy fuel, or by the clear separation of water from the fuel
Fuel Selectors (pictured)
Allows selection of fuel from various tanks, if installed
Common settings include, Left, Right, Both, Off
Both is not an option on all aircraft (swap between L / R)
Fuel Primer (assists with engine start)
Draws fuel from the tanks to vaporize directly into the cylinders prior to starting the engine
Fuel Gauges
Quantity Gauge(s) - Indicate amount of fuel in each tank
Certification rules only require accuracy in fuel gauges when they read “empty”
Always visually check the fuel level and compare it to the tank quantity indications
Pressure Gauge
If a fuel pump is installed, a fuel pressure gauge is included with it
Indicates the pressure in the fuel lines
Electrical Systems 										AI.II.E.K1f
General
Most aircraft are equipped with either a 14 or 28-volt direct current (DC) electrical system
A basic electrical system consists of the following:
Alternator/generator
Battery
Master/battery switch
Alternator/generator switch
Bus bar, fuses, and/or circuit breakers
Voltage regulator
Ammeter/loadmeter
Electrical wiring
Power Generation
Alternator or Generator supplies electric current to the electrical system and maintain a sufficient charge in the battery
Alternators have several advantages over generators
Can operate entire electrical system, even at low engine RPM
Electrical output is more constant through a wide range of engine speeds
Voltage Regulator (contained in most systems)
Controls the rate of charge to the battery by stabilizing generator / alternator output
The generator / alternator voltage should be higher than the battery voltage
The difference in voltage keeps the battery charged
Power Storage
Power is stored in batteries, primarily the main battery
Electrical power for engine start, and limited power in case of alternator / generator failure
Power Distribution (bus bars)
A bus bar is used to connect the main electrical system to the equipment using electricity
Distributes power from the alternator / generator / battery to the electrical components
Protection
Fuses or circuit breakers protect the circuits and equipment from electrical overload
Circuit breakers can be manually reset, rather than replaced (like a fuse), if an overload occurs
Indications
Ammeter
Monitors the performance of the electrical system
Indications
Zero in the center, negative to L, positive to R
Positive: shows battery charge rate
Negative: shows battery discharge rate
Full scale deflection (+ or -) indicates a malfunction
Not all aircraft have an ammeter – may just have a warning light to indicate a malfunction
Loadmeter
Shows load on alternator/generator (% of load on the system)
With all components off it reflects on the amount of charge demanded by the battery
Avionics 												AI.II.E.K1g
Avionics can vary greatly, especially with the advent and large-scale acceptance of glass displays
Electronic instrument displays, GPS’s, autopilots, radios, traditional instruments (vacuum, gyro, etc.)
G1000, Avidyne, etc.
Be familiar with the avionics displays and instruments associated with your aircraft and their use
Manage automation
Do not become distracted with the seemingly unlimited functionality of glass flight decks
Reference the avionics user manual(s)
Autopilot
Automatic flight control system that keeps an aircraft in level flight or on a set course
Can be directed by the pilot or coupled to a radio navigation signal
Reduces physical and mental demands on a pilot and increases safety
Autopilots vary greatly in complexity
The simplest systems use gyroscopic attitude indicators and magnetic compasses to control servos connected to the flight control system
The number and location of the servos depends on the complexity of the system
A single-axis autopilot controls the plane about the longitudinal axis (servo moves the ailerons)
A three-axis autopilot controls the aircraft about the longitudinal, lateral, and vertical axes
Three different servos actuate ailerons, elevator, and rudder
More advanced systems often include a vertical speed and/or indicated airspeed hold mode
Autopilots can be coupled to navigational aids through a flight director
Work with inertial navigation systems, GPS, and flight computers to control the aircraft
Most systems incorporate a disconnect to disengage the system automatically or manually
Allows the pilot to override an autopilot malfunction
Because avionics systems differ widely in their operation, refer to the operating instructions
Flight Instruments 										AI.II.E.K1h
Pitot-Static Flight Instruments
Airspeed Indicator, Altimeter, & Vertical Speed Indicator
How it Works
Utilizes the static and pitot pressure from the motion of the aircraft through the air
Static Pressure (still pressure) is measured at a flush static port where air is not disturbed
Pitot Pressure (impact pressure) is measured through a pitot tube pointed into the relative wind
The Pitot Tube connects to the Airspeed Indicator; the Static Port connects to all 3 instruments
Sensitive Altimeter
Measures absolute pressure of the ambient air, displays it as feet above selected pressure level
Principle of Operation
Static air pressure tries to compress aneroid wafers while natural springiness tries to expand them
Compression and expansion move gears/linkages to change the altitude displayed
Adjustable barometric scale (Kollsman window)
Allows you to set the reference pressure from which the altitude is measured
1” Hg is equal to 1,000’
Pressure Alt = 29.92” Hg
Indicated Alt = local altimeter setting
Errors (Mechanical and Inherent)
Nonstandard Temperature
Warmer than standard air is less dense, pressure levels are farther apart
True altitude > Indicated altitude
Colder than standard air is denser, pressure levels are closer together
True altitude < Indicated altitude
Nonstandard Pressure
High pressure to Low pressure
As pressure decreases, the altimeter registers it as a climb
Pilot descends to maintain altitude
True altitude < Indicated altitude
The opposite applies from Low pressure to High pressure – True alt > Indicated alt
REMEMBER: From hot to cold, or high to low, look out below!
Vertical Speed Indicator
Differential pressure instrument
Operation
Diaphragm and casing are connected to static pressure
Diaphragm is directly connected
Case has a delayed connection
During a climb / descent, the diaphragm expands / contracts immediately, while pressure in the case remains the same for a short period
The difference in pressure is displayed as rate of climb
Airspeed Indicator
Differential pressure gauge indicating the difference between pitot and static pressure
Operation
Diaphragm receives pressure from the pitot tube
Instrument case receives pressure from static port
Increasing pitot pressure / decreasing static pressure expands the diaphragm and vice versa
Gearing indicates changes in airspeed
Electronic Flight Display
General
Same information (airspeed, altitude, VSI) is displayed, but via new methods
Air Data Computer (ADC)
Information is still received from pitot / static inputs, but the processing is different
ADC takes the pitot / static inputs and displays airspeed, altitude, VSI
No diaphragms, gearing, linkages
Gyroscopic System
Attitude Indicator, Heading Indicator, Turn Coordinator
How it Works
Heavy, fast spinning wheel/rotor mounted to utilize characteristics of spin
The 2 characteristics of gyroscopes: Rigidity and Precession
Rigidity: Gyro remains in a fixed position in the plane in which it is spinning
Attitude/Heading instruments operate on the principle of rigidity
Precession: Any applied force is felt 90o from that point in the direction of rotation
Turn indicators/coordinators (rate instruments) operate on the principle of precession
Power Sources
Electrical
Pneumatic (vacuum) – Driven by jet of air impinging on buckets in the outside of the wheel
Venturi Tube
Air flows through venturi tubes mounted on the outside of the aircraft
The constricted part of the tube (low pressure) creates a suction for the instruments
Wet-Type Vacuum
Steel vane air pumps are used to evacuate the instrument cases
The vanes in the pumps are lubricated with oil which is discharged with the air
Dry-Air Pump
At high altitudes, more air is needed in the instruments as the air is less dense
Air pumps that do not mix oil with the discharge air are used in high flying
Vanes are made of a special formulation of carbon which do not need lubricating
Pressure
2 dry pumps (one per engine) with a regulator to maintain desired pressure
Inline filters remove contamination, from there into a manifold check valve
If either engine / pump fails, the check valve isolates the bad side / uses the good side
After driving the gyros, air is exhausted from the case
Gyro pressure gauge measures the pressure drop across the instruments
Attitude Indicator
Operation
Mounted in a horizontal plane
Double gimbal - allows display of pitch and roll
Horizon disk is attached to the gimbals
Remains in the same plane as the gyro and the plane pitches / rolls about it
Mini aircraft appears to be flying relative to the horizon
Errors
Free from most errors, but…
May be a slight nose-up indication during a rapid acceleration and vice versa
Possibility of a small bank angle and pitch error after a 180o turn
Tiny amounts of friction over time can cause precession / tilting – erection mechanism (pull the knob) returns the gyro to the proper position
Heading Indicator
Gyro turns on a vertical plane sensing rotation about the plane’s vertical axis
Compass is used to set the appropriate heading – Rigidity causes it to maintain this heading
Precession causes heading to drift & Earth rotates 15o an hour
Precession + Earth’s rotation means heading should be checked & reset every 15 min
Turn Indicators
General
Two types: Turn-and-slip, and Turn coordinators
Both instruments indicate turn direction and quality of turn (coordination)
Turn-and-slip shows direction and rate of turn
Turn coordinator (canted gyro) shows direction and rate of turn and rate of roll
Backup source of bank information if the attitude indicator fails
Operation
Gyro is powered by air or an electric motor
Small gyro mounted in a single gimbal
Yawing produces a force in the horizontal plane
Precession causes any yawing forces to tilt the gyro to the left or right
A spring works to maintain the center position
Turn-and-Slip Indicator
Direction and rate of turn is displayed by the turn needle as yawing forces tilt the gyro
Turn Coordinator (more common in GA aircraft)
Very similar to the turn-and-slip but gimbal is canted
Gyro can sense both rate of roll as well as rate of turn
A rapid roll rate causes the mini aircraft to bank more steeply than a slow roll rate
Used to establish and maintain a standard-rate turn (3o per second)
Align the wing of the mini aircraft with the turn index
Electronic Flight Display
Gyroscopic instruments replaced with AHRS (attitude and heading reference system)
AHRS
Spinning gyros are replaced with solid-state laser systems that do not tumble
Heading information comes from a magnetometer that senses earth’s lines of magnetic flux
All the information is processed and then sent to the PFD to be displayed
Environmental Systems 									AI.II.E.K1i
Heating
Many different types of heating systems (Exhaust, Fuel Fired, Combustion, Bleed Air)
Exhaust Heating Systems – Simplest type of heating system, used on most light aircraft
Outside air is ducted through a shroud around the muffler
Muffler is heated by exiting exhaust gases, and in turn heats the air around the muffler
Heated air is ducted to the cabin for heat and defrost
Exhaust must be in good condition / free of cracks to ensure gases don’t enter the cabin
Fuel Fired Heaters – A small mounted or portable space-heating device
Fuel is brough to the heater’s combustion chamber
A fan blows air into the chamber, and an ignition device ignites the fuel-air mixture
Air is ducted around the combustion chamber’s outer surface
A second fan blows the warm air into tubing which takes it to the cabin
Combustion Heater Systems – Often used to heat larger, more expensive aircraft
Operation
Burns the aircraft’s fuel in a combustion chamber or tube to develop heat
Air flowing around the tube is heated and ducted to the cabin
Exhaust exits through the heater’s exhaust pipe
System is activated by the thermostat (fuel is turned on/off based on cabin temperature)
Very Safe
Overheat switch – shuts off fuel in the case of a malfunction
Unlikely for carbon monoxide poisoning to occur
Low pressure in the combustion tube, high pressure outside the combustion tube
If there were a leak, high-pressure air would flow into the chamber / exit the exhaust
Bleed Air Heating Systems – Used on turbine-engine aircraft
Extremely hot, compressed engine bleed air is ducted into a chamber where it is mixed with ambient / re-circulated air to cool it to a useable temperature, and then is ducted into the cabin
Safety Features
Temperature sensors prevent excessive heat from entering the cabin
Check valves prevent losing bleed air during engine start and when full power is required
Engine sensors eliminate the bleed system if the engine becomes inoperative
Pressurization
General
Aircraft are flown at high altitudes for two reasons:
More efficient - Less fuel consumed for a given airspeed
Bad weather and turbulence may be avoided by flying above the storms
Pressurization is necessary to protect occupants from threats of high altitudes
How it Works
The cabin, flight and baggage compartments are a sealed unit capable of containing air under a higher pressure than the outside atmospheric pressure (Differential Pressure)
Differential Pressure –difference between the pressure acting on one side of a wall and the pressure acting on the other side of the wall (cabin pressure vs atmospheric pressure)
Atmospheric air is compressed. Different aircraft compress the air in in different ways:
Turbine aircraft – bleed air from the engine compressor is used to pressurize the cabin
Older turbine aircraft – superchargers are used to pump air into the sealed fuselage
Piston aircraft – Air from the turbocharger through a sonic venturi (flow limiter)
Compressed air is conditioned / sent to the cabin
Air exits the fuselage through an outflow valve
Cabin Pressure Control System
Cabin Pressure Regulator – controls cabin pressure
Outflow Valve
Air exits the fuselage through the outflow valve
Allows for a constant inflow of air, while maintaining the proper differential pressure
Cabin Air Pressure Safety Valve
Combination of a pressure relief, vacuum relief, and dump valve
Pressure relief valve prevents cabin pressure from exceeding maximum differential pressure
Vacuum relief valve prevents ambient pressure from exceeding cabin pressure
Dump valve dumps the cabin air into the atmosphere (emergency situations)
Instruments
Cabin Differential Pressure Gauge – Indicates the difference between inside & outside pressure
Cabin Altimeter – Shows the altitude inside the airplane
Differential pressure gauge and cabin altimeter can be combined into one instrument
Cabin Rate of Climb/Descent – Shows rate the cabin altitude is changing during
Deice & Anti-Ice Systems 									AI.II.E.K1j
Overview
Anti-ice equipment is designed to prevent the formation of ice
Deice equipment is designed to remove ice once it has formed
Protect numerous parts of the aircraft – leading edge of wing and tail, pitot / static ports, fuel tank vents, stall warning devices, windshields, propeller blades
Airfoil
Deicing Boots – Inflatable boots consisting of a rubber sheet bonded to the leading edge of the wing (pictured, top right)
Operation
Engine-driven pump, or engine bleed air, inflates the rubber boots breaking up the ice
Single cycle operation, or at automatic, timed intervals
Instruments – Suction and pneumatic pressure gauges
Thermal Anti-Ice System – Heat driven system
Hot air is directed from the engine compressor to the leading-edge surfaces to prevent ice
Should be activated prior to entering icing conditions
Weeping Wing (pictured, bottom right)
Antifreeze solution is pumped to the leading edge of the wings and weeps through small holes
Capable of deice and anti-ice
Antifreeze chemically breaks down the bond between the ice and airframe, allowing aerodynamic forces to remove the ice
Windscreen
Alcohol - Flow of alcohol is directed to the windscreen
Used early enough, prevents ice buildup on the windscreen
Electric Heat
Wires or other conductive material imbedded in the windscreen
Operated by a switch in the flight deck
Propeller
Alcohol - Used to prevent ice forming on the propeller’s leading edge
Released from nozzles, centrifugal force distributes it on props
Grooves in propeller boots to help direct the flow of alcohol
Electric Heat – Anti-ice boots with electrical wires to heat the props
Oxygen Systems 										AI.II.E.K1l
Fixed vs Portable Systems
Most high-altitude aircraft come with a fixed installation
Otherwise, portable is required – Often consists of a container, regulator, mask outlet, pressure gauge
Usually stored between 1,800-2,200 psi – pressure will drop with drops in ambient temperature
High pressure containers should be marked with the psi tolerance before filling
Masks & Cannulas
Masks
Various designs
Ensure properly fitted with minimum leakage and a microphone
Can allow oxygen to be delivered under pressure (see pressure-demand system below)
Passenger mask can be a simple rubber cup (like airlines)
Cannula (pictured right)
Ergonomic piece of plastic tubing running under the nose to administer oxygen
More comfortable than a mask but not as efficient at delivering oxygen
Current regs require aircraft with O2 systems and certified > 18,000’ to have masks instead of cannulas
Types of Oxygen Systems
Continuous Flow (pictured right, blue mask)
Usually provided for passengers
Mix of oxygen and ambient air
Typically has a reservoir bag that collects oxygen from the system while the user is exhaling
Diluter Demand (useable to 40,000’)
Supplies oxygen only when the user inhales through the mask
Can provide 100% oxygen or mix the cabin air and oxygen based on the user’s setting
Pressure Demand (some regulators are safe above 40,000’)
Oxygen is supplied under pressure at cabin altitudes above 34,000’
Allows the user’s lungs to be pressurized with oxygen
Electric Pulse-Demand
Conserves oxygen, reducing oxygen needed by 50-85% compared to continuous flow systems
Detect the user’s inhalation and provides oxygen during the initial portion of inhalation
Most have an internal barometer to automatically increase the amount of oxygen as altitude increases
Aviator’s Breathing Oxygen (Introduction to Aviation Physiology document)
Min purity requirement of 99.5%, may not contain more than 0.005 mg of water vapor per liter
Use Aviator’s oxygen - Different requirements exist for different types of oxygen and their uses
Care and Storage of High-Pressure Oxygen Bottles
If required, portable oxygen equipment must be accessible in flight
Be aware of the danger of fire when using oxygen
Thoroughly inspect/test all oxygen equipment before flight. Accomplish periodic inspections/servicing
Autopilot
Overview
Automatic flight control system to keep an aircraft in level flight or on a set course
Amount of automation varies based on the system – Reference POH/Operator’s Manual
Reduces pilot physical and mental demands
RM: Managing & Monitoring Automation							AI.II.E.R3
Managing: Automation is only as good as the inputs it’s given
Understand the system’s capabilities & ensure proper set up and programming
Monitoring: Follow along with the automation to ensure it’s doing what you intend, when you intend it
RM: Abnormalities & Failures 							AI.II.E.K2, AI.II.E.R1
Automated Systems 										AI.II.E.R3
Monitor indications - be familiar with expected operation, ranges & limitations & warning annunciations
Reference the POH and/or take action if indications are out of range
Recognizing Malfunctions or Failures
Specific to the aircraft and its systems (EFD warnings, caution/warning lights, gauge indications, etc.)
Managing a Failure (Airborne): M - A - T - L  							AI.II.E.R2
Maintain Aircraft Control
Fly the airplane - Get to a safe flight state (straight-and-level, etc.)
Trim and turn on automation, if possible
Maintain control throughout the malfunction
Analyze the Situation
Indications, lights, sounds, visual (i.e., smoke, leaks, fire, etc.), smells, etc.
Use all available information to determine the issue
Take Proper Action
Apply any memory items
Use the appropriate checklist from the POH
Land, as conditions require/permit
Based on the emergency, decide on a landing area (divert, field, ditching, etc.)
This may have to occur in conjunction with the checklist(s)
Managing a Failure (On the Ground)
Remain on the ground
Analyze the situation: Same as above
Take proper action: Run the appropriate checklist(s)
Decide whether to continue the flight, return to park, or evacuate
RM: Flight Instruction (Unfamiliar Aircraft, Systems & Avionics) 			AI.II.E.R4
Just because it’s legal, doesn’t mean it’s safe
Ensure proficiency in any aircraft you’re flying, let alone instructing in
Important for safety as well as the learner’s time, money, and education
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points
