Payload: Weight of the occupants, cargo and baggage
Standard Weights: Established weights for numerous items in weight and balance computations
Station: A location in the aircraft identified by a number designating its distance from the datum
Unusable Fuel: Fuel in the tanks that cannot be safely used in flight or drained on the ground
Usable Fuel: Fuel in the tanks that can be used for flight
Useful Load: Basic empty weight subtracted from the maximum allowable gross weight
Weight & Balance Control
The pilot is responsible
Aircraft owner/operator should ensure up to date information is available to the pilot
Determining Weight and Balance 								AI.II.F.K4
CG = Total Moment divided by Total Weight
RM: Weight Change and/or CG Shift (RM: Shifting, adding, and removing weight) 		AI.II.F.R6
Operating Limitations are in Chapter 2 of the POH
Limitations establish the boundaries for which the airplane can be safely operated
Adverse Effects
Attempting to takeoff or land without enough runway
Attempting to clear an obstacle that the airplane performance will not support
Not having enough fuel to reach the airport of intended landing
Using the wrong type of fuel
Exceeding the structural/aerodynamic limits (overweight or outside CG limits)
Exceeding the maximum crosswind component
standard_lessons.full_text:
II.F. Performance & Limitations
Introduction
How
Performance
Ability of an aircraft to accomplish certain things that make it useful for a certain purpose
Factors most affected by performance are:
TO/LDG distance, climb rate/ceiling, payload, range, speed, maneuverability, stability, fuel economy
Aircraft and powerplant design & characteristics dictate available performance
Manufacturer match aerodynamic configuration with a powerplant for the specific design conditions
POH charts and information are used to measure performance based on the specific conditions
Performance Factors
Atmospheric Conditions 									AI.II.F.K2a
Atmospheric Pressure
Under standard conditions at sea level, the average pressure is approx. 14.7 lbs. per sq. in
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded
Air density effects performance: As density increases, performance increases and vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)?
Barometric Pressure, Altitude, Temperature, and Humidity
Density Varies:
Directly with Pressure - As pressure increases, density increases & vice versa
Inversely with Altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases & vice versa
Inversely with Temperature – As temp increases, density decreases & vice versa
Inversely with Humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases & vice versa
For a given volume of atmospheric air, as humidity increases some of the dry air is replaced by water vapor. The molecular weight of dry air is about 29 grams/mol, while the molecular weight of water vapor (H20) is about 18 grams/mol (Grams/mol = Molar mass). As the proportion of water in the atmosphere (humidity) increases, the density (weight/volume) of the air decreases.
How it affects Performance
As the air becomes less dense, it reduces:
Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is being moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils
RM: Pilot Technique & Airplane Configuration 			AI.II.F.K2b, AI.II.F.K2c, AI.II.F.R3
(RM: Difference between calculated & actual performance)
Performance is based on specific aircraft configuration, procedures, airspeeds, etc.
Any technique or configuration that differs from POH criteria will change (likely reduce) performance
Airport Environment 										AI.II.F.K2d
Airport Runways & Layout
Runway Surface (paved, grass, dirt, gravel, etc.)
Any surface that is not hard and smooth increases ground roll
Braking Effectiveness
Soft surfaces slow an aircraft much faster than smooth and slick surfaces
Wet runways reduce braking effectiveness and can result in hydroplaning
Runway Gradient: The change in height over the length of the runway, expressed as a percentage
Runways available based on wind conditions
Surrounding Terrain & Factors (Obstacles, towers, buildings, etc.)
Can the aircraft clear the obstacles based on the specific conditions?
Is a max angle versus max rate of climb required
Are there specific noise abatement or climb rate procedures requiring specific performance
Loading and Weight & Balance								AI.II.F.K2e
Weight & Flight Performance
Added weight reduces aircraft performance
Manufacturer’s limit maximum weights to ensure aircraft performance / structural abilities
Effects of increased weight
Higher takeoff speed and longer takeoff run
Reduced rate and angle of climb & Lower maximum altitude
Slower cruise speed and reduced range, and increased fuel consumption
Reduced maneuverability
Higher stall speed
Higher approach speed and longer landing roll
Excessive weight on the nose / tail wheel
RM: Effects of Overloading (RM: Exceeding weight limits) 				AI.II.F.R4
Degraded climb performance, may not even be able to takeoff, inability to reach max altitude
Overheating during climbs, added wear on engine parts
Overstressing the aircraft
RM: Weight and Structure (RM: Exceeding weight limits) 				AI.II.F.R4
Structural failures from overloading are often progressive making it difficult to detect/repair
Airworthiness requirements require the aircraft withstand a specific load factor (3.8 Gs - Normal)
Any overload is amplified if the aircraft is stressed to these G limits
Ex. A 200 lb. overload imposes a potential structural overload of 740 lbs.
Stability & Controllability
Forward Loading
Problems controlling and raising the nose, especially at slow airspeeds (takeoff and landing)
“Heavier” and consequently slower than the same airplane with a further aft CG
Higher stall speed
More controllable in a stall
Aft loading
Very light control forces (easier to overstress)
“Lighter” and consequently faster than the same airplane with a more forward CG
Lower stall speed
Less controllable in a stall/spin
Serious effect upon longitudinal stability
The CG and Lateral Loading
Unbalanced loading can have adverse effects
Trim, or maintain constant control pressure
Increases drag, decreases efficiency
RM: Operating outside of CG limits can result in control difficulties 			AI.II.F.R5
Extremely nose or tail heavy – may not have control authority
Aerodynamics 											AI.II.F.K5
Straight-and-Level
To maintain straight-and-level, lift must equal weight and thrust must equal drag
Parasitic drag dominates at high speed, induced drag at low speed (pictured, top right)
Max level flight speed is obtained when power required equals max power/thrust available (lower right picture)
Min level flight speed is not defined by thrust/power requirements since stall occurs first (lower right picture)
Climb Performance
Kinetic Energy (KE): Energy of Speed
Directly proportional to the square of airspeed
m = mass, v = velocity
Potential Energy (PE): Stored Energy, Altitude
Directly proportional to the altitude
(m = mass, g = gravity, h = height)
Power & Thrust
Thrust: Force or pressure exerted on an object (pounds or newtons)
Power: Measurement of the rate of performing work or transferring energy (horsepower or kilowatts)
The motion (KE and PE) a force (thrust) creates when exerted on an object over a period of time
Positive climb performance occurs when an aircraft gains PE by increasing altitude
Two factors contribute to gaining altitude:
Factor One: Aircraft uses excess power above what’s required to maintain level flight
Factor Two: Aircraft converts airspeed (KE) to altitude (PE)
Angle of Climb (AOC)
Comparison of altitude gained relative to distance traveled
VX is used for max AOC performance
Max AOC occurs at the airspeed and AOA combination resulting in maximum excess thrust
This combination differs amongst aircraft types
Jet: Approximately L/DMAX
Propeller Plane: Below L/DMAX and just above stall speed
Rate of Climb (ROC)
Comparison of altitude gained relative to the time needed to reach that altitude (VY)
Max ROC occurs at the airspeed and AOA combination resulting in maximum excess power
Combination differs amongst aircraft types
Jet: Airspeed > L/DMAX and AOA < L/DMAX AOA
Propeller Plane: Airspeed and AOA combination close to L/DMAX
Climb Performance Factors
Weight, altitude, & configuration affect excess thrust/power and therefore climb performance
Increased weight/altitude and lowering the flaps/gear decrease excess thrust & power
Weight
Added weight means the aircraft must fly at a higher AOA to maintain a given altitude & speed
Increases drag requiring additional thrust
Additional thrust = less reserve thrust to climb
Altitude (pictured, right)
Climb performance diminishes with altitude
Increases power required, decreases power available
As altitude increases, max AOC/ROC & min/max level flight speeds converge at the absolute ceiling
At the absolute ceiling, there is no excess power and only one speed allows level flight
Range Performance
The ability to convert fuel into flying distance
Range vs Endurance
Range involves the consideration of flying distance
Endurance involves the consideration of flying time
Maximum Endurance (Time)
If max endurance is desired, the flight condition must provide minimum fuel flow (B in the chart)
Point A (low speed, high fuel flow) is takeoff and climb
As speed increases, power & fuel requirements decrease due to aerodynamic factors up to Point B
Beyond Point B, you must pay to go faster (more speed requires more power at the cost of fuel)
Maximum Range (Distance)
Costs aside, max range is the condition providing max NM per pound of fuel (or specific range)
Specific Range = NM / pounds of fuel
Ex: Specific range of 1.89 means for every pound of fuel, the aircraft could fly 1.89 miles
Obtained at L/DMAX and varies with gross weight, altitude, and configuration
As fuel burns gross weight changes, therefore optimum altitude, airspeed, & power changes
L/DMAX occurs at a specific AOA & lift coefficient, irrespective of weight
Changes in weight alter the specific airspeed and power required to attain L/DMAX
To maintain maximum range, optimum conditions must be maintained
Headwinds & Tailwinds
Theories say that speeding up in a headwind & slowing in a tailwind helps achieve max range
May be true in many cases, but there are many variables to every situation – no catch all rule
Reciprocating engines experience little, if any, variation in specific range up to absolute altitude
Performance Charts 										AI.II.F.K1
Airplane performance is found in Section 5 of the POH (Performance)
Using the performance charts, and the accompanying instructions, we can calculate
Cruise Performance
Stall Speeds based on airplane configuration
Wind Components (Crosswind and Headwind)
Takeoff Distance and Landing Distance
Climb Performance (In cruise and takeoff configurations as well as Balked Landing)
True Airspeed
Maximum Flight Duration (Pressure Altitude is combined with RPM to find % bhp, KTAS, GPH)
To make use of these charts we need to know the Pressure Altitude (PA)
PA: The altitude indicated when the altimeter setting window is set to 29.92
PA = 1,000 (29.92-Current Altimeter Setting) + Elevation
Ex. Altimeter=30.42, Elevation=808, so PA = 308’
From Pressure Altitude we can compute Density Altitude (DA)
DA: PA corrected for non-standard temperature (Directly related to airplane performance)
DA = 120(Current Temperature – ISA temperature) + PA  (estimate of DA, it’s not exact)
EX: Temp = 23oC and PA = 308’, so DA = 1,268’
Determining the Required Performance is Attainable
Use the performance charts and relate them to the airport information (runway lengths, etc.)
The charts will provide performance for all phases of flight
Remember, the charts don’t make allowance for pilot proficiency or mechanical deterioration
If conditions change, recalculate performance
RM: Inaccuracies (RM: Use of performance charts, tables, and data) 			AI.II.F.R1
Ensure you are using the proper chart
Many charts are imprecise, requiring you follow numerous small, detailed lines through various charts
Be as accurate as possible, double check and verify the performance information makes sense
RM: Calculated versus Actual Performance 						AI.II.F.R3
Calculated performance is based on the POH chart assumptions (configuration, airspeeds, etc.)
Anything different leads to different (generally, reduced) actual performance
Be conservative in performance calculations and precise in flying/operating procedures
Weight & Balance
Terms 												AI.II.F.K3
Reference Datum (RD): Imaginary vertical plane or line from which all measurements of arm are taken
Center of Gravity (CG): Point at which an airplane would balance if it were suspended at that point
Arm: Horizontal distance in inches from the reference datum line to the CG of an item
Basic Empty Weight: Weight of the airplane, optional equipment, unusable fuel, full operating fluids
CG Limits: Specified forward and aft points within which the CG must be located during the flight
Maximum Landing Weight: Greatest weight that an aircraft is normally allowed to have at landing
Maximum Ramp Weight: Total permitted weight of a loaded aircraft, including all fuel
Maximum Takeoff Weight: Maximum allowable weight for takeoff
Maximum Zero Fuel Weight: Maximum weight, exclusive of usable fuel
Moment: Product of the weight of an item multiplied by its arm - expressed in pound-inches
Moment Index: A moment divided by a constant such as 100, 1,000 or 10,000 (simplifies calculations)
Payload: Weight of the occupants, cargo and baggage
Standard Weights: Established weights for numerous items in weight and balance computations
Gas – 6lbs; Jet Fuel – 6.8 lbs.; Oil – 7.5 lbs.; Water – 8.35 lbs. (All per gallon)
Station: A location in the aircraft identified by a number designating its distance from the datum
Unusable Fuel: Fuel in the tanks that cannot be safely used in flight or drained on the ground
Usable Fuel: Fuel in the tanks that can be used for flight
Useful Load: Basic empty weight subtracted from the maximum allowable gross weight
Weight & Balance Control
The pilot is responsible
14 CFR Part 23.2100 requires establishment of ranges of weights and CGs within which aircraft may be safely operated - The manufacturer provides this information in the POH/AFM
Part 91.9 requires the PIC to comply with the operating limitations in the approved AFM
Aircraft owner/operator should ensure up to date information is available to the pilot
Determining Weight and Balance 								AI.II.F.K4
CG = Total Moment divided by Total Weight
Begin with the empty weight and make a list of everything that will be loaded in the airplane
Calculate the Moment of each item, then calculate the CG – (Total Moment/Total Weight)
RM: Weight Change and/or CG Shift (RM: Shifting, adding, and removing weight) 		AI.II.F.R6
Shifting Weight – If you know 3 of the components, you can solve for the 4th
Adding or Removing Weight – Solve for the missing component
RM: Exceeding Limitations 									AI.II.F.R2
Operating Limitations are in Chapter 2 of the POH
Limitations establish the boundaries for which the airplane can be safely operated
Adverse Effects
Attempting to takeoff or land without enough runway
Attempting to clear an obstacle that the airplane performance will not support
Not having enough fuel to reach the airport of intended landing
Using the wrong type of fuel
Exceeding the structural/aerodynamic limits (overweight or outside CG limits)
Exceeding the maximum crosswind component
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: II.G. National Airspace System
Introduction
How
Digital VFR Charts (to show airspace examples)
Class E Airspace 										AI.II.G.K1
Controlled airspace not designated A, B, C, or D
Operating Rules & Pilot/Equipment Requirements
Transponder Requirements (91.215)
At/above 10,000’ MSL in the contiguous 48 states & D.C., excluding airspace below 2,500’ AGL
Within 30 miles of class B primary airport, < 10,000’ MSL
Within/above all Class C airspace, up to 10,000’ MSL
Within 10 miles of certain designated airports
Excluding airspace outside Class D surface area / < 1,200’ AGL
Flying into, within, or across the ADIZ
ADS-B Requirements (91.225(d))
≥ 10,000’ MSL excluding at and below 2,500’ AGL
≥ 3,000’ MSL over Gulf of Mexico within 12 nm of the coast
Airspeeds Limits (91.117)
250 knots below 10,000’ MSL
200 kts below 2,500’ AGL within 4 nm of class C, D apt
200 knots underlying Class B/VFR corridor through B
Pilot Qualifications: Student pilot
ATC Services
VFR: No comm requirements, can request traffic advisories
IFR: ATC communication is required
Vertical Limits
Unless designated lower, 14,500’ to 17,999’ MSL over:
Contiguous 48 states including up to 12 miles off the coast
District of Columbia and Alaska
Extends from the surface or designated altitude to the overlying/adjacent controlled airspace
Segments of Class E Airspace
Class E and the Low Altitude Airway System
Airways: 1,200’ AGL up to, but not including, 18,000’ MSL
Normally 8 nm wide (4 nm each side of the centerline)
Class E and Airports
Extension to a Surface Area
Controlled airspace for IFR traffic transitioning between enroute / airport environments
When needed for IFR control purposes
Enroute Domestic Areas - Provide IFR ATC services where the Airway System is inadequate
Offshore Airspace Areas - Provide controlled airspace beyond 12 miles from the coast
Class D Airspace 										AI.II.G.K1
Definition
Normally surface to 2,500’ above field elevation / 4 nm radius
Part time control tower (Class E when closed)
Configured to the needs/instrument procedures of the area
Operating Rules and Pilot/Equipment Requirements
Pilot Certification - No specific certification required
Equipment - Two-way radio
Class C Airspace 										AI.II.G.K1
Definition
Surface to 4,000’ AFE
Operational control tower and radar approach control
5 NM core (surface - 4,000’ AFE), 10 NM shelf (1,200’ - 4,000’ AFE)
Operating Rules & Pilot/Equipment Requirements
Pilot Certification - No specific certification required
Equipment - Two-way radio, Mode C transponder
Communication required prior to entry
Class B Airspace 										AI.II.G.K1
Definition
Surface to 10,000’ MSL around nation’s busiest airports
Configuration is tailored to the needs of the area
Upside-down wedding cake
Designed to contain all instrument procedures
Operating Rules and Pilot/Equipment Requirements
For VFR Operations:
At least a Private Pilot Certificate is required
Or learner/recreational/sport pilot with endorsement
AIM 3-2-3b: Solo learner, sport, and recreational pilot operations are not permitted at certain class B airports
ATL, ORD, DFW, LAX, MIA, JFK, LGA, SFO, etc.
Specific ATC Clearance is required before entering
Two-way radio, 4096-code Mode C transponder
Mode C Veil transponder requirement - 30 nm of Class B airport, surface to 10,000’ MSL
For IFR operations:
VOR or TACAN receiver
Radar beacon transponder with auto altitude reporting
Class A Airspace 										AI.II.G.K1
18,000’ MSL up to/including FL600, including 12 NM off the coast of 48 contiguous states and Alaska
Operating Rules and Pilot/Equipment Requirements
Unless otherwise authorized, all operation is IFR
Class G Airspace 										AI.II.G.K1
Definition: Uncontrolled Airspace (everything that isn’t A-E)
Surface to the base of the overlying Class E airspace
VFR Weather Minimums Summary (Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAR 91.155)
Special VFR (FAR 91.157) 									AI.II.G.K5
Clearance to operate under VFR with less than VFR weather minimums
Only in Class B, C, D, or E surface areas, below 10,000’ MSL
Must be requested by the pilot
Special VFR is on the basis of weather conditions at the airport of intended landing/departure
Only approved if IFR traffic are not delayed
Special VFR may only be conducted
With an ATC clearance
Clear of clouds
With at least 1 statute mile flight visibility
At night (sunset to sunrise): With an instrument rated pilot and aircraft
May not takeoff or land under special VFR unless ground visibility is at least 1 statute mile
If not reported, flight visibility must be at least 1 statute mile
Prohibited at certain airports (mostly large class B airports) shown in Part 91 Appendix D Section 3
Special Use Airspace 										AI.II.G.K3
Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA) - Airspace governed by the rules described in Part 93
Normal rules don’t necessarily apply – special rules for operating in the boundaries of certain airspace
Ex: DC National Security, LA VFR Corridor, Grand Canyon National Park
Prohibited Areas - Published in the Federal Register and are depicted on aeronautical charts
Flight is prohibited - Established for security or other reasons associated with the national welfare
Restricted Areas - Published in the Federal Register and are depicted on aeronautical charts
Hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft, and while not wholly prohibited, are subject to restrictions
Warning Areas - Depicted on aeronautical charts
Extend from 3 nm outward from the coast, contain potentially hazardous activity
MOAs (Military Operation Areas) - Depicted on aeronautical charts
Separate military training activity from IFR traffic. No restriction against operating VFR
Alert Areas - Depicted on aeronautical charts
Advise pilots that a high volume of pilot training or unusual aerial activity is taking place
Controlled Firing Areas – Not displayed on charts
Activities that could be hazardous to aircraft, suspended when an aircraft is approaching the area
Other Airspace Areas 									AI.II.G.K3
Local Airport Advisory (LAA)
Area within 10 SM of an airport without operating tower, but with an FSS (provides local advisories)
Military Training Routes (MTR)
Routes used by military aircraft to maintain proficiency in tactical flying (IR and VR on sectional)
Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs) - www.tfr.faa.gov
An FDC NOTAM will be issued to designate a TFR
Parachute Jump Areas - Published in the Chart Supplement, and depicted on sectional charts
Published VFR Routes - Generally found on VFR terminal area planning charts
For transitioning around, under, or through complex airspace
Terminal Radar Service Areas (TRSA) – Depicted on sectionals/terminal area charts (solid black line)
Areas where participating pilots can receive radar services (participation is voluntary)
National Security Areas
Locations where there is a requirement for increased security and safety of ground facilities
Requested to voluntarily avoid - When necessary, flight can be temporarily prohibited
VFR Charts
Chart Symbology 										AI.II.G.K2
Aeronautical Chart User’s Guide (Pgs. 17-19: Airspace, Special Use & Other Airspace)
Chart Updates & Currency 									AI.II.G.K4
Terminal Area & Sectional Charts: Updated every 56 days
Wall Planning Chart: Updated annually
Information changes rapidly, it is important to check the effective dates on each chart/publication
To confirm currency, refer to the next scheduled edition date printed on the cover
Use the FAAs Dates of Latest Editions to verify you have the most current edition
Prior to expiration, check NOTAMs and Safety Alerts and Charting Notices for any changes
RM: Various classes & types of airspace 							AI.II.G.R1
The lesson as a whole is a discussion on the risks and requirements for each class of airspace
Conclusion: Brief review of each main point

WHAT
Airspace is defined as, “the portion of the atmosphere above a particular land area, especially above a nation.” The atmosphere above the United States is divided into several sectors, or classes and in each different airspace class, specific rules apply.

WHY
Different airspaces have been defined to efficiently manage the large amount of air traffic that traverses the sky each day.  To fly from place to place a pilot must know the rules and requirements regarding airspace.

paragraphs.text: II.H. Navigation Systems & Radar Services
Introduction
How
VOR/VORTAC (Very High Frequency Omnidirectional Range) 					AI.II.H.K1
What is it?
Omni means all - VHF radio projecting straight line courses (radials) in all directions
Referenced to magnetic north / 108.0 – 117.95 MHz
3 classes: Terminal, Low, High
RM: Limitations 				AI.II.H.R3
Radials projection depends on transmitter power
VHF signals are subject to line-of-sight restrictions
VOR MON (Minimum Operating Network)
NAS is transitioning to Performance Based Nav (PBN)
The number of VORs is being reduced (896 to 590 by 2030)
Two new, larger service volumes will enable near continuous navigation above 5,000’ AGL
Designed to enable aircraft, having lost GPS, to revert to conventional navigation procedures
Can use VOR station to station nav to reach a MON airport and fly a conventional approach
MON airport assured within 100 nm
New Service Volumes
Low: 70 nm from 5,000’ to 18,000’
High: 70 nm from 5,000’ to 14,500’
Three variations of VORs:
VOR – The VOR, by itself (magnetic courses)
VOR/DME – DME is installed with the VOR
VORTAC – TACAN (DME) is installed with a VOR
VOR Components
Ground - VOR station; transmits on assigned frequency
Aircraft - Antenna, Receiver, and VOR navigation instrument
Antenna – Picks up the VOR signal
Receiver – Processes the signal into navigation information
VOR Instrument – Displays the navigation information
OBS (Omnibearing Selector, or course selector)
Dial used to select desired radial or determine the radial on
CDI (Course Deviation Indicator) Needle
Indicates position in relation to the selected course/radial
Full scale deflection = ≥ 12o off selected course (2o per dot)
To/From Indicator
Shows whether the selected course takes the aircraft To or From the VOR
Does not indicate whether the aircraft is currently heading To or From the VOR
Flags
OFF flag indicates an unusable/unreliable signal
VOR Basics
RM: TIM (Tune, Identify, Monitor) (RM: Loss of a navigation signal) 			AI.II.H.R4
Loss of signal: If the morse code/identifier stops operating, do not use for navigation
Orientation
Rotate the OBS to center the CDI - note the course and the TO or FROM indication
TO indication displays the course to fly to the VOR
FROM indication displays the radial you’re currently on
Using a second VOR can provide an exact location at the intersection of the two radials
Tracking
Tune the VOR frequency and check the identifier to verify the desired VOR is being received
Rotate the OBS to center the CDI with a “TO” indication
Turn to the heading indicated on the VOR azimuth dial or course selector
Adjust for crosswind
Upon arriving, and passing the VOR station, the TO indication will change to a FROM indication
Reverse Sensing (not applicable to HSI)
If flying toward a VOR with a FROM indication, or away with TO, the CDI will indicate opposite
VOR Checks (FAR 91.171)
Not mandated for VFR flight
Checkpoints are listed in the Chart Supplement
FAA VOR Test Facility, Airborne Checkpoints, Ground Checkpoints, Dual VOR check
± 4o for ground checks, ± 6o for airborne checks
VOR Tips
Positively identify the station by its code or voice identification
VOR signals are line-of-sight
Don’t reset the course, correct for drift
When flying TO a station always fly the selected course with a TO indication
When flying FROM a station always fly the selected course with a FROM indication
Distance Measuring Equipment (DME) 							AI.II.H.K1
Function – Provides slant range distance from a station
With VOR and DME, a pilot can determine bearing as well as distance TO or FROM a station
How it Works
Aircraft transmits RF pulse to the DME on the ground, the DME responds with its own signal
Time between the sent signal and the reply signal determines distance
Ground speed can be provided on some systems
Operates on UHF frequencies between 962 MHz and 1213 MHz
Components
Ground Equipment - VOR/DME, VORTAC, ILS/DME, and LOC/DME
“Paired frequency” - auto selects the UHF DME frequency associated with the VORTAC
Airborne Equipment - Antenna and Receiver
RM: TIM (Tune, Identify, Monitor) the VOR (RM: Loss of a nav signal)			AI.II.H.R4
Do not use if the nav signal is lost
New DME Service Volumes for VOR MON
RM:  Errors & Limitations									AI.II.H.R3
DME signals are line-of-sight
Slant Range Distance
The mileage readout is the straight-line distance from the aircraft to the ground facility
This error is the smallest at low altitudes and long range
Negligible if 1 mile or more away from the facility for each 1,000’ above facility elevation
Automatic Direction Finder (ADF) & Nondirectional Radio Beacon (NDB) 		AI.II.H.K1
An NDB is a ground-based radio transmitter that transmits radio energy in all directions
The ADF needle in the airplane points to the NDB ground station to determine the relative bearing
Magnetic Heading + Relative Bearing = Magnetic Bearing
Mary Had + Roast Beef= Mary Barfed
NDB Components
The ground equipment: the NDB (transmits between 190 to 535 KHz)
Aircraft must be in operational range of the NDB - dependent on the strength of the station
ADF Components
The airborne equipment: 2 antennas, a receiver, and an indicator instrument
Two Antennas – used together to determine NDB direction
Receiver – Processes antenna information and to display on the instrument
Indicator Instrument (3 kinds)
Fixed Card ADF (or relative bearing indicator, RBI) (top picture)
Always indicates 0 at the top; Needle indicates RB to the station
Pilot must calculate MB based on MH and RB
Movable Card ADF (middle picture)
Automatically rotates to display aircraft heading
Head = MB to the station; Tail = MB from the station
Instrument provides MB, pilot doesn’t have to calculate it
RMI (bottom picture)
Automatically rotates to display aircraft heading
Can have two needles (ADF and/or VOR information)
ADF needle:
Head = MB To the station; Tail = MB From the station
VOR needle:
Head of needle points the bearing TO the station
Tail points to the radial the aircraft is currently on/crossing
RM: Limitations 										AI.II.H.R3
Lighting, precipitation, static, etc. result in erroneous bearing information
At night, NDBs are vulnerable to interference from distant stations
Noisy identification usually occurs when the ADF needle is erratic
Voice, music, or erroneous ID will usually be heard when a steady false bearing is displayed
ADF receivers do not have a flag to warn the pilot of erroneous bearing information
Using the NDB
RM: TIM (Tune, Identify, Monitor) (RM: Loss of a navigation signal) 			AI.II.H.R4
3-letter ID – very important since there is no flag to warn of erroneous information
Orientation (Fixed Card ADF)
The ADF needle points TO the station, showing Relative Bearing
Magnetic Heading + Relative Bearing = Magnetic Bearing
Movable Card/RMI
Turn toward the head of the needle indicating the MB to the station
Adjust for wind to maintain the desired course
Satellite Based Navigation 									AI.II.H.K2
GPS (Global Positioning System)
3 Major Segments
Space Segment: 31 satellites, 5 in view at any time (4 needed for operation)
UHF: Unaffected by weather, but subject to line-of-sight reference
Control Segment: Master control station, 5 monitoring stations, and 3 ground antennas
Updates/corrections are uplinked as satellites pass over ground antennas
User Segment: All components associated with GPS receivers
Solving for Location
The receiver utilizes the signals of at least 4 satellites to yield Latitude, Longitude, and Altitude
Navigating
VFR navigation with GPS can be as simple as selecting a destination and tracking the course
Course deviation is linear - no increase in sensitivity when approaching a waypoint
RM: RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) 					AI.II.H.R4
(RM: Loss of navigation signal & Limitations)
How the GPS verifies the integrity of the signals received from the satellites
Requires at least 5 satellites in view (or 4 satellites and a barometric altimeter)
Some receivers can use a 6th satellite to isolate and remove a corrupt satellite
RAIM Messages (generally, two types)
Not enough satellites available to provide RAIM
RAIM has detected a potential error exceeding the limit for the phase of flight
RM: GPS for VFR (RM: Limitations) 							AI.II.H.R3
In VFR operations, GPS receivers can vary between full IFR installation to handheld receivers
Many have no RAIM capability & antenna location is based on convenience, not performance
Limitations of the individual installation must be understood
Database Currency
No requirements exist for VFR ops; however, it is always a good idea to keep a current database
Violations
It is not FAA policy to initiate enforcement action against a pilot for having an expired database
However, if involved in an enforcement investigation and there is evidence that an out-of-date database contributed to the situation, it could be used in any enforcement action
WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System)
Basically, augmented GPS, to the point it may be used for precision approaches
Requires a position accuracy of 25’ or less at least 95% of the time
Designed to improve the accuracy, integrity, and availability of GPS signals
Approach Capabilities (IFR)
Improvement is sufficient to enable approach procedures with GPS/WAAS glidepaths
Eliminates cold temperature effects, incorrect altimeter setting / lack of a local altimeter source
Can be further enhanced with LAAS
LAAS (Local Area Augmentation System, also referred to as GBAS – Ground Based Augmentation System)
Like WAAS, but with more ground augmentation
Receivers around the airport send data to a central location which distributes it to aircraft
Aircraft uses the information fine tunes GPS signals
ATC Radar Services & Procedures (AIM 4-1-17 & 18) 					AI.II.H.K3
Radar equipped ATC facilities provide radar & navigation services to VFR aircraft, provided:
You can communicate with ATC, are within radar coverage, and can be radar identified
RM: Limitations
Based on controller discretion
Guidance information is advisory and responsibility for safe flying remains with the pilot
Cannot determine if flight into IMC will results from their instructions
Other services include:
Basic Radar Service – Safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited radar vectoring (workload permitting)
TRSA Service - Radar sequencing and separation for VFR aircraft in a TRSA
Class C services - Separation between IFR/VFR and sequencing of VFR traffic to the airport
Class B services - Separation based on IFR, VFR and/or weight and sequencing VFR arrivals
ADS-B Basics (Automatic Dependent Surveillance – Broadcast) 			AI.II.H.K4
What is it?
Foundation for NextGen, moving from ground radar to satellites
More precise tracking: Broadcasts every second vs a radar sweep every 5-12 seconds
ADS-B
Automatic: Automatically transmits information
Dependent: Position/velocity are derived from GPS/FMS
Surveillance: Allows 3D position and identification
Broadcast: Transmits the information to anyone with appropriate receiving equipment
ADS-B Out: Broadcasts GPS location, altitude, ground speed, more to ground stations/other aircraft
ADS-B In
Pilots can see what controllers see in the air as well as on the ground, and can provide weather
FIS-B (Flight Information Service Broadcast – available on 978 MHz UAT equipment)
Like XM weather, but more information
TIS-B (Traffic Information Service Broadcast – available to 1090ES and UAT equipment users)
Provides traffic information on all transponder-based aircraft in the vicinity of the ADS-B
Who Needs it?
FAR 91.225 – Effective Jan 1, 2020, ADS-B OUT is required in:
Class A, B, and C airspace (and above the ceiling of Class B and C airspace up to 10,000’ MSL)
Class E airspace at and above 10,000’ MSL, excluding at and below 2,500’ AGL
At and above 3,000’ MSL over the Gulf of Mexico within 12 nm of the coast
ADS-B IN is voluntary
Transponder 											AI.II.H.K4
Modes
A: Transmits 4-digit code that identifies an aircraft and its position
C: Mode A + ATC can see the aircraft’s altitude
S: Transmits a variety of information to ATC & other aircraft
Unique ICAO address (assigned to each aircraft)
Heading, speed, other flight related data
Integral to TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) and ADS-B
See lesson II.G. National Airspace System for transponder requirements
RM: EFBs & Automation (Navigation & Flight Systems) 				AI.II.H.R1, AI.II.H.R5
Pilots are responsible for proper use of an EFB and installed avionics
Pilots may be evaluated on the use and interpretation of an EFB or installed avionics
Although not required, always maintain current EFB charts and publications
Understand the abilities and limitations of the system(s) on your aircraft
RM: Distractions (Task Prioritization, Loss of SA, Disorientation) 			AI.II.H.R2
Distractions
Distractions are dangerous
Navigation systems, especially GPS/moving maps, can consume the pilot’s attention
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Navigation systems and radar services can be huge for situational awareness
Don’t be overdependent on a single system (like the GPS), if the GPS/VOR fails, have a backup
If SA is lost, admit it, and find a way to regain
Task Management
Divide attention between flying/navigating, scanning, and communicating
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

WHAT
This lesson discusses the different navigation systems in use, as well as radar services provided by ATC when in radar coverage and with established communication.

standard_lessons.full_text:
II.H. Navigation Systems & Radar Services
Introduction
How
VOR/VORTAC (Very High Frequency Omnidirectional Range) 					AI.II.H.K1
What is it?
Omni means all - VHF radio projecting straight line courses (radials) in all directions
Referenced to magnetic north / 108.0 – 117.95 MHz
3 classes: Terminal, Low, High
RM: Limitations 				AI.II.H.R3
Radials projection depends on transmitter power
VHF signals are subject to line-of-sight restrictions
VOR MON (Minimum Operating Network)
NAS is transitioning to Performance Based Nav (PBN)
The number of VORs is being reduced (896 to 590 by 2030)
Two new, larger service volumes will enable near continuous navigation above 5,000’ AGL
Designed to enable aircraft, having lost GPS, to revert to conventional navigation procedures
Can use VOR station to station nav to reach a MON airport and fly a conventional approach
MON airport assured within 100 nm
New Service Volumes
Low: 70 nm from 5,000’ to 18,000’
High: 70 nm from 5,000’ to 14,500’
Three variations of VORs:
VOR – The VOR, by itself (magnetic courses)
VOR/DME – DME is installed with the VOR
VORTAC – TACAN (DME) is installed with a VOR
VOR Components
Ground - VOR station; transmits on assigned frequency
Aircraft - Antenna, Receiver, and VOR navigation instrument
Antenna – Picks up the VOR signal
Receiver – Processes the signal into navigation information
VOR Instrument – Displays the navigation information
OBS (Omnibearing Selector, or course selector)
Dial used to select desired radial or determine the radial on
CDI (Course Deviation Indicator) Needle
Indicates position in relation to the selected course/radial
Full scale deflection = ≥ 12o off selected course (2o per dot)
To/From Indicator
Shows whether the selected course takes the aircraft To or From the VOR
Does not indicate whether the aircraft is currently heading To or From the VOR
Flags
OFF flag indicates an unusable/unreliable signal
VOR Basics
RM: TIM (Tune, Identify, Monitor) (RM: Loss of a navigation signal) 			AI.II.H.R4
Loss of signal: If the morse code/identifier stops operating, do not use for navigation
Orientation
Rotate the OBS to center the CDI - note the course and the TO or FROM indication
TO indication displays the course to fly to the VOR
FROM indication displays the radial you’re currently on
Using a second VOR can provide an exact location at the intersection of the two radials
Tracking
Tune the VOR frequency and check the identifier to verify the desired VOR is being received
Rotate the OBS to center the CDI with a “TO” indication
Turn to the heading indicated on the VOR azimuth dial or course selector
Adjust for crosswind
Upon arriving, and passing the VOR station, the TO indication will change to a FROM indication
Reverse Sensing (not applicable to HSI)
If flying toward a VOR with a FROM indication, or away with TO, the CDI will indicate opposite
VOR Checks (FAR 91.171)
Not mandated for VFR flight
Checkpoints are listed in the Chart Supplement
FAA VOR Test Facility, Airborne Checkpoints, Ground Checkpoints, Dual VOR check
± 4o for ground checks, ± 6o for airborne checks
VOR Tips
Positively identify the station by its code or voice identification
VOR signals are line-of-sight
Don’t reset the course, correct for drift
When flying TO a station always fly the selected course with a TO indication
When flying FROM a station always fly the selected course with a FROM indication
Distance Measuring Equipment (DME) 							AI.II.H.K1
Function – Provides slant range distance from a station
With VOR and DME, a pilot can determine bearing as well as distance TO or FROM a station
How it Works
Aircraft transmits RF pulse to the DME on the ground, the DME responds with its own signal
Time between the sent signal and the reply signal determines distance
Ground speed can be provided on some systems
Operates on UHF frequencies between 962 MHz and 1213 MHz
Components
Ground Equipment - VOR/DME, VORTAC, ILS/DME, and LOC/DME
“Paired frequency” - auto selects the UHF DME frequency associated with the VORTAC
Airborne Equipment - Antenna and Receiver
RM: TIM (Tune, Identify, Monitor) the VOR (RM: Loss of a nav signal)			AI.II.H.R4
Do not use if the nav signal is lost
New DME Service Volumes for VOR MON
RM:  Errors & Limitations									AI.II.H.R3
DME signals are line-of-sight
Slant Range Distance
The mileage readout is the straight-line distance from the aircraft to the ground facility
This error is the smallest at low altitudes and long range
Negligible if 1 mile or more away from the facility for each 1,000’ above facility elevation
Automatic Direction Finder (ADF) & Nondirectional Radio Beacon (NDB) 		AI.II.H.K1
An NDB is a ground-based radio transmitter that transmits radio energy in all directions
The ADF needle in the airplane points to the NDB ground station to determine the relative bearing
Magnetic Heading + Relative Bearing = Magnetic Bearing
Mary Had + Roast Beef= Mary Barfed
NDB Components
The ground equipment: the NDB (transmits between 190 to 535 KHz)
Aircraft must be in operational range of the NDB - dependent on the strength of the station
ADF Components
The airborne equipment: 2 antennas, a receiver, and an indicator instrument
Two Antennas – used together to determine NDB direction
Receiver – Processes antenna information and to display on the instrument
Indicator Instrument (3 kinds)
Fixed Card ADF (or relative bearing indicator, RBI) (top picture)
Always indicates 0 at the top; Needle indicates RB to the station
Pilot must calculate MB based on MH and RB
Movable Card ADF (middle picture)
Automatically rotates to display aircraft heading
Head = MB to the station; Tail = MB from the station
Instrument provides MB, pilot doesn’t have to calculate it
RMI (bottom picture)
Automatically rotates to display aircraft heading
Can have two needles (ADF and/or VOR information)
ADF needle:
Head = MB To the station; Tail = MB From the station
VOR needle:
Head of needle points the bearing TO the station
Tail points to the radial the aircraft is currently on/crossing
RM: Limitations 										AI.II.H.R3
Lighting, precipitation, static, etc. result in erroneous bearing information
At night, NDBs are vulnerable to interference from distant stations
Noisy identification usually occurs when the ADF needle is erratic
Voice, music, or erroneous ID will usually be heard when a steady false bearing is displayed
ADF receivers do not have a flag to warn the pilot of erroneous bearing information
Using the NDB
RM: TIM (Tune, Identify, Monitor) (RM: Loss of a navigation signal) 			AI.II.H.R4
3-letter ID – very important since there is no flag to warn of erroneous information
Orientation (Fixed Card ADF)
The ADF needle points TO the station, showing Relative Bearing
Magnetic Heading + Relative Bearing = Magnetic Bearing
Movable Card/RMI
Turn toward the head of the needle indicating the MB to the station
Adjust for wind to maintain the desired course
Satellite Based Navigation 									AI.II.H.K2
GPS (Global Positioning System)
3 Major Segments
Space Segment: 31 satellites, 5 in view at any time (4 needed for operation)
UHF: Unaffected by weather, but subject to line-of-sight reference
Control Segment: Master control station, 5 monitoring stations, and 3 ground antennas
Updates/corrections are uplinked as satellites pass over ground antennas
User Segment: All components associated with GPS receivers
Solving for Location
The receiver utilizes the signals of at least 4 satellites to yield Latitude, Longitude, and Altitude
Navigating
VFR navigation with GPS can be as simple as selecting a destination and tracking the course
Course deviation is linear - no increase in sensitivity when approaching a waypoint
RM: RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) 					AI.II.H.R4
(RM: Loss of navigation signal & Limitations)
How the GPS verifies the integrity of the signals received from the satellites
Requires at least 5 satellites in view (or 4 satellites and a barometric altimeter)
Some receivers can use a 6th satellite to isolate and remove a corrupt satellite
RAIM Messages (generally, two types)
Not enough satellites available to provide RAIM
RAIM has detected a potential error exceeding the limit for the phase of flight
RM: GPS for VFR (RM: Limitations) 							AI.II.H.R3
In VFR operations, GPS receivers can vary between full IFR installation to handheld receivers
Many have no RAIM capability & antenna location is based on convenience, not performance
Limitations of the individual installation must be understood
Database Currency
No requirements exist for VFR ops; however, it is always a good idea to keep a current database
Violations
It is not FAA policy to initiate enforcement action against a pilot for having an expired database
However, if involved in an enforcement investigation and there is evidence that an out-of-date database contributed to the situation, it could be used in any enforcement action
WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System)
Basically, augmented GPS, to the point it may be used for precision approaches
Requires a position accuracy of 25’ or less at least 95% of the time
Designed to improve the accuracy, integrity, and availability of GPS signals
Approach Capabilities (IFR)
Improvement is sufficient to enable approach procedures with GPS/WAAS glidepaths
Eliminates cold temperature effects, incorrect altimeter setting / lack of a local altimeter source
Can be further enhanced with LAAS
LAAS (Local Area Augmentation System, also referred to as GBAS – Ground Based Augmentation System)
Like WAAS, but with more ground augmentation
Receivers around the airport send data to a central location which distributes it to aircraft
Aircraft uses the information fine tunes GPS signals
ATC Radar Services & Procedures (AIM 4-1-17 & 18) 					AI.II.H.K3
Radar equipped ATC facilities provide radar & navigation services to VFR aircraft, provided:
You can communicate with ATC, are within radar coverage, and can be radar identified
RM: Limitations
Based on controller discretion
Guidance information is advisory and responsibility for safe flying remains with the pilot
Cannot determine if flight into IMC will results from their instructions
Other services include:
Basic Radar Service – Safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited radar vectoring (workload permitting)
TRSA Service - Radar sequencing and separation for VFR aircraft in a TRSA
Class C services - Separation between IFR/VFR and sequencing of VFR traffic to the airport
Class B services - Separation based on IFR, VFR and/or weight and sequencing VFR arrivals
ADS-B Basics (Automatic Dependent Surveillance – Broadcast) 			AI.II.H.K4
What is it?
Foundation for NextGen, moving from ground radar to satellites
More precise tracking: Broadcasts every second vs a radar sweep every 5-12 seconds
ADS-B
Automatic: Automatically transmits information
Dependent: Position/velocity are derived from GPS/FMS
Surveillance: Allows 3D position and identification
Broadcast: Transmits the information to anyone with appropriate receiving equipment
ADS-B Out: Broadcasts GPS location, altitude, ground speed, more to ground stations/other aircraft
ADS-B In
Pilots can see what controllers see in the air as well as on the ground, and can provide weather
FIS-B (Flight Information Service Broadcast – available on 978 MHz UAT equipment)
Like XM weather, but more information
TIS-B (Traffic Information Service Broadcast – available to 1090ES and UAT equipment users)
Provides traffic information on all transponder-based aircraft in the vicinity of the ADS-B
Who Needs it?
FAR 91.225 – Effective Jan 1, 2020, ADS-B OUT is required in:
Class A, B, and C airspace (and above the ceiling of Class B and C airspace up to 10,000’ MSL)
Class E airspace at and above 10,000’ MSL, excluding at and below 2,500’ AGL
At and above 3,000’ MSL over the Gulf of Mexico within 12 nm of the coast
ADS-B IN is voluntary
Transponder 											AI.II.H.K4
Modes
A: Transmits 4-digit code that identifies an aircraft and its position
C: Mode A + ATC can see the aircraft’s altitude
S: Transmits a variety of information to ATC & other aircraft
Unique ICAO address (assigned to each aircraft)
Heading, speed, other flight related data
Integral to TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System) and ADS-B
See lesson II.G. National Airspace System for transponder requirements
RM: EFBs & Automation (Navigation & Flight Systems) 				AI.II.H.R1, AI.II.H.R5
Pilots are responsible for proper use of an EFB and installed avionics
Pilots may be evaluated on the use and interpretation of an EFB or installed avionics
Although not required, always maintain current EFB charts and publications
Understand the abilities and limitations of the system(s) on your aircraft
RM: Distractions (Task Prioritization, Loss of SA, Disorientation) 			AI.II.H.R2
Distractions
Distractions are dangerous
Navigation systems, especially GPS/moving maps, can consume the pilot’s attention
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Navigation systems and radar services can be huge for situational awareness
Don’t be overdependent on a single system (like the GPS), if the GPS/VOR fails, have a backup
If SA is lost, admit it, and find a way to regain
Task Management
Divide attention between flying/navigating, scanning, and communicating
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: II.I. Navigation & Flight Planning
Introduction
How
Terms
Navigation Terminology
True North – Points directly to the geographic north pol
Magnetic North – Aligns with Earth’s magnetic field and points directly to the magnetic north pole
Variation – The angular difference between true north and magnetic north; isogonic lines on charts
True Course – The direction of flight as measured on a chart clockwise from true North
True Heading – The direction the longitudinal axis of the airplane points with respect to true North
Magnetic Course – True course corrected for magnetic variation
Magnetic Heading – Magnetic Course corrected for wind (direction and speed)
Compass Heading – Aircraft heading read from the compass
Deviation – Compass error due to magnetic disturbances from electrical/metal parts in the plane
Atmospheric Terminology
Standard Pressure – 29.92” Hg (at sea level)
Standard Temperature – 15o C/59oF (at sea level)
Altitude Terminology
Indicated Alt –Altitude read directly from the altimeter after it’s set to the current altimeter setting
Pressure Alt – Height above the standard pressure level of 29.92 in Hg -
Density Alt – Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperatures -
True Altitude – The true vertical distance of the aircraft above sea level
Absolute Altitude – The vertical distance of the aircraft above the surface of the earth (AGL)
Airspeed Terminology
Indicated (IAS) – The speed of an aircraft as shown on the airspeed Indicator
Calibrated (CAS) – Indicated airspeed of an aircraft, corrected for installation and instrument errors
Equivalent (EAS) – CAS corrected for adiabatic compressible flow for the particular altitude
True (TAS) – The speed an aircraft is moving relative to the surrounding air (CAS corrected for DA)
Groundspeed (GS) – The speed of the aircraft in relation to the ground (TAS corrected for wind)
Aeronautical Charts & Chart Supplement
Charts 											AI.II.I.K15
The roadmap for a pilot flying VFR
FAA Aeronautical Chart User’s Guide
Sectional Charts (Most commonly used by pilots) – revised every 56 days
Information provided: Airport data, nav aids, airspace, and topography. Revised semiannually
VFR Terminal Area Charts – revised every 56 days
More detailed map/information. Helpful in busy airspace and flying in or near Class B airspace
VFR Wall Planning Chart – revised annually (to be discontinued Aug 7, 2025)
Provides aeronautical and topographic information of the conterminous US
Airports, navaids, Class B airspace, Special use airspace
Proper and Current Aeronautical Charts
Always use current editions and discard obsolete charts and publications
Check Aeronautical Chart Bulletins & NOTAMs for important updates between publication cycles
Chart Supplement
Essential to planning
Digital Chart Supplements & FAA Chart Supplement description
Provides the most comprehensive information on a given airport
Detailed runway info, procedures, frequencies, hours of operation, lighting, services, and more
Also provides VFR waypoints, VOR checkpoints, chart bulletins, LAHSO operations, parachute jump areas, special notices and FAA, NWS, and facility phone numbers
Reference all potential airports during planning (departure, arrival, alternates)
Navigation 											AI.II.I.K10
Navigation Types
Pilotage – Navigation by reference to landmarks or checkpoints
Checkpoints used should be prominent features common to the area of flight
Easily recognizable and spaced at a comfortable frequency
Use features that can create boundaries (rivers, roads, mountain ranges, etc.)
Never place complete reliance on any single checkpoint
Turn based on time if the checkpoint is not in sight, do not continue blindly
Dead Reckoning – Navigation by computations based on time, airspeed, distance, and direction
Radio Navigation – Navigation by which a predetermined course is followed
There are three primary navigation systems available: VOR, NDB, and GPS
For more detailed information, see II.H. Navigation Systems and Radar Services
Ideally, pilotage, dead reckoning, and radio navigation should be used together
Magnetic Compass Errors 									AI.II.I.K9
Variation
Caused by the difference in the locations of the magnetic and geographic north pole
Isogonic Lines: Lines used to connect points with the same magnetic variation
Agonic Line: The line along which the two poles are aligned, and there is no variation
Deviation
Caused by local magnetic fields within the aircraft
Degrees of deviation is shown on a compass correction card
Finding the Compass Course – True Course corrected for Variation and Deviation
True Course ± Variation = Magnetic Course; Magnetic Course ± Deviation = Compass Course
Remember: East is Least, West is Best
East: Subtract variation from true course; West: Add variation to true course
Dip Errors (pictured below, left)
What’s Going On
Lines of magnetic flux leave the Earth at the magnetic N pole/enter at magnetic S pole
At both poles the lines are perpendicular to the surface
Over the equator the lines are parallel to the surface
Magnets align with these fields and near the poles they dip/tilt the float and card
Northerly and Southerly Turning Errors (basically, the compass pulls toward the North)
Starting a turn from a Southerly heading (turning to a Northerly direction):
Compass Leads – initially shows a more aggressive turn in the same direction
Undershoot Northerly headings to compensate (30o- N; 20o- 030/330; 10o- 060/300)
Starting a turn from a Northerly heading (turning to a Southerly direction):
Compass Lags – initially shows a turn in the opposite direction
Overshoot Southerly headings to compensate (30o- S; 20o- 150/210; 10o- 120/240)
Remember: Undershoot North, Overshoot South (no compensation needed for E/W)
Acceleration Error (only applicable on East and West headings) (pictured above, right)
Aft end of the compass tilts up when accelerating and down when decelerating
On an E or W heading, acceleration appears as a turn to the North, and deceleration a turn South
Remember: ANDS – Accelerate North, Decelerate South
Oscillation Error
A combination of all the other errors as well as the movement of the plane
It results in the compass card swinging back and forth around the heading being flown
Use the average indication
Flight Planning
Per the ACS, preparation, presentation, and explanation of a computer-generated flight plan is acceptable
The flight log provides the pilot an organized, point by point plan of the flight and other useful info
Plotting a Course 										AI.II.I.K1
First, draw the route - Consider terrain, airspace, weather, winds, navigation, etc.
Choose cruise altitude 									AI.II.I.K2
Fly Odd Thousands + 500’ when on a magnetic course between 0 & 179o
Fly Even Thousands + 500’ when on a magnetic course between 180 & 359o
Applies above 3,000’ AGL and up to 17,500’ MSL
Consider terrain, airspace, performance, glide distance, weather & wind, unique factors, etc. - Combine all factors with the FAR requirements
Checkpoints – Recognizable points along your route of flight used to maintain course 	AI.II.I.K3
Top of Climb (TOC) and Top of Descent (TOD) 						AI.II.I.K5a
Find additional checkpoints along the route to bridge the gap between the TOC and TOD
Record your TOC, TOD, and additional checkpoints on your Nav Log
Fuel Stops 											AI.II.I.K5c
Longer flights will have to incorporate multiple legs for fuel stops (create a separate log for each leg)
FAR 91.151 – fuel reserves (30 min during the day, 45 min during the night)
Completing the Nav Log 								AI.II.I.K5a, AI.II.I.K5b
Chooser a power setting 									AI.II.I.K4
Use the chart provided in the POH based on desired speed, fuel burn, altitude, etc.
Start by finding the True Airspeed for the trip and record it on your Nav Log
Find and input the distance between each of the checkpoints
Next, find the true course for each leg of the flight plan
Adjust True Course for wind to get True Heading, and record ground speed
Adjust the True Heading to obtain Magnetic Heading
If necessary, get your Compass Heading by adjusting for Deviation with the correction card
Calculate the estimated time for each leg
Based on expected departure time, you can calculate an expected arrival time
Convert to UTC
Use the time for each leg to find the fuel burn for each leg
RM: Fuel Planning Considerations 							AI.II.I.R6
Ensure fuel required for the trip plus an adequate reserve is available
Adequate reserve is a minimum of the FAR requirements (personal mins may be higher)
Account for engine start & taxi
Ensure fuel will allow deviation to an alternate airport/landing with reserves
Rate of fuel burn depends on many factors
Engine condition, propeller pitch, rpm, mixture setting, % of horsepower used
Enroute, compare expected burn to the actual burn and adjust as required
Electronic Flight Bag (EFB), if used								AI.II.I.K14
Apps such as ForeFlight can be great tools for flight planning, and cross-country flying
Ensure understanding and proficiency with the app used
VFR Flight Plan 									AI.II.I.K6, AI.II.I.K8, AI.II.I.K14
Not required but it is good operating practice since the info can be used for search and rescue
ICAO Flight Plans
ICAO Flight Plan Form
A great, short ICAO flight plan instructional video from AOPA
AIM ICAO Flight Plan instructions
FAA Aircraft Type Designators
AIM 5-1-6 – International Flight Plan - IFR Flights
Filing can be done on the ground or in the air
On the ground: Call the FSS (1 800-WX BRIEF), various apps such as ForeFlight have this ability
Airborne: FSS
Once filed, the flight plan will be held for an hour after the proposed departure time
Opening the Flight Plan
After takeoff, contact the FSS by radio and give them the takeoff time to activate the flight plan
Can also be done through ForeFlight
Don’t forget to close the flight plan
Should be done via telephone to avoid radio congestion
Can be done through ForeFlight
Weather Check & DECISION-MAKING								AI.II.I.K7
Preflight Weather Briefing – The first step to determine if the flight can be conducted safely
Often done in conjunction with filing the flight plan
See III.C. Weather Information for more details
FAR 91.103 requires familiarity with weather reports and forecasts for the flight
RM: Go/No Go
Good judgment is necessary in deciding whether to take the flight
RM: Apply the PAVE risk management checklist to flight					AI.II.I.R1
Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External Pressures
Continual process of decision making before and throughout the flight
Planned Calculations versus Actual Results 						AI.II.I.K11
Planned calculations are never perfect
Recognize deviations and adjust
The more familiar with the route, flight planning, & waypoints, the easier it is to recognize deviations

Don’t Panic
Five C’s: Climb, Communicate, Confess, Comply, Conserve

Use navigational radios (VOR/ADF) to attempt to plot your position (GPS if available)

The roadmap for a pilot flying VFR
FAA Aeronautical Chart User’s Guide
Sectional Charts (Most commonly used by pilots) – revised every 56 days
Information provided: Airport data, nav aids, airspace, and topography. Revised semiannually
Scale is 1:500,000 (1” = 6.86 NM)
VFR Terminal Area Charts – revised every 56 days
More detailed map/information. Helpful in busy airspace and flying in or near Class B airspace
Scale is 1:250,000 (1” = 3.43 NM)
VFR Wall Planning Chart – revised annually (to be discontinued Aug 7, 2025)
Provides aeronautical and topographic information of the conterminous US
Airports, navaids, Class B airspace, Special use airspace
Scale is 1:3,100,000 (1” = 43 NM)
Proper and Current Aeronautical Charts
Always use current editions and discard obsolete charts and publications
Check Aeronautical Chart Bulletins & NOTAMs for important updates between publication cycles
Chart Supplement
Essential to planning
Digital Chart Supplements & FAA Chart Supplement description
Provides the most comprehensive information on a given airport
Detailed runway info, procedures, frequencies, hours of operation, lighting, services, and more
Also provides VFR waypoints, VOR checkpoints, chart bulletins, LAHSO operations, parachute jump areas, special notices and FAA, NWS, and facility phone numbers
Reference all potential airports during planning (departure, arrival, alternates)
Navigation 											AI.II.I.K10
Navigation Types
Pilotage – Navigation by reference to landmarks or checkpoints
Checkpoints used should be prominent features common to the area of flight
Easily recognizable and spaced at a comfortable frequency
Use features that can create boundaries (rivers, roads, mountain ranges, etc.)
Never place complete reliance on any single checkpoint
Turn based on time if the checkpoint is not in sight, do not continue blindly
Dead Reckoning – Navigation by computations based on time, airspeed, distance, and direction
Radio Navigation – Navigation by which a predetermined course is followed
There are three primary navigation systems available: VOR, NDB, and GPS
For more detailed information, see II.H. Navigation Systems and Radar Services
Ideally, pilotage, dead reckoning, and radio navigation should be used together
Magnetic Compass Errors 									AI.II.I.K9
Variation
Caused by the difference in the locations of the magnetic and geographic north pole
Isogonic Lines: Lines used to connect points with the same magnetic variation
Agonic Line: The line along which the two poles are aligned, and there is no variation
Deviation
Caused by local magnetic fields within the aircraft
Degrees of deviation is shown on a compass correction card
Finding the Compass Course – True Course corrected for Variation and Deviation
True Course ± Variation = Magnetic Course; Magnetic Course ± Deviation = Compass Course
Remember: East is Least, West is Best
East: Subtract variation from true course; West: Add variation to true course
Dip Errors (pictured below, left)
What’s Going On
Lines of magnetic flux leave the Earth at the magnetic N pole/enter at magnetic S pole
At both poles the lines are perpendicular to the surface
Over the equator the lines are parallel to the surface
Magnets align with these fields and near the poles they dip/tilt the float and card
Northerly and Southerly Turning Errors (basically, the compass pulls toward the North)
Starting a turn from a Southerly heading (turning to a Northerly direction):
Compass Leads – initially shows a more aggressive turn in the same direction
Undershoot Northerly headings to compensate (30o- N; 20o- 030/330; 10o- 060/300)
Starting a turn from a Northerly heading (turning to a Southerly direction):
Compass Lags – initially shows a turn in the opposite direction
Overshoot Southerly headings to compensate (30o- S; 20o- 150/210; 10o- 120/240)
Remember: Undershoot North, Overshoot South (no compensation needed for E/W)
Acceleration Error (only applicable on East and West headings) (pictured above, right)
Aft end of the compass tilts up when accelerating and down when decelerating
On an E or W heading, acceleration appears as a turn to the North, and deceleration a turn South
Remember: ANDS – Accelerate North, Decelerate South
Oscillation Error
A combination of all the other errors as well as the movement of the plane
It results in the compass card swinging back and forth around the heading being flown
Use the average indication

Per the ACS, preparation, presentation, and explanation of a computer-generated flight plan is acceptable
The flight log provides the pilot an organized, point by point plan of the flight and other useful info

First, draw the route - Consider terrain, airspace, weather, winds, navigation, etc.
Choose cruise altitude 									AI.II.I.K2
FAR 91.159
Fly Odd Thousands + 500’ when on a magnetic course between 0 & 179o
Fly Even Thousands + 500’ when on a magnetic course between 180 & 359o
Applies above 3,000’ AGL and up to 17,500’ MSL
Consider terrain, airspace, performance, glide distance, weather & wind, unique factors, etc. - Combine all factors with the FAR requirements

Introduction
How

Contents: General Definitions, Abbreviations and Symbols, Rules of Construction

Requirements for issuing pilot, flight instructor, ground instructor certificates and ratings
Privileges and limitations of those certificates and ratings, and authorizations

Rules governing the operation of aircraft in the US, including the waters within 3 nm of the coast
Part 21 – Certification Procedures
Requirements for airworthiness certificates and airworthiness approvals

Rules governing maintenance, preventive maintenance, and rebuilding

Medical standards and certification for issuing medical certificates

Notification and reporting of aircraft incidents and accidents

Accident or serious incident (listed in 830.5a)
Aircraft is overdue and believed to have been involved in an accident
Information to be provided described in 830.6
Preservation of aircraft wreckage, mail, cargo, and records involving aircraft accidents
Advisory Circulars, INFOs & SAFOs

Used for information only and are not regulations

Respond to a request from a government entity (NTSB, Office of the Inspector General, etc.)

Commonly used ACs: The Backseat Pilot – Advisory Circulars

Information to meet requirements with low urgency or impact on safety
Ex: Updates to Cold Temperature Airports Program
InFO Database

Especially valuable to air carriers & the duty to provide service with the highest degree of safety
Ex: Recognizing & Mitigating GPS/GNSS Disruptions

SAFO Database

Used for information only and are not regulations

How

An instructor must sign the logbook of each person that instructor has given flight/ground training
Logbook entries must include (FAR 61.51):
Student Pilot Certificate Endorsements 					AI.II.K.K2, AI.II.K.K3
Student Pilot Endorsements (Examples shown in AC 61-65)
Special Federal Aviation Regulation (SFAR)
Mentioned in the ACS – Included here in case it comes up

Often issued with an expiration date that can be amended, extended or rescinded as needed
Ex: In 2020, the FAA issued an SFAR to provide regulatory relief to people/schools who were unable to comply with training, experience, testing, and checking requirements due to Covid
Practical Test Recommendation 								AI.II.K.K4
Endorsements 										AI.II.K.K4a
AC 61-65 A.1: Prerequisites for a Practical Test: 61.39(a)(6)(i) & (ii)
AC61-65 A.2: Aeronautical Knowledge Test Deficiencies: 61.39(a)(6)(iii)
As required
Sometimes combined with the above endorsement (Ex. AC 61-65 A.40: Instrument rating)
Other part 61 endorsement(s) for the category, class, rating, or privilege of certification sought
Example Endorsement – Single Engine Private Pilot
AC 61-65 A.1: Prerequisite for a Practical Test: § 61.39(a)(6)(i) & (ii)
AC 61.-65 A.2: Aeronautical Knowledge Test Deficiencies: § 61.39(a)(6)(iii)
AC 61-65 A.32: Aeronautical Knowledge Test: §§ 61.35(a)(1), 61.103(d), and 61.105
Part 61 required endorsement specific to the private pilot required knowledge training
AC 61-65 A.33: Flight Proficiency/Practical Test: §§ 61.103(f), 61.107(b), and 61.109
Part 61 required endorsement specific to the private pilot certificate
Endorsement References
The instructor/learner must complete the IACRA rating application online (iacra.faa.gov)
Or the instructor/learner must complete/sign a Form 8710-1 (rarely used)
Except in certain instances, applicant must hold at least a 3rd class medical: FAR 61.23 (a)(3)(iii)

Additional category and/or class (other than ATP), must have:
Instructor recommendations
Appropriate endorsements (vary by specific FAR 61 requirements )

Comply with the requirements of FAR 61.63 (described below)
Pass the practical test appropriate for the aircraft category, and if applicable, class rating sought

Endorsement stating competence in knowledge areas and proficient in areas of operation
AC 61-65 A.74: Additional aircraft category or class rating (other than ATP)
AC 61-65 A.1: Practical test endorsement
Other endorsement(s) as required, see example
Pass practical test
No need to meet the time requirements that apply to the class rating (see FAR for exception)
No knowledge test, provided applicant holds a rating at the certificate level

Complete training and have the applicable aeronautical experience required by FAR part 61
Endorsement stating competence in knowledge areas and proficient in areas of operation
AC 61-65 A.74: Additional aircraft category or class rating (other than ATP)
AC 61-65 A.1: Practical Test Endorsement
Other endorsement(s), as required
Pass practical test
No additional knowledge test, provided applicant holds a rating at the certificate level

Must have received the FAR required training for the aircraft
AC 61-65 A.72 – Solo PIC when the pilot doesn’t hold appropriate category/class
Additional Rating Example
Single engine private pilot wants to add multiengine class rating
AC 61-65 A.1: Prerequisite for a Practical Test: 61.39(a)(6)(i) & (ii)
AC 61-65 A.74: Additional Aircraft Category or Class Rating (other than ATP): 61.63(c)
AC 61-65 A.68: To act as Pilot in Command in a Complex Aircraft: 61.31(e)
Reapplying for a Practical Test
Following a Notice of Disapproval
Must have another endorsement in accordance with FAR 61.43(f) & 61.49(a)(2)
AC 61-65 A.73: Retesting after failure of a knowledge or practical test: 61.49
Instructor recommendation (8710/IACRA) is required for a retest
Get credit for areas of operation passed for 60 calendar-days from the date discontinued
Following a Letter of Discontinuance
No additional endorsements are required
Get credit for areas of operation passed for 60 calendar-days after the discontinuation date
Time Limits (Two Calendar Months vs 60 Calendar-Days)
60 Calendar-Day Time Limit
FAR 61.43(e) – Practical test can be discontinued for 4 reasons:
Fail one or more areas of operation, Inclement weather, Airworthiness, Safety of flight concern
FAR 61.43(f) – If discontinued per 61.43(e), applicant gets credit for the areas they passed, but
FAR 61.43(f)(1) – the remainder of the test must be completed within 60 calendar days
2 Calendar Month Time Limit
FAR 61.39(f) – If all increments of a practical test are not completed on the same date, all remaining increments must be completed within 2 calendar months
Increment may be because the test was discontinued for reasons stated in 61.43(e), or because it was planned to be conducted in increments
FAR 61.39(g): After 2 calendar months, the entire test must be accomplished
Separate time limit from the 60 calendar-day limit
Flight Review Endorsements 								AI.II.K.K5
After a satisfactory completion of a flight review, the instructor must endorse the pilot’s logbook
AC 61-65 A.65: Completion of a Flight Review: 61.56(a) & (c)
Instrument Proficiency Checks (IPC)
CFII is required
AC 61-65 A.67: Completion of an Instrument Proficiency Check: 61.57(d)
No logbook entry reflecting unsatisfactory performance is necessary for either flight review
Flight Instructor Responsibilities 							AI.II.K.K6
Records (FAR 61.189)
Must maintain a record that contains the following:
Name of each person endorsed for solo flight privileges, and the date of the endorsement
Name of each person endorsed for a knowledge or practical test, with the kind of test, date, results
Must retain the records for at least 3 years
RM: Limitations & Expiration Dates 								AI.II.K.R1
Failure to ensure proper endorsements is a serious deficiency in performance
Depending on the situation, the FAA could hold the instructor accountable
Required limitations & expiration dates are implemented for safety
Ensure proper endorsements and learner understanding of those endorsements
Training Initial Flight Instructor Applicants (reflects new requirements effective December 1, 2024)
Ground Training Options
Held the appropriate instructor certificate for 24+ months and given 40+ hours of ground training
Hold appropriate instructor certificate & given 100+ hours ground in an FAA-approved course
Flight Training Options
Held a flight instructor certificate for at least 24 months & given at least 200 hours of flight training
80% practical test pass rate for at least 5 applicants in the last 24 months
200 hrs. flight training & completed a FIEQTP (Flight Instructor Enhanced Qualification Training Program)
FIEQTP must be under Part 141 - training described in FAR 61.95(h)(3) & AC 61-145
Maintaining your CFI Certificate								AI.II.K.K7
Reflects removal of expiration date on CFI certificates & recent experience requirements effective Dec. 1, 2024
Duration
A certificate issued before December 1, 2024, expires 24 calendar months from the month in which it was issued, renewed, or reinstated, as appropriate (Exception: FAR 61.197(b))
A certificate issued on or after December 1, 2024, is issued without an expiration date
Recent Experience Requirements (FAR 61.197)
Must satisfy one of the following requirements within the previous 24 calendar months:
Pass a practical test for:
One of the ratings listed on your flight instructor certificate
An additional flight instructor rating
Submit documentation with the FAA for one of the following:
Endorsed 5 or more applicants for a checkride with ≥ 80% pass rate on their first attempt
Gold Seal Instructor Certificate (apply for renewal/gold seal together if desired)
Served as a company check pilot or check airman, chief flight instructor, Part 121 or 135 instructor, or in a position involving the regular eval of pilots in the past 24 calendar months
Completion of an approved instructor refresher course in the past 3 calendar months
AC 61-83: Flight Instructor Refresher Course
Passed a military instructor pilot or pilot examiner proficiency check in an aircraft in the past 24 calendar months (considerably more detail to this - reference FAR 61.197(4))
FAA-sponsored pilot proficiency program (i.e., WINGS) meeting the following requirements:
Hold a current flight instructor certificate
Complete ≥ 1 phase of an FAA-sponsored pilot proficiency program in the last 12 months
Evaluate & endorse 15 flight activities (at least 5 pilots) under the pilot proficiency program
WINGS Program
AC 61-91: WINGS – Pilot Proficiency Programs. See page 5, paragraph 6(e)
FAAST Team Notice – WINGS CFI Renewal Opportunity
Reinstatement of Flight Instructor Privileges (FAR 61.199)
Effective December 1, 2024 - If within 3 calendar months of the expiration date:
Privileges can be reinstated via an approved FIRC (flight instructor refresher course)
No instructional privileges during this reinstatement period
If more than 3 months have passed, the instructor must complete one of the following:
An instructor practical test for one of the ratings on the expired certificate per 61.183(h)
A practical test for an additional flight instructor rating
Passed a military instructor pilot or pilot examiner proficiency check
Completed a military instructor pilot/pilot examiner training course and received an additional rating appropriate to the flight instructor rating sought
Documentation
Submit an Airman Certificate and/or Rating Application (8710-1 or 8710-11) to validate experience
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points
