Reflects removal of expiration date on CFI certificates & recent experience requirements effective Dec. 1, 2024
Duration
FAR 61.19(d)
A certificate issued before December 1, 2024, expires 24 calendar months from the month in which it was issued, renewed, or reinstated, as appropriate (Exception: FAR 61.197(b))
A certificate issued on or after December 1, 2024, is issued without an expiration date
Recent Experience Requirements (FAR 61.197)
Must satisfy one of the following requirements within the previous 24 calendar months:
Pass a practical test for:
One of the ratings listed on your flight instructor certificate
An additional flight instructor rating
Submit documentation with the FAA for one of the following:
Endorsed 5 or more applicants for a checkride with ≥ 80% pass rate on their first attempt
Gold Seal Instructor Certificate (apply for renewal/gold seal together if desired)
Served as a company check pilot or check airman, chief flight instructor, Part 121 or 135 instructor, or in a position involving the regular eval of pilots in the past 24 calendar months
Completion of an approved instructor refresher course in the past 3 calendar months
AC 61-83: Flight Instructor Refresher Course
Passed a military instructor pilot or pilot examiner proficiency check in an aircraft in the past 24 calendar months (considerably more detail to this - reference FAR 61.197(4))
FAA-sponsored pilot proficiency program (i.e., WINGS) meeting the following requirements:
Hold a current flight instructor certificate
Complete ≥ 1 phase of an FAA-sponsored pilot proficiency program in the last 12 months
Evaluate & endorse 15 flight activities (at least 5 pilots) under the pilot proficiency program
WINGS Program
AC 61-91: WINGS – Pilot Proficiency Programs. See page 5, paragraph 6(e)
FAAST Team Notice – WINGS CFI Renewal Opportunity
Reinstatement of Flight Instructor Privileges (FAR 61.199)
Effective December 1, 2024 - If within 3 calendar months of the expiration date:
Privileges can be reinstated via an approved FIRC (flight instructor refresher course)
No instructional privileges during this reinstatement period
If more than 3 months have passed, the instructor must complete one of the following:
An instructor practical test for one of the ratings on the expired certificate per 61.183(h)
A practical test for an additional flight instructor rating
Passed a military instructor pilot or pilot examiner proficiency check
Completed a military instructor pilot/pilot examiner training course and received an additional rating appropriate to the flight instructor rating sought
Documentation
Submit an Airman Certificate and/or Rating Application (8710-1 or 8710-11) to validate experience

paragraphs.text: II.M. Night Operations
Introduction
How
Eyes at Night 							AI.II.M.K1
Rods and Cones
Light enters the eye through the cornea, travels through the lens, and falls on the retina
The retina has light sensitive cells that convert light into electrical impulses that are sent to the brain
Two types of light-sensitive cells:
Cones: Responsible for color, detail, far away objects; located in the center of the retina
Rods: Peripheral vision and provide vision in dim light; located in a ring around the cones
Rods, Cones, and Night Vision
Cones: Located in the center of the retina (center of vision)
Rods: Make night vision possible
Concentrated around the cones; used in dim light
Off center viewing is necessary at night
Slow to adapt to dark, but quick to lose adaptation
Summary: Night vision is based on the rods and off-center viewing is necessary
RM: Collision Avoidance 									AI.II.M.R3
Use off center viewing, as looking directly at an object may result in not seeing it
Avoid bright lights before and during a flight to maintain adequate night vision
Use red/green light in the flight deck
Flight deck lighting should be at a minimum
Lighting 												AI.II.M.K2
Taxiway Lighting
Taxiway Edge Lights
Steady blue lights outlining the edges of taxiways
Taxiway Centerline Lights
Steady green lights installed along the centerline of the taxiway
Clearance Bar Lights
Three in-pavement steady-burning yellow lights
Installed at holding positions on taxiways to increase visibility of the holding position
Runway Guard Lights
Pair of elevated flashing yellow lights on either side of the taxiway, or a row of in-pavement yellow lights across the entire taxiway at the runway holding position marking
Installed at taxiway/runway intersections
Enhance conspicuity of taxiway/runway intersections
Stop Bar Lights
A row of red, unidirectional, steady-burning in-pavement lights across the entire taxiway at the runway holding position, and elevated steady-burning red lights on each side
A controlled stop bar operates in conjunction with the taxiway centerline lead-on lights
Following ATC clearance, the stop bar is turned off and the lead-on lights are turned on
Used to confirm the ATC clearance to enter or cross the active runway in low visibility
Runway Lighting
Runway Edge Lights
White lights, except on instrument runways they’re yellow for the last 2,000’ or half of the runway, whichever is less
Mark the end of the runway emitting red toward the runway (takeoff) & green outward (landing)
Classified based on brightness: High Intensity Runway Lights (HIRL), Medium (MIRL), & Low (LIRL)
Runway End Identifier Lights (REIL)
Installed to provide rapid/positive identification of the approach end of a runway
Pair of synchronized flashing lights on each side of the runway threshold
Runway Centerline Lighting System (RCLS)
White in-pavement lights every 50’ until the last 3,000’ of the runway at which point they alternate red and white for 2,000’ and are red for the last 1,000’
Touchdown Zone Lights (TDZL)
Two rows of light bars set symmetrically about the centerline
Steady burning white lights starting 100’ beyond the landing threshold and extend to 3,000’ beyond the threshold or the midpoint of the runway, whichever is less
Taxiway Centerline Lead-Off Lights
Alternate green & yellow lights from the runway centerline to one light position beyond the holding position or ILS critical area holding position
Taxiway Centerline Lead-On Lights
Same as lead-off lights but leading onto the runway
Land and Hold Short Lights
Row of pulsing white lights across the runway at the hold short point
Off when LAHSO is not in effect
Approach Lighting
Approach Light System
Basic means to transition from instrument conditions to visual conditions for landing
Used to identify the runway
Configuration of lights from the threshold extending into the approach area
Visual Glideslope Indicators
Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI)
Provides visual descent guidance during approach
Visible from 3-5 miles during the day & > 20 at night
Safe obstruction clearance within ±10o of the centerline and 4 NM from the threshold
Most common visual glide system in use
Configuration
Light units arranged in bars
2-Bar VASI (most common) – Normally, 3o path
Each unit projects light with an upper white segment and a lower red segment
3 Bar: Near, middle & far bars, 2 glidepaths:
Lower (3o) & Upper (¼o higher)
Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI)
Uses light units like a VASI but in a single row usually on the left side of the runway
Other Glidepath Systems
Tri-Color System (pictured below, left)
Above – Amber, On – Green, Below - Red
Range: Day - ½ to 1 mile; Night - Up to 5 miles
Pulsating VASI (pictured below, right)
Single light-unit projecting a 2-color visual approach path (Range: 4 miles day, 10 miles night)
High: Pulsating white, On Path: Steady white, Slightly below: Steady red, Below: Pulsating red
Pulsating rate increases further above/below the glidepath
Airport Beacons
Used to identify airports as well as differentiate different types of airports
Colors and Combinations of Beacons
Land Airport: White and Green
Military Airport: White, White, and Green
Water Airport: White and Yellow
Lighted Heliport: Green, Yellow, and White
During the day, beacon operation often indicates ground visibility < 3 miles and/or ceiling < 1,000’
No regulatory requirement for daylight beacon operation
Pilot Control of Airport Lighting
Controlled Airport
Operation of approach light systems and runway lighting is controlled by the tower/FSS
Pilots may request the lights be turned on, off, or dimmed
Pilot Control of Airport Lighting
Radio control of lighting is available at some airports by keying the microphone
3 clicks for low, 5 for medium, and 7 for high (all clicks within 5 seconds – lasts 15 minutes)
Frequency is in Chart Supplement (usually CTAF)
Obstruction Lighting
Aviation Red Obstruction Lights: Flashing red beacons and steady-burning red lights
Medium Intensity Flashing White Obstruction Lights: Flashing white obstruction lights
Not normally installed on structures less than 200’ AGL
High Intensity White Obstruction Lights: Flashing white lights
Dual Lighting: Combination of flashing red beacons and steady burning red lights
Catenary Lighting: Light markers for high voltage transmission line catenary wires

High intensity flashing white lights are being used to identify some supporting structures of overhead transmission lines located across rivers, chasms, gorges, etc. & tall structures (chimneys, towers)
Beamed toward the companion structure and identify the area of the wire span
RM: Disorientation and Night Optical Illusions 		AI.II.M.K7, AI.II.M.R4, AI.II.M.R5
Combatting Disorientation / Illusions
Verify attitude by reference to the flight instruments (best tactic to combat disorientation/illusions)
Use vertical guidance as much as possible, especially at night (VASI/PAPI, glide slope, etc.)
Go around if unsure of your position
Autokinesis
Caused by staring at a single point of light on a dark background
The light appears to move on its own
Prevention: Focus on objects at varying distances / avoid fixating
Reversible Perspective Illusion
At night, an aircraft may appear to be moving away when it is approaching
If the light intensity increases, the aircraft is approaching, if it dims, it is moving away
Size-Distance Illusion
Light that is getting brighter or dimmer, may be interpreted as approaching or retreating
Flicker Vertigo
A light flickering between 4 and 20 cycles per second can produce unpleasant, dangerous reactions
Examples: nausea, vomiting, and vertigo. Convulsions/unconsciousness are possible, but rare
Proper scanning techniques at night can prevent flicker vertigo
False Horizon
The natural horizon is not readily apparent
Trust your instruments to maintain orientation
Featureless Terrain
An absence of ground features can create the illusion that the aircraft is higher than it actually is
Results in a tendency to fly a lower-than-normal approach
Ground Lighting
Can be mistaken for airport / runway / approach lights
Bright runway or approach lights can create the illusion the airplane is closer to the runway
Maintain situational awareness - know what to expect to see, and where to see it
Disorientation at Night 									AI.II.M.K6
Disregard false sensations and trust the instruments
Always verify aircraft attitude with the instruments at night
Night Ops
Pilot & Plane 										AI.II.M.K3, AI.II.M.K4
Night Currency (FAR 61.57(b))
To act as PIC carrying passengers from 1 hr. after sunset to 1 hr. before sunrise
3 full stop takeoffs/landings in last 90 days
Sole manipulator of the flight controls & in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type
RM: Current doesn’t imply proficient – Ensure proficiency				AI.II.M.R7
Equipment
Flashlight - Red and white light (White light is used to preflight, red is used in the flight deck)
Aeronautical Charts, Nav Logs
Be cautious of washout (red color on the chart is difficult to distinguish with a red light)
Regardless of equipment, organization eases the burden on the pilot
Preflight Inspection (FAR 91.205)
Required equipment for VFR flight at night
TOMATO FFLAAMES (day VFR) and FLAPS (additional night VFR requirements)
Fuses (if applicable)
Landing Light
Anti-Collision Lights
Position Lights
Source of Power
Instrument required equipment doesn’t hurt (safer is smarter)
Walk Around – Just like a normal walk around but be more vigilant with night equipment
Check all aircraft lights, and check the ramp for obstructions
RM: Inoperative Equipment 								AI.II.M.R1
If inoperative equipment is found, handle it the same as you would during the day, but with the additional night required equipment
Is it required by Kinds of Equipment List, Type Certificate, AD, FAR 91.205
And, of course, Personal Minimum requirements
Reference III.B. Airworthiness Requirements for more details
Engine Start & Taxi
Engine Start
Take extra precaution to be sure the propeller area is clear
Turn on the beacon, announce “clear prop” and scan carefully
To avoid excessive battery drain, leave all unnecessary electrical equipment off until after engine start
Taxiing 											AI.II.M.K8
Turn on the taxi and/or landing light (be sure not to blind other pilots)
Taxi slowly, particularly in congested areas
Orientation
Airport diagram (always have one out)
Understand the taxiway markings, lights, and signs
RM: Orientation & Situational Awareness (RM: Runway incursion)			AI.II.M.R6
Airport diagram (always have one out)
Understand the taxiway markings, lights, and signs
Taxi slowly to allow time to maintain situational awareness
If there is a loss of situational awareness, conflicting info, or doubt, stop and ask for clarification
Run-up
The before takeoff run-up should be performed with the checklist as usual
Forward movement of the airplane may not be easy to detect at night
Takeoff & Climb
General 											AI.II.M.K6
The most noticeable difference is the limited availability of outside visual references
Flight instruments should be used to a greater degree at night than in the day
Dim the flight deck lighting so the instruments are readable, without hindering night vision
Entering the Runway
Clear final approach for approaching traffic
Turn on all lights, except the landing light
Recommended to align 3’ off the centerline to prevent blending in with the runway lights
Verify correct runway
Takeoff Roll
Turn on landing light after receiving takeoff clearance or starting the roll at an uncontrolled field
Same as a day takeoff except many visual cues aren’t available (compensate with instruments)
Climb
Darkness makes it difficult to note whether the airplane is getting closer or farther from the surface
Verify with the airspeed indicator, the VSI and the altimeter
Pitch/bank adjustments should be made by referencing the attitude/heading indicators
In-Flight Orientation 										AI.II.M.K5
Clouds/Restricted Visibility
It is difficult to see clouds at night – be cautious to avoid flying into MVFR/IFR weather conditions
Be conservative, don’t expect to pop out the other side, take action to avoid flying into the clouds
Crossing Large Bodies of Water
Very easy to become disoriented with little to no horizon, and false horizons
Rely more heavily on the instruments
In the event of an engine failure, the pilot may not have any option other than ditching
Ground Based Lighting
Lighted runways, buildings, etc. may cause illusions when seen from different altitudes
RM: Nav Lights (Collision Hazards) 		AI.II.M.K9, AI.II.M.R3
Red on Left Wing, Green on Right Wing, White on the Tail
Technique to remember: Green & Right have the same number of letters
Navigating at Night
Although many day references are unavailable, numerous night references can be used instead
Anything with bright lights or a lot of lights - City light patterns, highways, airport beacons, etc.
Backup with NAVAIDS/GPS whenever possible
Traffic Pattern
Airport Environment
Identify runway/airport lights as soon as possible
It may be difficult to find the airport or runways (especially if they’re buried within a city)
Fly towards the beacon until you identify runway lights
Compare the runway lights with heading indicator
If possible, tune the localizer and/or use the GPS OBS function to view an extended centerline
Use any additional means available to help orient yourself and maintain situational awareness
Distance may be deceptive at night due to limited light conditions
More trust must be put on the instruments (particularly the altimeter and airspeed indicator)
RM: Ensure appropriate lights are on for collision avoidance 				AI.II.M.R3
Fly a normal traffic pattern
Approach & Landing
A stabilized approach should be made in the same manner as during the day
Use flight instruments more often (especially altimeter/airspeed indicator)
Final Approach
If there are no centerline lights, align the airplane between the edge lights
Maintain a stabilized approach (use any references available – VASI, PAPI, glideslope, etc.)
Roundout/Touchdown
A smooth, controlled roundout and touchdown should be made in the same way as in the day
Judgment of height, speed, and sink rate may be impaired due to lack of visual references
Tendency to round out high
Technique: Start the roundout when the landing lights reflect on the tire marks on the runway
If no landing light/can’t see tire marks, start the roundout when the runway lights at the far end appear to be rising higher than the nose of the airplane
Go Around
A prompt decision is even more necessary at night due to the restricted visibility
Fly the go around as normal, with a greater emphasis on the instrument crosscheck
RM: Hazards & Emergencies
Weather Considerations 									AI.II.M.R2
Narrow temperature/dewpoint spread leading to fog
Fog and clouds are more difficult to see at night
The wind’s effect on the airplane cannot be as easily detected at night as during the day
Night Emergencies
General
Don’t panic, maintain control, attempt to fix the problem/accomplish emergency procedures
As the checklist is completed, crosscheck the outside visual references (if any), and the instruments to ensure a safe flight attitude is maintained
Electrical Failure
In the case of a suspected problem, follow the checklist in the POH
Generally, reduce the electrical load as much as possible
If total electrical failure is expected, land at the nearest airport immediately
Transition to backup instruments if applicable
Engine Failure
ABCD – Airspeed, Best landing area, Checklist, Distress call
Don’t Panic - Establish a normal glide and turn toward an airport or suitable landing area
Check to determine the cause and correct it immediately, if possible (Engine restart checklist)
Always maintain positive control of the airplane!
Announce the emergency to ATC, UNICOM, and/or guard
If already on a frequency, talk to them, don’t change unless instructed to
Before landing checklist
Touchdown at the slowest possible airspeed
After landing, turn off all switches and evacuate as quickly as possible
Distractions, Situational Awareness & Task Prioritization 					AI.II.M.R4
Distractions
They’re dangerous
Remove distractions from view – if it’s a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Sterile flight deck (taxi, takeoff, descent, and landing)
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational Awareness
Plan thoroughly, have navigation backups, use flight following
Task Prioritization
On the ground, clearing takes precedence – take care of all heads down activities while stopped
Airborne, divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention full more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
“Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing problem
Collision Hazards 										AI.II.M.R3
Collision Avoidance
Scanning with off-center viewing
Clearing Procedures
Before Takeoff: Scan the runway and final approach for other traffic
Climbing: Execute gentle banks to allow scanning above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Uncontrolled Fields: Be conservative with spacing during takeoff, landing, and in the pattern
Clearly communicate intentions & location at uncontrolled fields
Operation Lights On
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Terrain
Be aware of terrain that could cause a hazard during the climb or descent into the airfield
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Use Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Many structures can significantly affect safety below 500’ AGL and particularly below 200’ AGL
Become familiar with any obstacles nearby airports
Obstacles can be found in the NOTAMs, and the Terminal Procedures (IFR document)
Antenna Towers
Numerous antennas extend over 1,000’-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which are very difficult to see
Avoid structures by ≥ 2,000’ - guy wires can extend 1,500’ horizontally from structures
Vehicles, Persons, Wildlife, etc.
Be alert for anyone/anything that may cause a hazard
Often the ATIS/NOTAMs will inform of potential vehicles/persons working around the airport
Takeoff: Reject the takeoff or delay takeoff, if required
Landing: Go around
Taxiing: Stop until safe (taxi slowly to ensure the ability to stop if something suddenly appears)
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

standard_lessons.full_text:
II.M. Night Operations
Introduction
How
Eyes at Night 							AI.II.M.K1
Rods and Cones
Light enters the eye through the cornea, travels through the lens, and falls on the retina
The retina has light sensitive cells that convert light into electrical impulses that are sent to the brain
Two types of light-sensitive cells:
Cones: Responsible for color, detail, far away objects; located in the center of the retina
Rods: Peripheral vision and provide vision in dim light; located in a ring around the cones
Rods, Cones, and Night Vision
Cones: Located in the center of the retina (center of vision)
Rods: Make night vision possible
Concentrated around the cones; used in dim light
Off center viewing is necessary at night
Slow to adapt to dark, but quick to lose adaptation
Summary: Night vision is based on the rods and off-center viewing is necessary
RM: Collision Avoidance 									AI.II.M.R3
Use off center viewing, as looking directly at an object may result in not seeing it
Avoid bright lights before and during a flight to maintain adequate night vision
Use red/green light in the flight deck
Flight deck lighting should be at a minimum
Lighting 												AI.II.M.K2
Taxiway Lighting
Taxiway Edge Lights
Steady blue lights outlining the edges of taxiways
Taxiway Centerline Lights
Steady green lights installed along the centerline of the taxiway
Clearance Bar Lights
Three in-pavement steady-burning yellow lights
Installed at holding positions on taxiways to increase visibility of the holding position
Runway Guard Lights
Pair of elevated flashing yellow lights on either side of the taxiway, or a row of in-pavement yellow lights across the entire taxiway at the runway holding position marking
Installed at taxiway/runway intersections
Enhance conspicuity of taxiway/runway intersections
Stop Bar Lights
A row of red, unidirectional, steady-burning in-pavement lights across the entire taxiway at the runway holding position, and elevated steady-burning red lights on each side
A controlled stop bar operates in conjunction with the taxiway centerline lead-on lights
Following ATC clearance, the stop bar is turned off and the lead-on lights are turned on
Used to confirm the ATC clearance to enter or cross the active runway in low visibility
Runway Lighting
Runway Edge Lights
White lights, except on instrument runways they’re yellow for the last 2,000’ or half of the runway, whichever is less
Mark the end of the runway emitting red toward the runway (takeoff) & green outward (landing)
Classified based on brightness: High Intensity Runway Lights (HIRL), Medium (MIRL), & Low (LIRL)
Runway End Identifier Lights (REIL)
Installed to provide rapid/positive identification of the approach end of a runway
Pair of synchronized flashing lights on each side of the runway threshold
Runway Centerline Lighting System (RCLS)
White in-pavement lights every 50’ until the last 3,000’ of the runway at which point they alternate red and white for 2,000’ and are red for the last 1,000’
Touchdown Zone Lights (TDZL)
Two rows of light bars set symmetrically about the centerline
Steady burning white lights starting 100’ beyond the landing threshold and extend to 3,000’ beyond the threshold or the midpoint of the runway, whichever is less
Taxiway Centerline Lead-Off Lights
Alternate green & yellow lights from the runway centerline to one light position beyond the holding position or ILS critical area holding position
Taxiway Centerline Lead-On Lights
Same as lead-off lights but leading onto the runway
Land and Hold Short Lights
Row of pulsing white lights across the runway at the hold short point
Off when LAHSO is not in effect
Approach Lighting
Approach Light System
Basic means to transition from instrument conditions to visual conditions for landing
Used to identify the runway
Configuration of lights from the threshold extending into the approach area
Visual Glideslope Indicators
Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI)
Provides visual descent guidance during approach
Visible from 3-5 miles during the day & > 20 at night
Safe obstruction clearance within ±10o of the centerline and 4 NM from the threshold
Most common visual glide system in use
Configuration
Light units arranged in bars
2-Bar VASI (most common) – Normally, 3o path
Each unit projects light with an upper white segment and a lower red segment
3 Bar: Near, middle & far bars, 2 glidepaths:
Lower (3o) & Upper (¼o higher)
Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI)
Uses light units like a VASI but in a single row usually on the left side of the runway
Other Glidepath Systems
Tri-Color System (pictured below, left)
Above – Amber, On – Green, Below - Red
Range: Day - ½ to 1 mile; Night - Up to 5 miles
Pulsating VASI (pictured below, right)
Single light-unit projecting a 2-color visual approach path (Range: 4 miles day, 10 miles night)
High: Pulsating white, On Path: Steady white, Slightly below: Steady red, Below: Pulsating red
Pulsating rate increases further above/below the glidepath
Airport Beacons
Used to identify airports as well as differentiate different types of airports
Colors and Combinations of Beacons
Land Airport: White and Green
Military Airport: White, White, and Green
Water Airport: White and Yellow
Lighted Heliport: Green, Yellow, and White
During the day, beacon operation often indicates ground visibility < 3 miles and/or ceiling < 1,000’
No regulatory requirement for daylight beacon operation
Pilot Control of Airport Lighting
Controlled Airport
Operation of approach light systems and runway lighting is controlled by the tower/FSS
Pilots may request the lights be turned on, off, or dimmed
Pilot Control of Airport Lighting
Radio control of lighting is available at some airports by keying the microphone
3 clicks for low, 5 for medium, and 7 for high (all clicks within 5 seconds – lasts 15 minutes)
Frequency is in Chart Supplement (usually CTAF)
Obstruction Lighting
Aviation Red Obstruction Lights: Flashing red beacons and steady-burning red lights
Medium Intensity Flashing White Obstruction Lights: Flashing white obstruction lights
Not normally installed on structures less than 200’ AGL
High Intensity White Obstruction Lights: Flashing white lights
Dual Lighting: Combination of flashing red beacons and steady burning red lights
Catenary Lighting: Light markers for high voltage transmission line catenary wires
High intensity flashing white lights are being used to identify some supporting structures of overhead transmission lines located across rivers, chasms, gorges, etc. & tall structures (chimneys, towers)
Beamed toward the companion structure and identify the area of the wire span
RM: Disorientation and Night Optical Illusions 		AI.II.M.K7, AI.II.M.R4, AI.II.M.R5
Combatting Disorientation / Illusions
Verify attitude by reference to the flight instruments (best tactic to combat disorientation/illusions)
Use vertical guidance as much as possible, especially at night (VASI/PAPI, glide slope, etc.)
Go around if unsure of your position
Autokinesis
Caused by staring at a single point of light on a dark background
The light appears to move on its own
Prevention: Focus on objects at varying distances / avoid fixating
Reversible Perspective Illusion
At night, an aircraft may appear to be moving away when it is approaching
If the light intensity increases, the aircraft is approaching, if it dims, it is moving away
Size-Distance Illusion
Light that is getting brighter or dimmer, may be interpreted as approaching or retreating
Flicker Vertigo
A light flickering between 4 and 20 cycles per second can produce unpleasant, dangerous reactions
Examples: nausea, vomiting, and vertigo. Convulsions/unconsciousness are possible, but rare
Proper scanning techniques at night can prevent flicker vertigo
False Horizon
The natural horizon is not readily apparent
Trust your instruments to maintain orientation
Featureless Terrain
An absence of ground features can create the illusion that the aircraft is higher than it actually is
Results in a tendency to fly a lower-than-normal approach
Ground Lighting
Can be mistaken for airport / runway / approach lights
Bright runway or approach lights can create the illusion the airplane is closer to the runway
Maintain situational awareness - know what to expect to see, and where to see it
Disorientation at Night 									AI.II.M.K6
Disregard false sensations and trust the instruments
Always verify aircraft attitude with the instruments at night
Night Ops
Pilot & Plane 										AI.II.M.K3, AI.II.M.K4
Night Currency (FAR 61.57(b))
To act as PIC carrying passengers from 1 hr. after sunset to 1 hr. before sunrise
3 full stop takeoffs/landings in last 90 days
Sole manipulator of the flight controls & in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type
RM: Current doesn’t imply proficient – Ensure proficiency				AI.II.M.R7
Equipment
Flashlight - Red and white light (White light is used to preflight, red is used in the flight deck)
Aeronautical Charts, Nav Logs
Be cautious of washout (red color on the chart is difficult to distinguish with a red light)
Regardless of equipment, organization eases the burden on the pilot
Preflight Inspection (FAR 91.205)
Required equipment for VFR flight at night
TOMATO FFLAAMES (day VFR) and FLAPS (additional night VFR requirements)
Fuses (if applicable)
Landing Light
Anti-Collision Lights
Position Lights
Source of Power
Instrument required equipment doesn’t hurt (safer is smarter)
Walk Around – Just like a normal walk around but be more vigilant with night equipment
Check all aircraft lights, and check the ramp for obstructions
RM: Inoperative Equipment 								AI.II.M.R1
If inoperative equipment is found, handle it the same as you would during the day, but with the additional night required equipment
Is it required by Kinds of Equipment List, Type Certificate, AD, FAR 91.205
And, of course, Personal Minimum requirements
Reference III.B. Airworthiness Requirements for more details
Engine Start & Taxi
Engine Start
Take extra precaution to be sure the propeller area is clear
Turn on the beacon, announce “clear prop” and scan carefully
To avoid excessive battery drain, leave all unnecessary electrical equipment off until after engine start
Taxiing 											AI.II.M.K8
Turn on the taxi and/or landing light (be sure not to blind other pilots)
Taxi slowly, particularly in congested areas
Orientation
Airport diagram (always have one out)
Understand the taxiway markings, lights, and signs
RM: Orientation & Situational Awareness (RM: Runway incursion)			AI.II.M.R6
Airport diagram (always have one out)
Understand the taxiway markings, lights, and signs
Taxi slowly to allow time to maintain situational awareness
If there is a loss of situational awareness, conflicting info, or doubt, stop and ask for clarification
Run-up
The before takeoff run-up should be performed with the checklist as usual
Forward movement of the airplane may not be easy to detect at night
Takeoff & Climb
General 											AI.II.M.K6
The most noticeable difference is the limited availability of outside visual references
Flight instruments should be used to a greater degree at night than in the day
Dim the flight deck lighting so the instruments are readable, without hindering night vision
Entering the Runway
Clear final approach for approaching traffic
Turn on all lights, except the landing light
Recommended to align 3’ off the centerline to prevent blending in with the runway lights
Verify correct runway
Takeoff Roll
Turn on landing light after receiving takeoff clearance or starting the roll at an uncontrolled field
Same as a day takeoff except many visual cues aren’t available (compensate with instruments)
Climb
Darkness makes it difficult to note whether the airplane is getting closer or farther from the surface
Verify with the airspeed indicator, the VSI and the altimeter
Pitch/bank adjustments should be made by referencing the attitude/heading indicators
In-Flight Orientation 										AI.II.M.K5
Clouds/Restricted Visibility
It is difficult to see clouds at night – be cautious to avoid flying into MVFR/IFR weather conditions
Be conservative, don’t expect to pop out the other side, take action to avoid flying into the clouds
Crossing Large Bodies of Water
Very easy to become disoriented with little to no horizon, and false horizons
Rely more heavily on the instruments
In the event of an engine failure, the pilot may not have any option other than ditching
Ground Based Lighting
Lighted runways, buildings, etc. may cause illusions when seen from different altitudes
RM: Nav Lights (Collision Hazards) 		AI.II.M.K9, AI.II.M.R3
Red on Left Wing, Green on Right Wing, White on the Tail
Technique to remember: Green & Right have the same number of letters
Navigating at Night
Although many day references are unavailable, numerous night references can be used instead
Anything with bright lights or a lot of lights - City light patterns, highways, airport beacons, etc.
Backup with NAVAIDS/GPS whenever possible
Traffic Pattern
Airport Environment
Identify runway/airport lights as soon as possible
It may be difficult to find the airport or runways (especially if they’re buried within a city)
Fly towards the beacon until you identify runway lights
Compare the runway lights with heading indicator
If possible, tune the localizer and/or use the GPS OBS function to view an extended centerline
Use any additional means available to help orient yourself and maintain situational awareness
Distance may be deceptive at night due to limited light conditions
More trust must be put on the instruments (particularly the altimeter and airspeed indicator)
RM: Ensure appropriate lights are on for collision avoidance 				AI.II.M.R3
Fly a normal traffic pattern
Approach & Landing
A stabilized approach should be made in the same manner as during the day
Use flight instruments more often (especially altimeter/airspeed indicator)
Final Approach
If there are no centerline lights, align the airplane between the edge lights
Maintain a stabilized approach (use any references available – VASI, PAPI, glideslope, etc.)
Roundout/Touchdown
A smooth, controlled roundout and touchdown should be made in the same way as in the day
Judgment of height, speed, and sink rate may be impaired due to lack of visual references
Tendency to round out high
Technique: Start the roundout when the landing lights reflect on the tire marks on the runway
If no landing light/can’t see tire marks, start the roundout when the runway lights at the far end appear to be rising higher than the nose of the airplane
Go Around
A prompt decision is even more necessary at night due to the restricted visibility
Fly the go around as normal, with a greater emphasis on the instrument crosscheck
RM: Hazards & Emergencies
Weather Considerations 									AI.II.M.R2
Narrow temperature/dewpoint spread leading to fog
Fog and clouds are more difficult to see at night
The wind’s effect on the airplane cannot be as easily detected at night as during the day
Night Emergencies
General
Don’t panic, maintain control, attempt to fix the problem/accomplish emergency procedures
As the checklist is completed, crosscheck the outside visual references (if any), and the instruments to ensure a safe flight attitude is maintained
Electrical Failure
In the case of a suspected problem, follow the checklist in the POH
Generally, reduce the electrical load as much as possible
If total electrical failure is expected, land at the nearest airport immediately
Transition to backup instruments if applicable
Engine Failure
ABCD – Airspeed, Best landing area, Checklist, Distress call
Don’t Panic - Establish a normal glide and turn toward an airport or suitable landing area
Check to determine the cause and correct it immediately, if possible (Engine restart checklist)
Always maintain positive control of the airplane!
Announce the emergency to ATC, UNICOM, and/or guard
If already on a frequency, talk to them, don’t change unless instructed to
Before landing checklist
Touchdown at the slowest possible airspeed
After landing, turn off all switches and evacuate as quickly as possible
Distractions, Situational Awareness & Task Prioritization 					AI.II.M.R4
Distractions
They’re dangerous
Remove distractions from view – if it’s a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Sterile flight deck (taxi, takeoff, descent, and landing)
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational Awareness
Plan thoroughly, have navigation backups, use flight following
Task Prioritization
On the ground, clearing takes precedence – take care of all heads down activities while stopped
Airborne, divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention full more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
“Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing problem
Collision Hazards 										AI.II.M.R3
Collision Avoidance
Scanning with off-center viewing
Clearing Procedures
Before Takeoff: Scan the runway and final approach for other traffic
Climbing: Execute gentle banks to allow scanning above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Uncontrolled Fields: Be conservative with spacing during takeoff, landing, and in the pattern
Clearly communicate intentions & location at uncontrolled fields
Operation Lights On
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Terrain
Be aware of terrain that could cause a hazard during the climb or descent into the airfield
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Use Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Many structures can significantly affect safety below 500’ AGL and particularly below 200’ AGL
Become familiar with any obstacles nearby airports
Obstacles can be found in the NOTAMs, and the Terminal Procedures (IFR document)
Antenna Towers
Numerous antennas extend over 1,000’-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which are very difficult to see
Avoid structures by ≥ 2,000’ - guy wires can extend 1,500’ horizontally from structures
Vehicles, Persons, Wildlife, etc.
Be alert for anyone/anything that may cause a hazard
Often the ATIS/NOTAMs will inform of potential vehicles/persons working around the airport
Takeoff: Reject the takeoff or delay takeoff, if required
Landing: Go around
Taxiing: Stop until safe (taxi slowly to ensure the ability to stop if something suddenly appears)
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: II.N. Supplemental Oxygen
Introduction
How
The High-Altitude Flight Environment
FAR 61.31(g) considers all flight operations conducted above 25,000’ MSL to be high altitude, however many effects of higher altitudes can be felt well below 25,000’
Regulatory Requirements (FAR 91.211) 							AI.II.N.K1
Supplemental oxygen is required for the minimum required flight crew:
From 12,500’ MSL up to/including 14,000’ MSL for greater than 30 minutes
At all times above 14,000’ MSL
AND all occupants of the aircraft above 15,000’ MSL cabin pressure altitude
Cannot operate a pressurized cabin above:
FL 250 without at least 10 minutes of supplemental oxygen plus any oxygen required above, in the case there is a loss of cabin pressure
FL 350, unless a pilot at the controls is using an oxygen mask
Mask must supply oxygen at all times or automatically when cabin pressure exceeds 14,000’
Exception: At/below FL410 with two pilots are at the controls and both have quick don masks
Above 350, if one pilot leaves the controls, the other will wear their mask
RM: Physiological Hazards (RM: High altitude flight) 				AI.II.N.K2, AI.II.N.R1
The human body functions normally from sea level to 12,000’ MSL
Above 12,000’ oxygen saturation continues to decrease and affect performance
Hypoxia 								AI.II.N.K2a, AI.II.N.K2b, AI.II.N.K2c
Oxygen deficiency in the blood, tissues, or cells sufficient to cause impairment of body functions
The concern is getting enough oxygen to the brain, since it is particularly vulnerable to deprivation
Symptoms: Cyanosis, headache, delayed reactions, impaired judgment, euphoria, visual Impairment, drowsiness, lightheaded or dizzy, tingling in the fingers or toes, numbness
Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC)
Max time to make and carry out rational, lifesaving decisions at a given altitude
> 10,000’ symptoms increase in severity, & TUC rapidly decreases
Treatment: Lower altitudes (emergency descent) and supplemental oxygen
For more details, see II.A. Human Factors - Hypoxia
Types of Oxygen Systems 									AI.II.N.K3a
Continuous Flow (usually provided for passengers)
Mix of oxygen and ambient air
Typically has a reservoir bag that collects oxygen from the system while the user is exhaling
Diluter Demand (useable to 40,000’)
Supplies oxygen only when the user inhales through the mask
Can provide 100% oxygen or mix the cabin air and oxygen based on the user’s setting
Pressure Demand (some regulators are safe above 40,000’)
Oxygen is supplied under pressure at cabin altitudes above 34,000’
Allows the user’s lungs to be pressurized with oxygen
Electric Pulse-Demand

paragraphs.text: II.O. Pressurization
Introduction
How
High-Altitude Flight Environment
FAR 61.31(g) considers all flight operations conducted above 25,000’ MSL to be high altitude, however many effects of higher altitudes can be felt well below 25,000’
RM: Physiological Hazards (RM: High altitude flight) 				AI.II.O.K2, AI.II.O.R1
The human body functions normally from sea level to 12,000’ MSL
Above 12,000’ oxygen saturation continues to decrease and affect performance
Hypoxia 			AI.II.O.K2a, AI.II.O.K2b, AI.II.O.K2c
Oxygen deficiency in the blood, tissues, or cells sufficient to cause impairment of body functions
The concern is getting enough oxygen to the brain, since it is particularly vulnerable to deprivation
Time of Useful Consciousness (TUC)
Max time to make and carry out rational, lifesaving decisions at a given altitude
> 10,000’, symptoms increase in severity & TUC decreases rapidly
Treatment: Lower altitudes (emergency descent) and supplemental oxygen
Vision tends to deteriorate with altitude
Lack of oxygen to the rods significantly reduces their sensitivity
Trapped Gas
Gases expand with a decrease in pressure (climb) and compress with increased pressure (descent)
The body has several cavities that contain varying amounts of gas
Most cavities can allow the gas to escape, but if the gas gets trapped it can result in pain
Problem areas include middle ear, sinuses, teeth, and GI tract
Nitrogen Absorption (Decompression Sickness - DCS)
If pressure drops sufficiently, nitrogen in the body comes out of solution, forming bubbles in the body
Symptoms include impairment or severe pain, but in extreme cases can result in death
Pressurization in Airplanes 								AI.II.O.K1
Compression of air to maintain a cabin altitude lower than the flight altitude
How it Works
The cabin, flight, baggage compartments are a sealed unit that can withstand high pressure
Compressed/Conditioned air is brought into the fuselage
Turbine aircraft use engine bleed air
Piston aircraft use turbocharger air
Air exits at a controlled rate through an outflow valve
Allows the system to maintain constant pressure
Cabin pressure control system
Pressure regulation, pressure relief, vacuum relief, and the means for selecting the desired cabin altitude
Safety Valve - Allows for pressure and vacuum relief
Instruments
Cabin Differential Pressure: Difference between inside/outside pressure
Cabin Altimeter: Shows altitude inside the airplane
Cabin Rate of Climb/Descent: Cabin rate of change
RM: Malfunctions/Failure Modes  AI.II.O.R2
Reference the POH checklist
Be prepared for reduced pressurization or decompression (supplemental oxygen/emergency descent)
Rapid Decompression 									AI.II.O.K2d
Decompression is the inability of the pressurization system to maintain its designed pressure differential
Categories of Decompression
Explosive Decompression: Pressure changes faster than the lungs can decompress (< 0.5 seconds)
Rapid Decompression: Lungs can decompress faster than the aircraft
Indications of a Rapid or Explosive Decompression
Noise, may feel dazed, the cabin will fill with fog, dust, and flying debris
Air will rush from the mouth and nose due to the escape of air from the lungs
The primary danger of decompression is hypoxia – use oxygen equipment quickly and properly
Another potential danger is decompression sickness, as discussed above
Supplemental oxygen and a rapid emergency descent are necessary
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: II.A. Human Factors
References:
Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25); Chapter 17 pgs. 1-19
Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3) Chapter5 pg. 3
AIM – Chapter 8
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story

Safety in the aircraft requires knowledge of the factors that can lead to negative consequences if we were unaware or unable to treat them. Hypoxia, for example, can result in symptoms of euphoria and the inability to make any sort of rational decision, which is obviously not a good thing while you’re trying to fly a plane. (There are many good hyperbaric chamber/hypoxia videos on you tube)
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What

Human factors involve several health and physiological factors that can influence a pilot and his or her ability to fly safely. Some are minor, while others require special attention to ensure safety and survival.
Why
Many of these factors not only affect the health and well-being of the pilot but can quickly lead to in-flight emergencies.
How:
Hypoxia 												AI.II.A.K1a
Hypoxia means “reduced oxygen” or “not enough oxygen”
The greatest concern is getting oxygen to the brain, since it is particularly vulnerable to oxygen deprivation
Hypoxia can be caused by several factors including:
An insufficient supply of oxygen
Inadequate transportation of oxygen
Inability of the body tissues to use oxygen
Hypoxic Hypoxia
A result of insufficient oxygen available to the lungs
A blocked airway or drowning are examples of how the lungs can be deprived of oxygen
For Pilots: The reduction in partial pressure of oxygen at high altitude is a common example
Partial Pressure: amount of pressure that a single gas (out of a mixture) contributes to the total pressure
Although the percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere is constant with changes in altitude, partial pressure decreases as altitude increases
As you ascend, the percentage of each gas remains the same, but the molecules no longer have the pressure required to drive oxygen into the respiratory system
The decrease of oxygen molecules at sufficient pressure leads to hypoxic hypoxia
Hypemic Hypoxia
Occurs when the blood is not able to take up and transport sufficient oxygen to the cells in the body
Hypemic means “not enough blood”
This type of hypoxia is a result of oxygen deficiency in the blood
Possible Causes:
Not enough blood volume
Can be caused by severe bleed or blood donation
Certain blood diseases, such as anemia
Hemoglobin, the molecule that transports oxygen, is unable to bind oxygen molecules
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Stagnant Hypoxia
Stagnant means “not flowing;” stagnant hypoxia results when the oxygen rich blood in the lungs isn’t moving to the tissues that need it
Ex. An arm or leg “falling asleep” because the blood flow has been restricted
This type of hypoxia can result from:
Shock
The heart failing to pump blood effectively
A constricted artery
During flight, stagnant hypoxia can occur when pulling excessive positive Gs
Cold temperatures can also decrease the blood supplied to extremities
Histotoxic Hypoxia
The inability of the cells to effectively use oxygen
“Histo” refers to tissues or cells, and “Toxic” means poison
In this case, oxygen is being transported to the cells, but they are unable to use it
Causes:
Alcohol and other drugs, such as narcotics and poison
Drinking an ounce of alcohol is equivalent to an additional 2,000’ of altitude
Symptoms of Hypoxia
The first symptoms are euphoria and a carefree feeling. With increased oxygen starvation, the extremities become less responsive and flying becomes less coordinated.
As it worsens, vision narrows, concentration and instrument interpretation become difficult
Common symptoms include:
Cyanosis (blue fingernails and lips)
Headache
Delayed reactions
Impaired judgment
Euphoria
Visual Impairment
Drowsiness
Lightheaded or dizzy sensation
Tingling in fingers or toes
Numbness
Even with all of these symptoms, the effects of hypoxia can cause a pilot to have a false sense of security and be deceived into believing that everything is normal (euphoria)
Useful Consciousness
Describes the maximum time the pilot has to make rational, lifesaving decisions and carry them out at a given altitude without supplemental oxygen
Above 10,000 ft., symptoms increase in severity, and time of useful consciousness rapidly decreases
Treatment
Flying at lower altitudes (Emergency Descent)
Use supplemental oxygen immediately
FAA Physiology Training – One day course in OK. Altitude chamber and vertigo demonstrations
Experiencing and witnessing the effects of hypoxia can be very helpful to recognizing its onset
Hyperventilation 											AI.II.A.K1b
Occurs when experiencing emotional stress, fright, or pain, and the breathing rate and depth increase
Result is an excessive loss of carbon dioxide from the body, which can lead to unconsciousness while the respiratory system attempts to override your actions and regain control of breathing
Pilots encountering a stressful situation may unconsciously increase their breathing rate
At higher altitudes, with or without oxygen, a pilot may tend to breathe more rapidly than normal, which can lead to hyperventilation
Hyperventilation symptoms are similar to hypoxia so it’s important to treat the proper condition
Common Symptoms:
Visual Impairment
Unconsciousness
Lightheaded or dizzy sensation
Tingling sensations
Hot and cold sensations
Muscle spasms
Treatment
Involves restoring the proper carbon dioxide level in the body
If using supplemental oxygen, check the equipment and flow rate to ensure it’s not hypoxia
If unsure, hypoxia is the more threatening situation and should be treated
Breathing normally is the best prevention and the best cure for hyperventilation
Breathing into a paper bag or talking aloud helps
Recovery is usually rapid once breathing is returned to normal
Middle Ear and Sinus Problems 									AI.II.A.K1c
Middle Ear Problems
Explanation
Difference between the outside air pressure and the air inside the middle ear and nasal sinuses
The middle ear is a small cavity located in the bone of the skull
Normally, the pressure differences are equalized by the Eustachian Tube
A tube leading from inside each ear to the back of the throat on each side
Tubes are usually closed, but open with chewing, yawning or swallowing to equalize pressure
Symptoms
Pain is the primary indicator
Large pressure differences can lead to excessive pain and eardrum damage
Temporary reduction in hearing sensitivity
Relation to flying
Climb: Eardrum bulges outward as pressure in the eustachian tube remains the same while outside air pressure decreases, resulting in discomfort
Descent: Eardrum bulges inward causing discomfort as outside pressure increases while pressure in the Eustachian tube remains at altitude
Excessive pressure in either situation can result in pain and a ruptured ear drum
Treatment
If minor, chew gum or stretch the jaw to attempt to equalize pressure
Pinch the nostrils, close the mouth, and blow slowly and gently in the mouth and nose
Forces air into the Eustachian tube allowing the pressure to equalize
May not be possible to equalize the pressure with a cold, an ear infection, or sore throat
Be cautious in a climb, forcing air into the Eustachian tube can add more pressure and force the eardrum farther outward leading to increased pain
If experiencing minor congestion, nose drops, or nasal sprays may reduce painful ear blockage
Sinus Problems
Explanation
Air pressure in the sinuses equalizes with the pressure in the flight deck through small openings that connect the sinuses to the nasal passages
An upper respiratory infection (cold or sinusitis) or a nasal allergic condition can produce enough congestion to slow equalization
Symptoms
Pain over the sinus area (pain can become excessive)
Some sinus blocks can make the upper teeth ache
Bloody mucus may discharge from the nasal passages
Relation to flying
As the difference in pressure increases, congestion may plug the sinus’ openings
“Sinus block” occurs most frequently during descents
Treatment
Use slow descent rates
Do not fly with sinus problems
Spatial Disorientation 										AI.II.A.K1d
Explanation
Orientation: The awareness of the position of the aircraft and of oneself in relation to a specific reference point
Spatial Disorientation refers to the lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude, or movement of the airplane in space
The body uses three systems to ascertain orientation and movement in space
Visual: The eye, by far the largest source of information
Somatosensory: Nerves in the skin, muscles, and joints that, along with hearing, sense position based on gravity, feeling, and sound
Vestibular System: A very sensitive motion sensing system located in the inner ears
Reports head position, orientation, and movement in 3-dimensional space
When all 3 systems agree you have a clear idea of where and how the body is moving
When they don’t agree is when you become disoriented
Relation to flight
Flying can result in conflicting information being sent to the brain, leading to disorientation
Visual System (eyes)
Flight in VMC
Eyes are the major orientation system and can usually prevail over false sensations
Flight in IMC
Without visual cues, the eyes can’t correct for false sensations which leads to disorientation
Vestibular System (inner ear)
Allows the pilot to sense movement and determine orientation in the surrounding environment
Two major parts: Semicircular Canals and Otolith Organs
Semicircular Canals
Explanation
Detect angular acceleration
Three tubes at right angles to each other (one on each axis)
Each canal is filled with Endolymph Fluid
In the center of the canal is the cupola
Gelatinous structure resting on sensory hairs at the end of the vestibular nerves
How they work: In a Turn
Turn Detection
Unaccelerated, Straight & Level Flight
Hair cells are upright, and the brain doesn’t sense a turn
Turning Flight
Semicircular canal and its fluid are put into motion
Fluid lags behind the canal walls
Canal wall and cupola move in the opposite direction of the fluid
Brain interprets the hair movement as a turn
Only detects turns of a short duration
After about 20 seconds, the fluid catches up with the canal walls and the hairs are no longer bent (unaccelerated, straight & level flight)
Hairs detect no relative movement so the sensation of turning ceases
Returning to straight-and-level flight, the fluid moves in the opposite direction
Falsely interpreted as a turn in the opposite direction
To correct for this, the pilot reenters the original turn

Demonstration: Establish a 30o bank turn, tell the student to close their eyes and let you know when the aircraft is flying straight. Try it again, but this time once they believe the aircraft is straight, roll out of the bank. The student will feel like the aircraft is turning in the opposite direction.
Otolith Organs
Explanation
Detect linear acceleration/gravity
A gelatinous membrane containing chalk like crystals covers the sensory hairs
When you tilt your head, the weight of the crystals causes the membrane to shift due to gravity and sensory hairs detect the shift
Acceleration
Forward acceleration gives the illusion of the head tilting backward and deceleration gives the illusion of the head tilting forward
Somatosensory System (nerves)
Nerves in the body’s skin, muscles, and joints constantly send signals to the brain which signals the body’s relation to gravity
Ex. Acceleration will be felt as the pilot is pushed back into the seat
False Sensations
Forces created in turns can lead to false sensations of the direction of gravity
The brain cannot differentiate between the forces of a turn and the force of gravity
Turbulence can create motions that confuse the brain
Fatigue or illness can exacerbate these sensations
Countering the sensations
Recognize the problem, disregard the false sensations, and rely totally on the flight instruments
Understand the problem and control the aircraft using only instrument indications
Motion Sickness 											AI.II.A.K1e
Cause
Caused by the brain receiving conflicting messages about the state of the body
Anxiety and stress also affect motion sickness
Symptoms
General discomfort
Nausea
Dizziness
Paleness
Sweating
Vomiting
Treatment
Open fresh air vents
Focus on objects outside the airplane
Avoid unnecessary head movement
Take control of the aircraft and fly smooth, straight and level
Letting someone else fly can make the situation worse
Usually goes away after a few flight lessons
More used to flying and stress/anxiety are reduced
Carbon Monoxide Poisoning 									AI.II.A.K1f
How it Happens – In the Plane
Carbon Monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas produced by all internal combustion engines
If the exhaust system is damaged or leaking, heat/defrost vents can provide CO a way into the cabin
How it Happens – In the Body
CO attaches itself to the hemoglobin in the blood
It does this about 200 times easier than oxygen
CO prevents the hemoglobin from carrying oxygen to the cells resulting in Hypemic Hypoxia
Can take up to 48 hours for the body to dispose of CO
If severe enough, CO poisoning can result in death
Effects of CO poisoning
Headache
Blurred vision
Dizziness
Drowsiness
Loss of muscle power
Detecting and Correction
Disposable, inexpensive CO detectors are widely available
If a strong odor of exhaust gases is detected, assume CO is present
CO may be present in dangerous amounts even if no exhaust odor is detected
If exhaust odor is noticed or symptoms are experienced, immediate actions should be taken
Turn off the heater
Open fresh air vents and windows
Use supplemental oxygen, if available
Land
Fatigue and Stress
Fatigue 												AI.II.A.K1h
Effects
Degradation of attention and concentration
Impaired coordination
Decreased ability to communicate
Causes
Sleep loss
Exercise
Physical work
Stress and prolonged performance of cognitive work can result in mental fatigue
Categories of Fatigue (Acute and Chronic)
Acute Fatigue (short term)
Definition
Short term, and a normal occurrence in everyday life
Tiredness felt after a period of strenuous effort, excitement, or lack of sleep
Skill Fatigue – A special type of acute fatigue affecting piloting skill. Effects include:
Timing Disruption
Appearing to perform a normal task, but the timing of each component is slightly off
Pattern of operation is less smooth as each component is performed as a separate part instead of part of a single, integrated activity
Disruption of the perceptual field
Concentrating attention upon movements or objects in the center of vision and neglecting those in the periphery
May be accompanied by a loss of accuracy/smoothness in control movements
Causes
Mild hypoxia
Physical stress
Psychological stress
Depletion of physical energy resulting from psychological stress
Sustained psychological stress
Prevention
Proper diet
Prevents the body from having to consume its own tissues as an energy source
Adequate rest and sleep
Maintains the body’s store of vital energy
The difference between flying fatigued and rested can be night and day,
Chronic Fatigue
Definition
Fatigue extending over a long period of time
Usually has psychological roots, an underlying disease is sometimes responsible
Causes
Continuous high-stress levels produce chronic fatigue
Symptoms
Weakness
Tiredness
Palpitations of the heart
Breathlessness
Headaches
Irritability
Stomach or intestinal problems (rare)
Generalized aches and pains throughout the body
Emotional Illness (when conditions become serious enough)
Prevention
Usually requires treatment by a physician
Prevention
If suffering from acute fatigue, stay on the ground
Fatigue in the flight deck cannot be overcome through training or experience
Getting adequate rest is the only way to prevent fatigue
Avoid flying
Without a full night’s rest
After working excessive hours
After an especially exhausting or stressful day
Suspected chronic fatigue should be treated by a physician
Stress 												AI.II.A.K1g
Body’s response to physical and psychological demands placed upon it
Body’s Reaction
Releasing chemical hormones (such as adrenaline) into the blood
Increasing metabolism to provide more energy to the muscles
Blood sugar, heart rate, respiration, blood pressure, and perspiration all increase
Stressors (elements that cause an individual to experience stress)
Physical stress (noise or vibration)
Physiological stress (fatigue)
Psychological stress (difficult work or personal situations)
Categories of Stress (Acute and Chronic)
Acute Stress (short term)
Involves an immediate threat that is perceived as danger
The type of stress that triggers a “fight or flight” response in an individual
Normally, a healthy person can cope with acute stress and prevent stress overload
On-going acute stress can develop into chronic stress
Chronic Stress (long term)
Presents an intolerable burden, exceeds the ability to cope, causes performance to fall sharply
Causes
Unrelenting psychological pressures
Ex. Loneliness, financial worries, and relationship or work problems
Do not fly. Consult a physician
Dehydration & Nutrition										 AI.II.A.K1i
Dehydration
Critical loss of water from the body
Causes
Hot flight decks/flight lines, wind, humidity, diuretic drinks (coffee, tea, alcohol, caffeinated soda)
Effects
First noticeable effect is fatigue
Top physical and mental performance is difficult, if not impossible
Headache, cramps, tingling, sleepiness, and dizziness
How it affects flying
Hot temperatures and high altitudes increase susceptibility to dehydration
Dry air at altitude increases the body’s rate of water loss
Fatigue progresses to dizziness, weakness, nausea, tingling hands & feet, abdominal cramps, and extreme thirst
Attention is taken from flying and skills diminish
Prevention
Carry an ample supply of water (recommended to drink 2 quarts of water per day)
Stay ahead – don’t wait until you’re thirsty to drink
Wear light colored, porous clothing and a hat
Keep the flight deck well ventilated
Limit caffeine and alcohol intake
Nutrition
Ensure properly fed and nourished
Causes: Missing/postponing meals and/or poor eating habits
Effects
Low energy and/or low blood sugar
Stomach contractions, distraction, breakdown in habit patterns, and shortened attention span
Insufficient vitamin A can impair night vision
Prevention: Eat healthy, regularly spaced and sized meals
Hypothermia 											AI.II.A.K1j
How it Happens
The body loses heat faster than it can be produced
Normal body temperature is 98.6o F (37o C), hypothermia occurs below 95o F (35o C)
Mechanisms of heat loss
Radiated heat: Most heat loss is due to heat radiated from unprotected parts of the body
Direct contact: In contact with something very cold, heat is conducted away from the body
Heat is lost much faster in cold water than cold air
Heat loss if much faster if clothes are wet
Wind: Carries away the thin layer of warm air at the surface of your skin
Causes
Clothes that aren’t warm enough for the weather
Too much time in the cold
Falling into cold water
Unable to get out of wet clothes or move to a warm, dry location
Symptoms
Shivering
Slurred speech or mumbling
Slow, shallow breathing
Weak pulse
Clumsiness
Drowsiness
Confusion or memory loss (can prevent the person from knowing they have hypothermia)
Bright red, cold skin
Prevention (COLD)
Cover: Wear protective clothing
Cover your head, face, and neck. Wear mittens instead of gloves
Overexertion
Avoid activities that result in a lot of sweat
Wet clothing + cold weather causes body heat to be lost more quickly
Layers
Loose fitting, layered, lightweight clothing
Wool, silk or polypropylene inner layers hold heat better than cotton
Tightly woven, water repellent material is best for wind protection
Dry
Stay dry – get out of wet clothing as soon as possible
Optical Illusions 											AI.II.A.K1k
Runway Width Illusion
Reason
A narrower than usual runway
A wider than usual runway
Illusion
Narrow: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it is
Wide: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a lower altitude than it is
Result
Narrow: The pilot who doesn’t recognize this will fly a lower approach, with the risk of striking objects along the approach path or landing short
Wide: the pilot who doesn’t recognize this will fly a higher approach, with the risk of leveling out high and landing hard or overshooting the runway
Runway and Terrain Slope Illusion
Reason
An up-sloping runway, up sloping terrain, or both
A down sloping runway, down sloping terrain, or both
Illusion
Upslope: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it is
Downslope: Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a lower altitude than it is
Result
Upslope: The pilot who does not recognize this will fly a lower approach
Downslope: The pilot who does not recognize this will fly a higher approach
Featureless Terrain Illusion
Reason
An absence of ground features, as when landing over water, darkened areas, and terrain made featureless by snow
Illusion
Can create the illusion that the aircraft is at a higher altitude than it is
Result
The pilot who doesn’t recognize this will fly a lower approach
Atmospheric Illusions
Reason
Rain on the windscreen
Atmospheric Haze
Penetration of fog
Illusion
Rain - Can create the illusion of greater height
Atmospheric Haze: Can create the illusion of being a greater distance from the runway
Penetration of Fog: Can create the illusion of pitching up
Result
Rain & Haze: The pilot who does not recognize these illusions will fly a lower approach
Fog: The pilot who does not recognize this will steepen the approach, often quite abruptly
Ground Lighting Illusions
Reason: Lights along a straight path, such as a road, and even lights on moving trains
Illusions: Can create the illusion of runway and approach lights
Result: The pilot may attempt to land on a path, road, or train
Reason: Bright runway and approach lighting systems
Illusion: Can create the illusion of less distance to the runway
Especially where few lights illuminate the surrounding terrain
Result: The pilot who does not recognize this illusion will fly a higher approach
Preventing Landing Illusions
Anticipate them during approaches
Aerial visual inspection of unfamiliar airports before landing
Using glide slope or VASI/PAPI systems whenever possible
Maintaining optimum proficiency in landing procedures
Nitrogen and Scuba Diving 										AI.II.A.K1i
Why it’s a Danger
Scuba diving results in a significant increase in the amount of nitrogen dissolved in the body
The deeper the dive, the greater the nitrogen
At sea level, the nitrogen inside and outside the body is in equilibrium
When atmospheric pressure is reduced, nitrogen leaves the body
If the nitrogen leaves too quickly, bubbles may form causing a variety of symptoms
Bubbles can form in the bloodstream, spinal cord or brain
Symptoms include impairment or severe pain - extreme cases can result in death
Scuba Diving and Flying
If enough time isn’t provided, DCS can occur as low as 5,000’ and create an in-flight emergency
In normal conditions, most cases of DCS occur at altitudes of 25,000’ or higher
Wait at least 12 hrs. after a dive not requiring a controlled ascent before flight up to 8,000’ MSL
24 hrs. for flight above 8,000’
Wait at least 24 hrs. after a dive that requires a controlled ascent before flight up to 8,000’ MSL
If a decompression occurs, DCS symptoms can be brought on quickly
Alcohol and Other Drugs 									AI.II.A.K2. AI.II.A.K3
DON’T drink and fly
Even in small amounts, alcohol can impair judgement, decrease sense of responsibility, affect coordination, constrict visual field, diminish memory, reduce reasoning ability, lower attention span
Altitude multiplies the effects of alcohol on the brain
Alcohol interferes with the brains ability to utilize oxygen (form of histotoxic hypoxia)
A hangover can impair anyone attempting to fly
FAR 91.17 – 8 hrs. ‘from bottle to throttle’ (8 hrs. and not feeling the effects of alcohol is better)
Considerable amounts of alcohol can remain in the body for over 16 hours – be cautious
Medications
FAR 61.53 (Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency) prohibits flying if you:
Are taking medication/receiving treatment that would prevent you from obtaining a medical
FAR 91.17 prohibits use of drugs affecting a person’s faculties in any way contrary to safety
Medication can absolutely affect pilot performance
Side effects can impair judgment, memory, alertness, coordination, vision, can cause confusion, dizziness, headaches, nausea, mood swings, anxiety, balance problems, hearing problems, etc.
Drugs that cause no apparent side effects on the ground can create serious problems airborne
Basically: Do not fly while taking any medication(s), unless approved by the FAA
ADM, CRM, & SRM 											AI.II.A.K4
RM: Distractions (Task Prioritization, Loss of SA, Disorientation) 					AI.II.A.R3
Human factors can present significant, distractions, disorientation, and an inability to manage tasks
The pilot must perform an honest evaluation of themselves prior to flight
IMSAFE:
Illness – Symptoms?
Medication – Taking any?
Stress – Family, money, relationships, work, etc.
Alcohol – Been drinking?
Fatigue – Well rested?
Emotion – Emotionally upset?
In flight, be alert to factors that can affect performance and lead to disorientation, etc.
RM: Combat confirmation/expectation bias 							AI.II.A.R4
Your expectations can influence behavior
Individuals are vulnerable to thinking they see (or hear) what they expect to see (or hear)
Don’t assume everything will be OK, because it’s always been OK
If something doesn’t feel right (i.e., hypoxia symptoms), take action
Stress Management
Learning to cope with stress is an effective ADM tool
A certain amount of stress is good – keeps you alert and prevents complacency
Stress is cumulative, too much can amount to an intolerable burden
Performance increases with the onset of stress, peaks, then falls rapidly as stress gets too high
Stressors can increase risk of error
Physical: Associated with the environment (temperature, noise, vibration, lack of oxygen)
Physiological: Physical conditions (fatigue, lack of physical fitness, missed meals)
Psychological: Social or emotional factors (divorce, death in the family, sick child)
Recognize when stress affect performance
RM: Hazardous Attitudes 									AI.II.A.R2
Attitude affects the quality of decisions
5 hazardous attitudes that can interfere with the ability to make sound decisions
Contribute to poor judgement
Recognizing is the first step to neutralizing these attitudes
Once recognizing a thought as hazardous, label it as hazardous and state the antidote
Attitudes & Antidotes
Use all Resources
Use all available resources – Don’t depend solely on yourself
Internal Resources
Equipment (autopilot, GPS, etc.), systems, charts, books, etc.
Ingenuity, knowledge, and skill
Other passengers (even if they are not pilots)
External Resources
ATC, FSS, Guard, etc. (Traffic advisories, vectors, weather info, emergency assistance)
Workload Management
Plan, prioritize, and sequence to prevent overload
Prepare for high workload situations
Don’t wait until you’re in the situation (i.e., prepare for the approach before it begins)
Be able to recognize high workloads
Faster paced work along with divided attention
Stay ahead as much as possible to prevent high workloads
Manage tasks in order of importance when behind
“Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing/threatening issue
RM: Aeromedical & Physiological Issues 								AI.II.A.R2
The lesson as a whole is a discussion of managing risk associated with aeromedical issues
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

There are many factors a pilot needs to be aware of to ensure a safe flight and to understand the medical risks involved with flying. Recognize conditions and symptoms associated with physiological issues and take action to maintain safety, whether that means supplemental oxygen, trusting the instruments, or diverting and landing as soon as possible.
